The issue is how deep the foundations have to be to make the house safe.”

永远不要屈服于压力。再想想和承包商谈判的例子。如果他提出雇用你的姐夫，条件是你必须在房屋地基深度上做出让步，你会怎么做？你可能会回答：“我姐夫的工作和房子能否安全地建在那个深度的地基上毫无关系。” 如果承包商接着威胁要提高价格呢？你的回答也一样：“这个问题我们也要根据实际情况来决定。看看其他承包商做这种工程要多少钱。”或者“把你的成本清单给我，我们来算出一个合理的利润率。” 如果承包商说：“别装了，你相信我，对吧？” 你会回答：“信任是另一回事。关键是地基要多深才能保证房子的安全。”

Pressure can take many forms: a bribe, a threat, a manipulative appeal to trust, or a simple refusal to budge. In all these cases, the principled response is the same: invite them to state their reasoning, suggest objective criteria you think apply, and refuse to budge except on this basis. Never yield to pressure, only to principle.

压力可以采取多种形式：贿赂、威胁、操纵信任，或者仅仅是拒绝让步。在所有这些情况下，遵循原则的回应都是一样的：邀请对方陈述理由，提出你认为适用的客观标准，并且除非基于这些标准，否则绝不让步。永远不要屈服于压力，只坚守原则。

Who will prevail? In any given case it is impossible to say, but in general you will have an edge. For in addition to your willpower, you also have the power of legitimacy and the persuasiveness of remaining open to reason. It will be easier for you to resist making an arbitrary concession than it will be for them to resist advancing some objective standards. A refusal to yield except in response to sound reasons is an easier position to defend—publicly and privately—than is a refusal to yield combined with a refusal to advance sound reasons.

谁将胜出？具体情况难以预料，但总体而言，你会占据优势。因为除了意志力之外，你还拥有合法性的力量，以及保持理性、接受劝说的能力。你更容易拒绝做出武断的让步，而他们则更难拒绝提出客观标准。除非有充分的理由，否则拒绝让步的立场——无论公开还是私下——都比拒绝让步并拒绝提出充分理由的立场更容易辩护。

At the least, you will usually prevail on the question of process; you can usually shift the process from positional bargaining to a search for objective criteria. In this sense principled negotiation is a dominant strategy over positional bargaining. One who insists that negotiation be based on the merits can bring others around to playing that game, since that becomes the only way to advance their substantive interests.

至少，你通常会在谈判程序问题上占上风；你通常可以将谈判从立场博弈转向寻求客观标准。从这个意义上讲，原则性谈判比立场博弈更具优势。坚持谈判必须基于事实的人能够促使其他人也参与到这种博弈中来，因为这成为推进自身实质性利益的唯一途径。

On substance, too, you are likely to do well. Particularly for those who might otherwise be browbeaten by a positional bargainer, principled negotiation allows you to hold your own and still be fair. Principle serves as your hardhearted partner who will not let you yield to pressure. It is a form of “right makes might.”

在实质内容方面，你也很有可能取得成功。尤其对于那些可能被强势谈判者压制的人来说，坚持原则的谈判能让你既能维护自身权益，又能保持公平。原则就像你坚定的伙伴，不会让你屈服于压力。这是一种“正义即力量”的体现。

If the other side truly will not budge and will not advance a persuasive basis for their position, then there is no further negotiation. You now have a choice like the one you face when you walk into a store that has a fixed, nonnegotiable price on what you want to buy. You can take it or leave it. Before leaving it you should see if you have overlooked some objective standard that makes their offer a fair one. If you find such a standard and if you would rather reach agreement on that basis than have no agreement, do so. The availability of that relevant standard avoids the cost of giving in to an arbitrary position.

如果对方确实毫不让步，也无法提出令人信服的理由来支持其立场，那么谈判就到此为止。你现在面临的选择，就像走进一家商店，商品标价固定且不接受议价一样。你可以接受，也可以放弃。在放弃之前，你应该思考一下是否忽略了某种客观标准，使得对方的报价显得合理。如果你找到了这样的标准，并且宁愿以此为基础达成协议，也不愿无协议脱身，那就这样做。有了这样的标准，就能避免因对方的武断立场而付出代价。

If there is no give in their position and you find no principled basis for accepting it, you should assess what you might gain by accepting their unjustified position rather than going to your best alternative. You should weigh that substantive benefit against the benefit to your reputation as a principled negotiator that could come from walking away.

如果对方立场坚定，毫无让步余地，而你又找不到任何原则性的理由接受，那么你应该评估接受他们不合理的立场，而不是寻求最佳替代方案，你能从中获得什么。你应该权衡这种实质性的利益与放弃谈判可能损害你作为一位有原则的谈判者的声誉之间的利弊。

Shifting discussion in a negotiation from the question of what the other side is willing to do to the question of how the matter ought to be decided does not end argument, nor does it guarantee a favorable result. It does, however, provide a strategy you can vigorously pursue without the high costs of positional bargaining.

在谈判中，将讨论的重点从对方愿意做什么转移到如何解决这个问题，并不能结束争论，也不能保证取得有利的结果。然而，这确实提供了一种策略，你可以积极运用，而无需付出高昂的立场谈判代价。

“It’s company policy”

“这是公司政策。”

Let’s look at a real case where one party used positional bargaining and the other principled negotiation. Tom, one of our colleagues, had his parked car totally destroyed by a dump truck. The car was covered by insurance, but the exact amount Tom could recover remained for him to work out with the insurance adjuster.

我们来看一个真实案例，一方采用立场谈判，另一方则采用原则谈判。我们的同事汤姆停在路边的车被一辆自卸卡车彻底撞毁了。虽然车辆有保险，但汤姆最终能获得多少赔偿，还需要他与保险理赔员协商。

Insurance Adjuster

保险理赔员

Tom

汤姆

We have studied your case and we have decided the policy applies. That means you’re entitled to a settlement of $13,600.

我们已对您的案件进行了研究，并认定该保单适用。这意味着您有权获得 13,600 美元的赔偿。

I see. How did you reach that figure?

我明白了。你是怎么得出这个数字的？

That’s how much we decided the car was worth.

我们最终决定这辆车值多少钱。

I understand, but what standard did you use to determine that amount? Do you know where I can buy a comparable car for that much?

我明白了，但是您是用什么标准来确定这个价格的？您知道哪里能买到价格差不多的同级别车吗？

How much are you asking for?

你要多少钱？

Whatever I’m entitled to under the policy. I found a secondhand car just about like it for $17,700. Adding the sales and excise tax, it would come to about $19,000.

根据保单条款，我有权获得赔偿。我找到一辆和它差不多的二手车，价格是 17,700 美元。加上销售税和消费税，总共大约要 19,000 美元。

$19,000! That’s too much!

19000美元！太多了！

I’m not asking for $19,000 or $18,000 or $20,000, but for fair compensation. Do you agree that it’s only fair I get enough to replace the car?

我不是要19000美元、18000美元或者20000美元，而是要公平的赔偿。您是否同意，我理应获得足够的赔偿金来更换车辆？

OK, I’ll offer you $15,000. That’s the highest I can go. Company policy.

好吧，我给你15000美元。这是我能给的最高价了。公司规定。

How does the company figure that?

公司是如何计算的？

Look, $15,000 is all you’ll get. Take it or leave it.

听着，你只能拿到15000美元。要不要随你。

$15,000 may be fair. I don’t know. I certainly understand your position if you’re bound by company policy. But unless you can state objectively why that amount is what I’m entitled to, I think I’ll do better in court. Why don’t we study the matter and talk again? Is Wednesday at eleven a good time to talk?

15000美元或许合理。我也不确定。如果你受公司政策约束，我当然理解你的立场。但除非你能客观地说明我为什么有权获得这笔钱，否则我觉得上法庭会更有胜算。不如我们先研究一下这件事，然后再谈谈？周三上午11点方便吗？

. . .

OK, Mr. Griffith, I’ve got an ad here in today’s paper offering a car exactly the same make, model, and year as yours for $14,800.

好的，格里菲斯先生，我这里有一则广告，刊登在今天的报纸上，出售一辆与您的汽车品牌、型号和年份完全相同的汽车，售价为 14,800 美元。

I see. What does it say about the mileage?

我明白了。里程数显示是多少？

49,000. Why?

49,000。为什么？

Because mine only had 25,000 miles. How many dollars does that increase the worth in your book?

因为我的车只跑了25000英里。在你看来，这能增加多少价值？

Let me see . . . $1,650.

让我看看……1650美元。

Assuming the $14,800 as one possible base, that brings the figure to $16,450. Does the ad specify the technology package?

假设14800美元是一个可能的基准价，那么总价就是16450美元。广告中是否明确说明了技术套餐的内容？

No.

不。

How much extra for that in your book?

你觉得这要额外花多少钱？

$1,100.

How about an autodimming mirror?

自动防眩光后视镜怎么样？

. . .

A half hour later Tom walked out with a check for $18,024.

半小时后，汤姆拿着一张18024美元的支票走了出来。

6 What If They Are More Powerful?

6 如果他们更强大呢？

( Develop Your BATNA—Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement)

（制定你的最佳替代方案——谈判协议之外的最佳选择）

I f what use is talking about interests, options, and standards if the other side has a stronger bargaining position? What do you do if the other side is richer or better connected, or if they have a larger staff or more powerful weapons?

如果对方拥有更强的谈判地位，那么谈论利益、选择和标准又有什么用呢？如果对方更富有、人脉更广，或者拥有更多的人员或更强大的武器，你又该怎么办？

No method can guarantee success if all the leverage lies on the other side. No book on gardening can teach you to grow lilies in a desert or a cactus in a swamp. If you enter an antique store to buy a sterling silver George IV tea set worth thousands of dollars and all you have is one hundred-dollar bill, you should not expect skillful negotiation to overcome the difference. In any negotiation there exist realities that are hard to change. In response to power, the most any method of negotiation can do is to meet two objectives: first, to protect you against making an agreement you should reject and second, to help you make the most of the assets you do have so that any agreement you reach will satisfy your interests as well as possible. Let’s take each objective in turn.

如果对方掌握了绝对优势，任何方法都无法保证成功。任何园艺书籍都无法教你如何在沙漠中种植百合花，或在沼泽中种植仙人掌。如果你走进一家古董店，想买一套价值数千美元的乔治四世时期纯银茶具，而你身上只有一张百元大钞，那么你不应该指望高超的谈判技巧能够弥补资金缺口。任何谈判都存在一些难以改变的现实。面对强大的力量，任何谈判方法最多只能实现两个目标：第一，避免你被迫接受你本不该接受的协议；第二，帮助你最大限度地利用现有资源，使你达成的任何协议都能尽可能地满足你的利益。让我们逐一分析这两个目标。

Protecting yourself

保护自己

When you are trying to catch an airplane your goal may seem tremendously important; looking back on it, you see you could have caught the next plane. Negotiation will often present you with a similar situation. You will worry, for instance, about failing to reach agreement on an important business deal in which you have invested a great deal of yourself. Under these conditions, a major danger is that you will be too accommodating to the views of the other side—too quick to go along. The siren song of “Let’s all agree and put an end to this” becomes persuasive. You may end up with a deal you should have rejected.

当你赶飞机时，你的目标可能看起来无比重要；但事后回想起来，你会发现自己本可以赶上下一班。谈判也常常会让你面临类似的情况。例如，你可能会担心无法就一项你投入了大量心血的重要商业交易达成一致。在这种情况下，一个主要的危险是你会过于迁就对方的观点——太容易妥协。“我们都同意，结束这一切吧”的诱惑力十足。最终，你可能会接受一项你本应该拒绝的交易。

The costs of using a bottom line. Negotiators commonly try to protect themselves against such an outcome by establishing in advance the worst acceptable outcome—their “bottom line.” If you are buying, a bottom line is the highest price you would pay. If you are selling, a bottom line is the lowest amount you would accept. You and your spouse might, for example, ask $300,000 for your house and agree between yourselves to accept no offer below $260,000.

设定底线的代价。谈判者通常会预先设定一个最差的可接受结果——他们的“底线”，以此来避免出现这种情况。如果你是买家，底线就是你愿意支付的最高价格。如果你是卖家，底线就是你愿意接受的最低价格。例如，你和你的配偶可能会为你们的房子要价30万美元，并约定不接受低于26万美元的报价。

Having a bottom line makes it easier to resist pressure and temptations of the moment. In the house example, it might be impossible for a buyer to pay more than $244,000, and everyone involved may know that you bought the house not so long ago for only $235,000. In this situation, where you have the power to produce agreement and the buyer does not, the brokers and anyone else in the room may turn to you. Your predetermined bottom line may save you from making a decision you would later regret.

设定底线能让你更容易抵制当下的压力和诱惑。以买房为例，买家可能根本不可能出价超过24.4万美元，而且所有相关人员可能都知道你不久前才以23.5万美元的价格买下这套房子。在这种情况下，你有能力促成交易而买家却无能为力，经纪人和在场的其他人可能会向你寻求帮助。你预先设定的底线或许能让你避免做出日后会后悔的决定。

If there is more than one person on your side, jointly adopting a bottom line helps ensure that no one will indicate to the other side that you might settle for less. It limits the authority of a lawyer, broker, or other agent. “Get the best price you can, but you are not authorized to sell for less than $260,000,” you might say. If your side is a loose coalition of newspaper unions negotiating with an association of publishers, agreement on a bottom line reduces the risk that one union will be split off by offers from the other side.

如果你们一方有多人，共同设定底线有助于确保没有人会向对方暗示你们可能会接受更低的价格。这也能限制律师、经纪人或其他代理人的权限。你们可以这样说：“尽力争取最高价格，但你们无权以低于26万美元的价格出售。” 如果你们一方是由报业工会组成的松散联盟，与出版商协会进行谈判，那么就底线达成一致可以降低一方工会因对方报价而分裂的风险。

But the protection afforded by adopting a bottom line involves high costs. It limits your ability to benefit from what you learn during negotiation. By definition, a bottom line is a position that is not to be changed. To that extent you have shut your ears, deciding in advance that nothing the other party says could cause you to raise or lower that bottom line.

但设定底线所带来的保护代价高昂。它限制了你从谈判过程中获取信息的能力。顾名思义，底线就是一个不容更改的立场。从某种程度上说，你等于充耳不闻，预先决定对方的任何言论都不能让你提高或降低底线。

A bottom line also inhibits imagination. It reduces the incentive to invent a tailor-made solution that would reconcile differing interests in a way more advantageous for both you and them. Almost every negotiation involves more than one variable. Rather than simply selling your place for $260,000, you might serve your interests better by settling for $235,000 with a first refusal on resale, a delayed closing, the right to use the barn for storage for two years, and an option to buy back two acres of the pasture. If you insist on a bottom line, you are not likely to explore an imaginative solution like this. A bottom line—by its very nature rigid—is almost certain to be too rigid.

底线也会扼杀想象力。它降低了你构思量身定制的解决方案的动力，而这种方案本可以更好地调和双方不同的利益。几乎所有谈判都涉及多个变量。与其简单地以 26 万美元的价格出售你的房产，不如考虑以 23.5 万美元的价格成交，并附带优先转售权、延迟交割、两年内使用谷仓作为仓库的权利以及回购两英亩牧场的选择权，这样或许更符合你的利益。如果你坚持底线，就不太可能去探索这样富有创意的解决方案。底线——就其本质而言——几乎肯定过于僵化。

Moreover, a bottom line is likely to be set too high. Suppose you are sitting around the breakfast table with your family trying to decide the lowest price you should accept for your house. One family member suggests $200,000. Another replies, “We should get at least $240,000.” A third chimes in, “$240,000 for our house? That would be a steal. It’s worth at least $300,000.” Who sitting at the table will object, knowing they will benefit from a higher price? Once decided upon, such a bottom line may be hard to change and may prevent your selling the house when you should. Under other circumstances a bottom line may be too low; rather than selling at such a figure, you would have been better off renting.

此外，底价往往设定得过高。假设你和家人围坐在餐桌旁，商量着房子的最低售价。一位家人提议20万美元。另一位回应说：“我们至少应该卖24万美元。”第三位插话说：“24万美元？简直是白菜价。它至少值30万美元。”餐桌上还有谁会反对呢？毕竟，更高的价格对他们更有利。一旦底价定下，就很难更改，甚至可能让你错失本该卖房的机会。在其他情况下，底价也可能过低；与其以这样的价格出售，还不如租房。

In short, while adopting a bottom line may protect you from accepting a very bad agreement, it may keep you both from inventing and from agreeing to a solution it would be wise to accept. An arbitrarily selected figure is no measure of what you should accept.

简而言之，虽然设定底线可以避免你接受非常糟糕的协议，但它也可能阻碍你和对方找到并达成一个明智的解决方案。随意设定的数字并不能作为你应该接受的底线标准。

Is there an alternative to the bottom line? Is there a measure for agreements that will protect you against both accepting an agreement you should reject and rejecting an agreement you should accept? There is.

除了底线之外，还有其他选择吗？有没有什么措施可以保护你免于接受本应拒绝的协议，以及免于拒绝本应接受的协议？答案是肯定的。

Know your BATNA. When a family is deciding on the minimum price for their house, the right question for them to ask is not what they “ought” to be able to get, but what they will do if by a certain time they have not sold the house. Will they keep it on the market indefinitely? Will they rent it, tear it down, turn the land into a parking lot, let someone else live in it rent-free on condition they paint it, or what? Which of those alternatives is most attractive, all things considered? And how does that alternative compare with the best offer received for the house? It may be that one of those alternatives is more attractive than selling the house for $260,000. On the other hand, selling the house for as little as $224,000 may be better than holding on to it indefinitely. It is most unlikely that any arbitrarily selected bottom line truly reflects the family’s interests.

了解你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。当一个家庭决定房屋的最低售价时，他们真正应该问自己的问题不是“应该”卖多少钱，而是如果到某个时间点房子还没卖出去该怎么办。他们会无限期地把房子挂牌出售吗？他们会出租吗？会拆掉房子吗？会把地改成停车场吗？会让别人免费住，条件是他们负责粉刷吗？还是别的什么？综合考虑所有因素，哪个方案最有吸引力？这个方案与收到的最佳报价相比如何？也许某个方案比以26万美元的价格卖掉房子更有吸引力。另一方面，即使只卖22.4万美元，也可能比无限期地持有房子要好。任何随意设定的底线都不太可能真正反映出这个家庭的利益。

The reason you negotiate is to produce something better than the results you can obtain without negotiating. What are those results? What is that alternative? What is your BATNA—your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement? That is the standard against which any proposed agreement should be measured. That is the only standard that can protect you both from accepting terms that are too unfavorable and from rejecting terms it would be in your interest to accept.

谈判的目的是为了达成比不谈判更好的结果。那么，不谈判能得到的结果是什么？更好的替代方案是什么？你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）是什么？任何拟议协议都应以此为标准来衡量。只有这样，才能保护双方免于接受过于不利的条款，也免于拒绝那些本应符合自身利益的条款。

Your BATNA not only is a better measure but also has the advantage of being flexible enough to permit the exploration of imaginative solutions. Instead of ruling out any solution that does not meet your bottom line, you can compare a proposal with your BATNA to see whether it better satisfies your interests.

你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）不仅是一种更优的衡量标准，而且其优势在于足够灵活，可以探索更具创意的解决方案。与其直接排除任何不符合你底线的方案，不如将某个方案与你的BATNA进行比较，看看哪个方案更能满足你的利益。

The insecurity of an unknown BATNA. If you have not thought carefully about what you will do if you fail to reach an agreement, you are negotiating with your eyes closed. You may, for instance, be too optimistic and assume that you have many other choices: other houses for sale, other buyers for your secondhand car, other plumbers, other jobs available, other wholesalers, and so on. Even when your alternative is fixed, you may be taking too rosy a view of the consequences of not reaching agreement. You may not be appreciating the full agony of a lawsuit, a contested divorce, a strike, an arms race, or a war.

未知的替代方案带来的不安全感。如果你没有认真考虑过如果无法达成协议该怎么办，那么你的谈判就如同闭着眼睛。例如，你可能过于乐观，认为自己还有很多其他选择：其他待售房屋、其他二手车买家、其他水管工、其他工作机会、其他批发商等等。即使你的替代方案是确定的，你也可能对无法达成协议的后果过于乐观。你可能没有充分意识到诉讼、离婚纠纷、罢工、军备竞赛或战争带来的痛苦。

One frequent mistake is psychologically to see your alternatives in the aggregate. You may be telling yourself that if you do not reach agreement on a salary for this job, you could always go to California, or go south, or go back to school, or write, or work on a farm, or live in Paris, or do something else. In your mind you are likely to find the sum of these alternatives more attractive than working for a specific salary in a particular job. The difficulty is that you cannot have the sum total of all those other alternatives; if you fail to reach agreement, you will have to choose just one.

一个常见的心理误区是把所有选择看作一个整体。你可能会想，如果这份工作的薪资谈不拢，你还可以去加州，或者去南方，或者重返校园，或者写作，或者去农场工作，或者住在巴黎，或者做其他事情。在你看来，这些选择的总和可能比在某份工作中拿着固定的薪水更有吸引力。但问题在于，你不可能拥有所有这些选择的总和；如果无法达成协议，你只能从中选择一个。

In most circumstances, however, the greater danger is that you are too committed to reaching agreement. Not having developed any alternative to a negotiated solution, you are unduly pessimistic about what would happen if negotiations broke off.

然而，在大多数情况下，更大的危险在于你过于执着于达成协议。由于没有制定任何替代谈判方案，你对谈判破裂后的后果过于悲观。

As valuable as knowing your BATNA may be, you may hesitate to explore alternatives. You hope this buyer or the next will make you an attractive offer for the house. You may avoid facing the question of what you will do if no agreement is reached. You may think to yourself, “Let’s negotiate first and see what happens. If things don’t work out, then I’ll figure out what to do.” But having at least a tentative answer to the question is absolutely essential if you are to conduct your negotiations wisely. Whether you should or should not agree on something in a negotiation depends entirely upon the attractiveness to you of the best available alternative.

了解你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）固然重要，但你可能仍然会犹豫是否要探索其他选择。你或许希望这位买家或下一位买家能给你一个有吸引力的报价。你可能刻意回避如果无法达成协议该怎么办的问题。你可能会想：“先谈判看看结果如何。如果谈判不成，我再想办法。” 但要想明智地进行谈判，至少对这个问题有一个初步的答案至关重要。在谈判中是否应该同意某项条款，完全取决于你对最佳替代方案的接受程度。

Formulate a trip wire. Although your BATNA is the true measure by which you should judge any proposed agreement, you may want another test as well. To give you early warning that the content of a possible agreement is beginning to run the risk of being too unattractive, it is useful to identify one far from perfect agreement that is better than your BATNA. Before accepting any agreement worse than this trip-wire package, you should take a break and reexamine the situation. Like a bottom line, a trip wire can limit the authority of an agent. “Don’t sell for less than $258,000, the price I paid plus interest, until you’ve talked to me.”

设定一个“诱饵”。虽然你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）才是衡量任何拟议协议的真正标准，但你可能还需要另一个测试。为了及早发现潜在协议的内容可能过于糟糕，最好先找到一个远非完美但比你的BATNA更好的协议。在接受任何比这个“诱饵”更差的协议之前，你应该冷静下来，重新审视情况。就像底线一样，“诱饵”可以限制经纪人的权限。“在你跟我谈过之前，不要以低于25.8万美元的价格出售，这是我的购买价格加上利息。”

A trip wire should provide you with some margin in reserve. If after reaching the standard reflected in your trip wire you decide to call in a mediator, you have left him with something on your side to work with. You still have some room to move.

设置触发条件应该给你留有一定的余地。如果达到触发条件所设定的标准后，你决定寻求调解，那么你也给调解员留下了一些有利条件。你仍然有一定的回旋余地。

Making the most of your assets

充分利用你的资产

Protecting yourself against a bad agreement is one thing. Making the most of the assets you have to produce a good agreement is another. How do you do this? Again the answer lies in your BATNA.

避免签订糟糕的协议是一回事，充分利用自身优势达成一份好的协议则是另一回事。那么，该如何做到这一点呢？答案依然在于你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。

The better your BATNA, the greater your power. People think of negotiating power as being determined by resources like wealth, political connections, physical strength, friends, and military might. In fact, the relative negotiating power of two parties depends primarily upon how attractive to each is the option of not reaching agreement.

你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）越好，你的谈判筹码就越大。人们通常认为谈判筹码取决于财富、政治关系、体力、人脉和军事实力等资源。但实际上，双方的相对谈判筹码主要取决于双方对不达成协议这一选项的接受程度。

Consider a wealthy tourist who wants to buy a small brass pot for a modest price from a vendor at the Mumbai railroad station. The vendor may be poor, but she is likely to know the market. If she does not sell the pot to this tourist, she can sell it to another. From her experience she can estimate when and for how much she could sell it to someone else. The tourist may be wealthy and “powerful,” but in this negotiation he will be weak indeed unless he knows approximately how much it would cost and how difficult it would be to find a comparable pot elsewhere. He is almost certain either to miss his chance to buy such a pot or to pay too high a price. The tourist’s wealth in no way strengthens his negotiating power. If apparent, it weakens his ability to buy the pot at a low price. To convert that wealth into negotiating power, the tourist would have to apply it to learn about the price at which he could buy an equally or more attractive brass pot somewhere else.

设想一位富有的游客想在孟买火车站从一位摊贩那里以适中的价格购买一个小铜壶。摊贩或许并不富裕，但她很可能了解市场行情。即使她不把铜壶卖给这位游客，她也可以卖给其他人。凭借经验，她可以估算出何时以什么价格能把铜壶卖给其他人。这位游客或许富有且“有权势”，但在谈判中，除非他大致了解铜壶的价格以及在其他地方找到类似铜壶的难度，否则他将处于绝对劣势。他几乎肯定会错过购买机会，或者支付过高的价格。游客的财富丝毫不会增强他的议价能力。如果说财富有所体现，那反而会削弱他以低价购买铜壶的能力。要想将财富转化为议价能力，这位游客必须利用财富去了解在其他地方购买同等或更精美铜壶的价格。

Think for a moment about how you would feel walking into a job interview with no other job offers—only some uncertain leads. Think how the talk about salary would go. Now contrast that with how you would feel walking in with two other job offers. How would that salary negotiation proceed? The difference is power.

试想一下，如果你没有其他工作机会，只有一些不太确定的线索，走进面试室会是什么感觉？想想薪资谈判会如何进行。现在，对比一下，如果你已经有了两份工作邀请，走进面试室又会是什么感觉？薪资谈判又会如何进行？区别就在于掌握主动权。

What is true for negotiations between individuals is equally true for negotiations between organizations. The relative negotiating power of a large industry and a small town trying to raise taxes on a factory is determined not by the relative size of their respective budgets, or their political clout, but by each side’s best alternative. In one case, a small town negotiated a company with a factory just outside the town limits from a “goodwill” payment of $300,000 a year to one of $2,300,000 a year. How?

适用于个人之间谈判的原则同样适用于组织之间的谈判。大型企业和试图提高工厂税收的小镇之间的谈判实力，并非取决于各自预算规模或政治影响力的相对大小，而是取决于双方各自的最佳替代方案。例如，在一个案例中，一个小镇成功地将一家工厂（工厂位于镇郊）每年30万美元的“善意”付款提高到了230万美元。这是如何做到的呢？

The town knew exactly what it would do if no agreement was reached: It would expand the town limits to include the factory and then tax the factory the full residential rate of some $2,500,000 a year. The corporation had committed itself to keeping the factory; it had developed no alternative to reaching agreement. At first glance the corporation seemed to have a great deal of power. It provided most of the jobs in the town, which was suffering economically; a factory shutdown or relocation would devastate the town. And the taxes the corporation was already paying helped provide the salaries of the very town leaders who were demanding more. Yet all of these assets, because they were not converted into a good BATNA, proved of little use. Having an attractive BATNA, the small town had more ability to affect the outcome of the negotiation than did one of the world’s largest corporations.

如果无法达成协议，小镇很清楚该怎么做：它会扩大城镇范围，将工厂纳入其中，然后对工厂征收每年约250万美元的全额居民税。公司已经承诺要保留这家工厂；它没有提出任何达成协议之外的替代方案。乍一看，这家公司似乎拥有巨大的权力。它为这个经济低迷的小镇提供了大部分工作岗位；工厂的关闭或搬迁将对小镇造成毁灭性打击。而且，公司已经缴纳的税款也用于支付那些要求更多税收的镇领导的薪水。然而，所有这些优势，由于没有转化为一个好的最佳替代方案（BATNA），最终都无济于事。如果拥有一个有吸引力的BATNA，这个小镇在谈判结果上的影响力甚至超过了世界最大的公司之一。

Develop your BATNA. Vigorous exploration of what you will do if you do not reach agreement can greatly strengthen your hand. Attractive alternatives are not just sitting there waiting for you; you usually have to develop them. Generating possible BATNAs requires three distinct operations: (1) inventing a list of actions you might conceivably take if no agreement is reached; (2) improving some of the more promising ideas and converting them into practical alternatives; and (3) selecting, tentatively, the one alternative that seems best.

制定你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。积极探索如果无法达成协议你将采取的行动，可以极大地增强你的谈判筹码。有吸引力的替代方案并非唾手可得；你通常需要主动开发它们。生成可能的最佳替代方案需要三个不同的步骤：（1）列出如果无法达成协议你可能采取的行动；（2）改进一些更有前景的想法，并将它们转化为切实可行的替代方案；（3）初步选择目前看来最佳的方案。

The first operation is inventing. If, by the end of the month, Company X does not make you a satisfactory job offer, what are some things you might do? Take a job with Company Y? Look in another city? Start a business on your own? What else? For a labor union, alternatives to a negotiated agreement would presumably include calling a strike, working without a contract, giving a sixty-day notice of a strike, asking for a mediator, and calling on union members to “work to rule.”

第一种方法是创新。如果到月底，X公司没有给你提供满意的工作机会，你可以做些什么？去Y公司工作？去其他城市找工作？自己创业？还有其他办法吗？对于工会来说，除了协商达成协议之外，其他选择可能包括：发起罢工、无合同工作、提前六十天发出罢工通知、请求调解以及呼吁工会成员“按章工作”。

The second stage is to improve the best of your ideas and turn the most promising into real alternatives. If you are thinking about working in Chicago, try to turn that idea into at least one job offer there. With a Chicago job offer in hand (or even having discovered that you are unable to produce one) you are much better prepared to assess the merits of a New York offer. While a labor union is still negotiating, it should convert the ideas of calling in a mediator and of striking into drafts of specific operational decisions ready for execution. The union might, for instance, take a vote of its membership to authorize a strike if a settlement is not achieved by the time the contract expires.

第二阶段是完善你最好的想法，并将最有前景的想法转化为切实可行的方案。如果你正在考虑去芝加哥工作，那就努力争取至少获得一份芝加哥的工作机会。有了芝加哥的工作机会（或者即便你发现自己无法获得），你也能更好地评估纽约工作机会的优劣。工会在谈判期间，应该将引入调解人和罢工的想法转化为具体的操作决策草案，以便随时执行。例如，如果在合同到期前未能达成协议，工会可以进行会员投票，授权罢工。

The final step in developing a BATNA is selecting the best among the alternatives. If you do not reach agreement in the negotiations, which of your realistic alternatives do you now plan to pursue?

制定最佳替代方案的最后一步是从所有备选方案中选择最佳方案。如果谈判未能达成协议，您现在计划采取哪些切实可行的替代方案？

Having gone through this effort, you now have a BATNA. Judge every offer against it. The better your BATNA, the greater your ability to improve the terms of any negotiated agreement. Knowing what you are going to do if the negotiation does not lead to agreement will give you additional confidence in the negotiating process. It is easier to break off negotiations if you know where you’re going. The greater your willingness to break off negotiations, the more forcefully you can present your interests and the basis on which you believe an agreement should be reached.

经过一番努力，你现在有了最佳替代方案（BATNA）。用它来评估每一个报价。你的BATNA越好，你就越有能力改善任何谈判协议的条款。知道如果谈判未能达成协议该如何应对，会让你在谈判过程中更有信心。如果你知道自己的下一步行动，那么终止谈判就更容易。你越愿意终止谈判，就越能有力地表达你的利益以及你认为应该达成协议的基础。

The desirability of disclosing your BATNA to the other side depends upon your assessment of the other side’s thinking. If your BATNA is extremely attractive—if you have another customer waiting in the next room—it is in your interest to let the other side know. If they think you lack a good alternative when in fact you have one, then you should almost certainly let them know. However, if your best alternative to a negotiated agreement is worse for you than they think, disclosing it will weaken rather than strengthen your hand.

是否应该向对方披露你的最佳替代方案（BATNA），取决于你对对方想法的判断。如果你的最佳替代方案极具吸引力——例如，你还有一位客户在隔壁房间等着——那么告知对方对你有利。如果对方认为你缺乏好的替代方案，而实际上你有，那么你几乎肯定应该告知他们。然而，如果你的最佳替代方案比对方想象的更不利，那么披露它反而会削弱你的优势。

Consider the other side’s BATNA. You should also think about the alternatives to a negotiated agreement available to the other side. The more you can learn of their alternatives, the better prepared you are for negotiation. Knowing their alternatives, you can realistically estimate what you can expect from the negotiation.

考虑对方的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。你也应该考虑对方除了谈判达成协议之外的其他选择。你越了解他们的替代方案，就越能为谈判做好充分准备。了解他们的替代方案，你就能更实际地评估谈判的预期结果。

They may be unduly optimistic about what they can do if no agreement is reached. Perhaps they have a vague notion that they have a great many alternatives and are under the influence of their cumulative total. If they appear to overestimate their BATNA, you will want to help them think through whether their expectations are realistic.

他们可能对无法达成协议的情况下自己能做的事情过于乐观。或许他们模糊地认为自己有很多选择，并受到这些选择累积效应的影响。如果他们似乎高估了最佳替代方案（BATNA），你需要帮助他们思考自己的预期是否现实。

Their BATNA may be better for them than any fair solution you can imagine. Suppose you are a community group concerned about the potential noxious gases to be emitted by a power plant now under construction. The power company’s BATNA is either to ignore your protests altogether or to keep you talking while they finish building the plant. To get them to take your concerns seriously, you may have to file a lawsuit seeking to have their construction permit revoked. In other words, if their BATNA is so good they don’t see any need to negotiate on the merits, consider what you can do to change it.

他们的最佳替代方案（BATNA）可能比你能想象到的任何公平解决方案都更适合他们。假设你是一个社区团体，担心一座正在建设中的发电厂可能会排放有害气体。电力公司的最佳替代方案要么是完全无视你们的抗议，要么是让你们一直争论下去，同时他们完成电厂的建设。为了让他们认真对待你们的担忧，你可能不得不提起诉讼，要求撤销他们的施工许可证。换句话说，如果他们的最佳替代方案如此完美，以至于他们认为没有必要就实质内容进行谈判，那么请考虑你可以做些什么来改变它。

If both sides have attractive BATNAs, the best outcome of the negotiation—for both parties—may well be not to reach agreement. In such cases a successful negotiation is one in which you and they amicably and efficiently discover that the best way to advance your respective interests is for each of you to look elsewhere and not to try further to reach agreement.

如果双方都有有吸引力的替代方案（BATNA），那么对双方而言，谈判的最佳结果很可能是不达成协议。在这种情况下，成功的谈判就是双方友好高效地发现，推进各自利益的最佳途径是各自寻找其他方案，而不是继续尝试达成协议。

When the other side is powerful

当对方实力强大时

If the other side has big guns, you do not want to turn a negotiation into a gunfight. The stronger they appear in terms of physical or economic power, the more you benefit by negotiating on the merits. To the extent that they have muscle and you have principle, the larger a role you can establish for principle the better off you are.

如果对方实力雄厚，你肯定不想把谈判变成枪战。对方在武力或经济实力上越强，你就越应该基于实力进行谈判。如果对方拥有武力而你坚守原则，那么你越能发挥原则的作用，就越有利于谈判。

Having a good BATNA can help you negotiate on the merits. You can convert such resources as you have into effective negotiating power by developing and improving your BATNA. Apply knowledge, time, money, people, connections, and wits into devising the best solution for you independent of the other side’s assent. The more easily and happily you can walk away from a negotiation, the greater your capacity to affect its outcome.

拥有一个好的最佳替代方案（BATNA）能帮助你进行基于事实的谈判。通过发展和完善你的BATNA，你可以将现有资源转化为有效的谈判力量。运用知识、时间、金钱、人脉、关系和智慧，独立于对方的同意，为你找到最佳解决方案。你越能轻松愉快地结束谈判，就越能影响谈判结果。

Developing your BATNA thus not only enables you to determine what is a minimally acceptable agreement, it will probably raise that minimum. Developing your BATNA is perhaps the most effective course of action you can take in dealing with a seemingly more powerful negotiator.

因此，制定你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）不仅能帮助你确定最低可接受的协议标准，还有可能提高这个最低标准。在与看似更强大的谈判者交锋时，制定最佳替代方案或许是你所能采取的最有效策略。

# ↩

7 What If They Won’t Play?

7 如果他们不参加比赛怎么办？

(Use Negotiation Jujitsu)

（运用谈判技巧）

T alking about interests, options, and standards may be a wise, efficient, and amicable game, but what if the other side won’t play? While you try to discuss interests, they may state their position in unequivocal terms. You may be concerned with developing possible agreements to maximize the gains of both parties. They may be attacking your proposals, concerned only with maximizing their own gains. You may attack the problem on its merits; they may attack you. What can you do to turn them away from positions and toward the merits?

讨论利益、选择和标准或许是明智、高效且友好的策略，但如果对方不愿配合呢？当你试图探讨利益时，他们可能会毫不含糊地表明立场。你可能致力于达成双方都能从中获益的协议，而他们可能只关心自身利益最大化，并攻击你的提议。你可能着眼于问题的本质，他们也可能攻击你。你该如何引导他们放下立场，关注问题的本质呢？

There are three basic approaches for focusing their attention on the merits. The first centers on what you can do. You yourself can concentrate on the merits, rather than on positions. This method, the subject of this book, is contagious; it holds open the prospect of success to those who will talk about interests, options, and criteria. In effect, you can change the game simply by starting to play a new one.

有三种基本方法可以帮助人们将注意力集中在优点上。第一种方法侧重于你能做什么。你可以专注于优点本身，而不是地位。本书的主题就是这种方法，它具有感染力；它为那些愿意谈论利益、选择和标准的人打开了成功的大门。实际上，你只需开始玩一种新的游戏，就能改变游戏规则。

If this doesn’t work and they continue to use positional bargaining, you can resort to a second strategy that focuses on what they may do. It counters the basic moves of positional bargaining in ways that direct their attention to the merits. This strategy we call negotiation jujitsu.

如果这种方法行不通，对方继续使用立场谈判，你可以采取第二种策略，重点关注他们可能采取的行动。这种策略能够有效应对立场谈判的基本手段，引导他们关注谈判的实质内容。我们称这种策略为谈判柔术。

The third approach focuses on what a third party can do. If neither principled negotiation nor negotiation jujitsu gets them to play, consider including a third party trained to focus the discussion on interests, options, and criteria. Perhaps the most effective tool a third party can use in such an effort is the one-text mediation procedure.

第三种方法侧重于第三方的作用。如果原则性谈判和谈判技巧都无法促使双方参与，可以考虑引入一位受过专门训练的第三方，引导讨论聚焦于利益、选择和标准。在这种情况下，第三方最有效的工具或许就是单次文本调解程序。

The first approach—principled negotiation—has already been discussed. Negotiation jujitsu and the one-text procedure are explained in this chapter. The chapter ends with a dialogue based on an actual landlord-tenant negotiation that illustrates in detail how you might persuade an unwilling party to play, using a combination of principled negotiation and negotiation jujitsu.

第一种方法——原则性谈判——已在前文讨论过。本章将解释谈判技巧和单文本谈判程序。本章最后以一个真实的房东房客谈判案例对话作为结尾，详细阐述了如何运用原则性谈判和谈判技巧相结合的方法，说服不愿谈判的一方参与谈判。

Negotiation jujitsu

谈判柔术

If the other side announces a firm position, you may be tempted to criticize and reject it. If they criticize your proposal, you may be tempted to defend it and dig yourself in. If they attack you, you may be tempted to defend yourself and counterattack. In short, if they push you hard, you will tend to push back.

如果对方明确表态，你可能会忍不住批评并拒绝。如果他们批评你的提议，你可能会忍不住捍卫它，并坚持己见。如果他们攻击你，你可能会忍不住自卫并反击。简而言之，如果他们咄咄逼人，你往往会奋起反击。

Yet if you do, you will end up playing the positional bargaining game. Rejecting their position only locks them in. Defending your proposal only locks you in. And defending yourself sidetracks the negotiation into a clash of personalities. You will find yourself in a vicious cycle of attack and defense, and you will waste a lot of time and energy in useless pushing and pulling.

然而，如果你这样做，最终只会陷入立场博弈的陷阱。拒绝对方的立场只会让他们更加固执己见；捍卫自己的提议只会让自己更加进退维谷；而为自己辩护则会让谈判演变成一场人身攻击。你会发现自己陷入攻防的恶性循环，在无谓的拉锯战中浪费大量时间和精力。

If pushing back does not work, what does? How can you prevent the cycle of action and reaction? Do not push back. When they assert their positions, do not reject them. When they attack your ideas, don’t defend them. When they attack you, don’t counterattack. Break the vicious cycle by refusing to react. Instead of pushing back, sidestep their attack and deflect it against the problem. As in the Oriental martial arts of judo and jujitsu, avoid pitting your strength against theirs directly; instead, use your skill to step aside and turn their strength to your ends. Rather than resisting their force, channel it into exploring interests, inventing options for mutual gain, and searching for independent standards.

如果反击行不通，那什么才行得通？如何才能打破这种行动与反击的恶性循环？不要反击。当他们坚持己见时，不要反驳。当他们攻击你的观点时，不要为自己辩护。当他们攻击你时，不要反击。拒绝回应，打破恶性循环。与其反击，不如绕开他们的攻击，并将其转化为解决问题的动力。就像柔道和柔术等东方武术一样，避免直接与对方对抗；相反，运用你的技巧巧妙地避开对方，并将对方的力量转化为你的优势。与其抵抗对方的力量，不如将其转化为探索自身利益、创造互利共赢方案以及寻求独立标准的动力。

How does “negotiation jujitsu” work in practice? How do you sidestep their attack and deflect it against the problem?

“谈判柔术”在实践中是如何运作的？如何躲避对方的攻击并将其转化为解决问题的动力？

Typically their “attack” will consist of three maneuvers: asserting their position forcefully, attacking your ideas, and attacking you. Let’s consider how a principled negotiator can deal with each of these.

通常，他们的“攻击”包含三种策略：强硬地表明立场、攻击你的观点以及攻击你本人。让我们来看看一位有原则的谈判者应该如何应对每一种策略。

Don’t attack their position, look behind it. When the other side sets forth their position, neither reject it nor accept it. Treat it as one possible option. Look for the interests behind it, seek out the principles that it reflects, and think about ways to improve it.

不要攻击对方的立场，要探究其背后的原因。当对方阐述立场时，既不要否定也不要接受。将其视为一种可能的选项。探究其背后的利益诉求，探寻其所体现的原则，并思考如何改进它。

Let’s say you represent an association of teachers striking for higher pay and for seniority as the only criterion in layoffs. The school board has proposed a $2,000 raise across the board plus retention of the right to decide unilaterally who gets laid off. Mine their position for the interests that lie below the surface. “What exactly are the budget trade-offs involved in raising the salary schedule more than $2,000?” “Why do you feel a need to maintain complete control over layoffs?”

假设你代表一个教师协会，他们正在罢工，要求提高工资，并要求裁员时只以资历为标准。校董会提议全员加薪2000美元，同时保留单方面决定裁员的权力。你需要深入挖掘他们的立场，找出隐藏的利益。“如果工资涨幅超过2000美元，预算方面究竟有哪些权衡取舍？”“你们为什么觉得有必要完全掌控裁员？”

Assume every position they take is a genuine attempt to address the basic concerns of each side; ask them how they think it addresses the problem at hand. Treat their position as one option and objectively examine the extent to which it meets the interests of each party, or might be improved to do so. “How will a $2,000 across-the-board increase keep our schools’ salaries competitive with others in the area and thus assure that the students will have high-quality teachers?” “How could you satisfy the teachers that your evaluation procedure for layoffs would be fair? We believe that you personally would be fair, but what would happen if you left? How can we leave our livelihoods and our families’ wellbeing up to a potentially arbitrary decision?”

假设他们提出的每一个立场都是真诚地试图解决双方的基本关切；询问他们认为该立场如何解决当前问题。将他们的立场视为一种选择，客观地审视它在多大程度上满足了各方的利益，或者是否可以改进以更好地满足各方的利益。“全面加薪2000美元如何才能使我们学校的薪资水平与该地区其他学校保持竞争力，从而确保学生拥有高质量的教师？”“您如何才能让教师们相信您的裁员评估程序是公平的？我们相信您本人会公平行事，但如果您离职了怎么办？我们怎能将我们的生计和家庭福祉交由一个可能带有随意性的决定来决定？”

Seek out and discuss the principles underlying the other side’s positions. “What is the theory that makes $2,000 a fair salary increase? Is it based on what other schools pay or what others with comparable qualifications make?” “Do you believe that the town’s least experienced teachers should be laid off first or the most experienced—who, of course, have higher salaries?”

找出并讨论对方立场背后的原则。“是什么理论认为2000美元的加薪是合理的？是基于其他学校的薪资水平，还是基于其他具有类似资历的人的薪资水平？”“你认为应该先解雇镇上经验最少的教师，还是经验最丰富的教师——当然，他们的薪水更高？”

To direct their attention toward improving the options on the table, discuss with them hypothetically what would happen if one of their positions was accepted. In 1970, an American lawyer had a chance to interview President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt on the subject of the Arab-Israeli conflict. He asked Nasser, “What do you want [Israel’s Prime Minister] Golda Meir to do?”

为了引导他们关注如何改进现有方案，可以和他们假设性地讨论一下，如果他们提出的某个立场被接受会发生什么。1970年，一位美国律师有机会就阿以冲突采访埃及总统贾迈勒·阿卜杜勒·纳赛尔。他问纳赛尔：“您希望（以色列总理）戈尔达·梅厄怎么做？”

Nasser replied, “Withdraw!”

纳赛尔回答说：“撤退！”

“Withdraw?” the lawyer asked.

“撤回申请？”律师问道。

“Withdraw from every inch of Arab territory!”

“从阿拉伯的每一寸领土撤军！”

“Without a deal? With nothing from you?” the American asked incredulously.

“没有协议？你们什么都没给？”美国人难以置信地问道。

“Nothing. It’s our territory. She should promise to withdraw,” Nasser replied.

“没什么。这是我们的地盘。她应该承诺撤军。”纳赛尔回答道。

The American asked, “What would happen to Golda Meir if tomorrow morning she appeared on Israeli radio and television and said, ‘On behalf of the people of Israel, I hereby promise to withdraw from every inch of territory occupied in 1967: the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, Jerusalem, the Golan Heights. And I want you to know, I have no commitment of any kind from any Arab whatsoever.’”

这位美国人问道：“如果戈尔达·梅厄明天早上出现在以色列的广播和电视上，说：‘我谨代表以色列人民，在此承诺从1967年占领的每一寸领土撤军：西奈半岛、加沙地带、西岸、耶路撒冷、戈兰高地。而且我要让你们知道，我没有得到任何阿拉伯人的任何承诺。’那她会怎么样？”

Nasser burst out laughing. “Oh, would she have trouble at home!”

纳赛尔哈哈大笑起来。“哦，她回家可就麻烦了！”

Understanding what an unrealistic option Egypt had been offering Israel may have contributed to Nasser’s stated willingness later that day to accept a cease-fire in the ongoing hostilities.

意识到埃及向以色列提供的选择多么不切实际，可能促使纳赛尔当天晚些时候表示愿意接受停火，结束正在进行的敌对行动。

Don’t defend your ideas, invite criticism and advice. A lot of time in negotiation is spent criticizing. Rather than resisting the other side’s criticism, invite it. Instead of asking them to accept or reject an idea, ask them what’s wrong with it. “What concerns of yours would this salary proposal fail to take into account?” Examine their negative judgments to find out their underlying interests and to improve your ideas from their point of view. Rework your ideas in light of what you learn from them, and thus turn criticism from an obstacle in the process of working toward agreement into an essential ingredient of that process. “If I understand you, you’re saying you can’t afford to give 750 teachers more than a $2,000 across-the-board raise. What if we accept that with the stipulation that any money saved by hiring fewer than 750 full-time teachers will be distributed as a monthly bonus to those teachers who are working?”

不要为自己的想法辩护，而是要接受批评和建议。谈判中，批评往往占据了大量时间。与其抵制对方的批评，不如欣然接受。与其要求对方接受或拒绝某个想法，不如问问他们这个想法有什么问题。“您认为这份薪资方案有哪些方面没有考虑到？”仔细审视他们的负面评价，找出他们的潜在利益，并从他们的角度改进你的想法。根据你从他们那里学到的东西调整你的想法，从而将批评从达成协议的障碍转化为协议过程中不可或缺的要素。“如果我理解正确的话，您的意思是说您无法为750名教师提供超过2000美元的统一加薪。如果我们接受这个方案，但附加一个条件：如果全职教师人数少于750人，节省下来的资金将以月度奖金的形式发放给仍在职的教师，您觉得如何？”

Another way to channel criticism in a constructive direction is to turn the situation around and ask for their advice. Ask them what they would do if they were in your position. “If your jobs were at stake, what would you do? Our members are feeling so insecure about their jobs and frustrated by their shrinking dollars they’re talking about inviting a militant union in to represent them. If you were leading this association, how would you act?” Thus, you lead them to confront your half of the problem. In doing so, they may be able to invent a solution that meets your concerns. “Part of the problem here seems to be that the teachers feel no one’s listening. Would it help to have regular sessions at which teachers could meet with the school board?”

另一种引导批评走向建设性方向的方法是转换视角，征求他们的意见。问问他们，如果他们处在你的位置会怎么做。“如果你们的工作岌岌可危，你们会怎么做？我们的成员对自己的工作感到非常没有安全感，而且收入不断缩水，他们甚至在讨论是否要邀请一个激进的工会来代表他们。如果你领导这个协会，你会怎么做？” 这样，你就能引导他们正视你这部分的问题。通过这种方式，他们或许能够找到一个既能满足你需求又能解决问题的方案。“问题的一部分似乎在于，教师们觉得没有人倾听他们的声音。定期召开会议，让教师们与校董会成员会面，会不会有所帮助？”

Recast an attack on you as an attack on the problem. When the other side attacks you personally—as frequently happens—resist the temptation to defend yourself or to attack them. Instead, sit back and allow them to let off steam. Listen to them, show you understand what they are saying, and when they have finished, recast their attack on you as an attack on the problem. “When you say that a strike shows we don’t care about the children, I hear your concern about the children’s education. I want you to know that we share this concern: they are our children and our students. We want the strike to end so we can go back to educating them. What can we both do now to reach an agreement as quickly as possible?”

将针对你的攻击转化为对问题的攻击。当对方对你进行人身攻击时——这种情况经常发生——要克制住想要为自己辩护或反击的冲动。相反，要冷静下来，让他们发泄情绪。认真倾听，让他们知道你理解他们的意思，等他们说完后，再把他们对你发起的攻击转化为对问题的攻击。“你说罢工表明我们不在乎孩子，我理解你对孩子教育的担忧。我想让你知道，我们和你一样关心这个问题：他们是我们的孩子，是我们的学生。我们希望罢工结束，这样我们才能恢复正常的教育。我们现在可以做些什么来尽快达成协议呢？”

Ask questions and pause. Those engaged in negotiation jujitsu use two key tools. The first is to use questions instead of statements. Statements generate resistance, whereas questions generate answers. Questions allow the other side to get their points across and let you understand them. They pose challenges and can be used to lead the other side to confront the problem. Questions offer them no target to strike at, no position to attack. Questions do not criticize, they educate. “Do you think it would be better to have teachers cooperating in a process they felt they were participating in, or actively resisting one they felt was imposed on them and failed to take their concerns into account?”

提问并稍作停顿。精通谈判技巧的人会运用两个关键工具。首先，要用提问代替陈述。陈述会引发抵触情绪，而提问则能带来答案。提问能让对方表达观点，并帮助你理解他们。提问能够提出挑战，引导对方直面问题。提问不会给对方留下攻击的目标，也不会让他们找到攻击的立足点。提问不是为了批评，而是为了启发。“您认为，让教师们积极参与到他们感觉自己真正参与其中的过程中，还是让他们积极抵制他们感觉被强加于身且未考虑他们诉求的过程，哪种情况更好？”

Silence is one of your best weapons. Use it. If they have made an unreasonable proposal or an attack you regard as unjustified, the best thing to do may be to sit there and not say a word.

沉默是你最好的武器之一。善用它。如果他们提出了不合理的提议或对你进行了你认为毫无道理的攻击，最好的做法或许就是坐在那里一言不发。

If you have asked an honest question to which they have provided an insufficient answer, just wait. People tend to feel uncomfortable with silence, particularly if they have doubts about the merits of something they have said. For example, if a teacher’s representative asks, “Why shouldn’t teachers have a say in layoff policy?” the school board chairman might find himself at a loss: “Layoffs are a purely administrative matter. . . . Well, of course teachers have an interest in layoff policy, but they really aren’t the best qualified to know who’s a good teacher. . . . Uh, what I mean is . . . .”

如果你问了一个真诚的问题，但对方的回答却不够充分，那就耐心等待。人们往往不喜欢沉默，尤其当他们对自己所说的话有所怀疑时。例如，如果一位教师代表问道：“为什么教师不应该对裁员政策有发言权？”，校董会主席可能会一时语塞：“裁员纯粹是行政事务……嗯，教师当然关心裁员政策，但他们真的不是最有资格评判谁是好老师的人……呃，我的意思是……”

Silence often creates the impression of a stalemate that the other side will feel impelled to break by answering your question or coming up with a new suggestion. When you ask questions, pause. Don’t take them off the hook by going right on with another question or some comment of your own. Some of the most effective negotiating you will ever do is when you are not talking.

沉默往往会给人一种僵局感，迫使对方通过回答你的问题或提出新的建议来打破僵局。提问时，要稍作停顿。不要立刻提出另一个问题或发表自己的评论，以免让对方轻松脱身。一些最有效的谈判技巧，恰恰是在你保持沉默的时候。

Consider the one-text procedure

考虑单文本程序

You will probably call in a third party only if your own efforts to shift the game from positional bargaining to principled negotiation have failed. The problem you face may be illustrated by a simple story of a negotiation between a husband and wife who plan to build a new house.

只有当你自己努力将谈判从立场博弈转向原则性谈判的努力失败后，你才会考虑引入第三方。你面临的问题可以用一对计划建造新房的夫妇之间的谈判故事来说明。

The wife is thinking of a two-story house with a chimney and a bay window. The husband is thinking of a modern one-story ranch-style house with a den and a garage with a lot of storage space. In the process of negotiating, each asks the other a number of questions, like “What are your views on the living room?” and “Do you really insist on having it your way?” Through answering such questions, two separate plans become more and more fixed. They each ask an architect to prepare first a sketch and then more detailed plans, ever more firmly digging themselves into their respective positions. In response to the wife’s demand for some flexibility, the husband agrees to reduce the length of the garage by one foot. In response to his insistence on a concession, the wife agrees to give up a back porch, which she says she had always wanted but which did not even appear on her plan. Each argues in support of one plan and against the other. In the process, feelings are hurt and communication becomes difficult. Neither side wants to make a concession, since it will likely lead only to requests for more concessions.

妻子想要一栋带烟囱和凸窗的两层楼房。丈夫则想要一栋现代的单层牧场式住宅，带书房和储物空间充足的车库。在协商过程中，双方互相询问了一系列问题，例如“你对客厅有什么想法？”以及“你真的坚持要按你的方式来吗？”通过回答这些问题，两个不同的方案逐渐定型。他们各自请建筑师先绘制草图，然后制定更详细的方案，更加坚定地维护各自的立场。为了回应妻子提出的灵活要求，丈夫同意将车库的长度缩短一英尺。为了回应丈夫的坚持，妻子同意放弃一个她一直想要但却从未出现在她方案中的后廊。双方都力挺自己的方案，反对对方的方案。在这个过程中，彼此都受到了伤害，沟通也变得困难重重。双方都不愿做出让步，因为这很可能导致对方提出更多让步的要求。

This is a classic case of positional bargaining. If you cannot change the process to one of seeking a solution on the merits, perhaps a third party can. More easily than one of those directly involved, a mediator can separate the people from the problem and direct the discussion to interests and options. Further, he or she can often suggest some impartial basis for resolving differences. A third party can also separate inventing from decision-making, reduce the number of decisions required to reach agreement, and help the parties know what they will get when they do decide. One process designed to enable a third party to do all this is known as the one-text procedure.

这是一个典型的立场式谈判案例。如果无法将谈判过程转变为基于事实寻求解决方案，或许可以借助第三方的力量。与直接参与谈判的各方相比，调解员更容易将人与问题分开，引导讨论聚焦于各方的利益和选择。此外，调解员通常还能提出一些公正的解决分歧的依据。第三方还可以将方案的构思与决策分开，减少达成协议所需的决策次数，并帮助各方了解最终决策的结果。一种旨在使第三方能够完成所有这些工作的流程被称为“单文本程序”。

In the house-designing negotiation between husband and wife, an independent architect is called in and shown the latest plans reflecting the present positions of the husband and the wife. Not all third parties will behave wisely. One architect, for example, might ask the parties for clarification of their positions, press them for a long series of concessions, and make them even more emotionally attached to their particular solutions. But an architect using the one-text procedure would behave differently. Rather than ask about their positions he asks about their interests: not how big a bay window the wife wants, but why she wants it. “Is it for morning sun or afternoon sun? Is it to look out or look in?” He would ask the husband, “Why do you want a garage? What things do you need to store? What do you expect to do in your den? Read? Look at television? Entertain friends? When will you use the den? During the day? Weekends? Evenings?” And so forth.

在夫妻双方就房屋设计进行协商时，通常会请一位独立建筑师介入，并向他们展示反映双方当前立场的最新方案。并非所有第三方都能明智行事。例如，有的建筑师可能会要求双方澄清各自的立场，迫使他们做出一系列让步，并让他们更加执着于自己提出的方案。但采用“一键沟通”模式的建筑师则会采取不同的做法。他不会询问双方的立场，而是关注他们的需求：不是妻子想要多大的凸窗，而是她为什么想要。“是为了享受早晨的阳光还是下午的阳光？是为了欣赏窗外景色还是欣赏室内景色？”他会问丈夫：“你为什么想要车库？你需要存放什么？你打算在书房里做什么？读书？看电视？招待朋友？你会在什么时间使用书房？白天？周末？晚上？”等等。

The architect makes clear he is not asking either spouse to give up a position. Rather, he is exploring the possibility that he might be able to make a recommendation to them—but even that is uncertain. At this stage he is just trying to learn all he can about their needs and interests.

这位建筑师明确表示，他并非要求夫妻双方放弃任何职位。相反，他只是在探讨是否有可能向他们提出建议——但即便如此，结果也尚不确定。现阶段，他只是想尽可能多地了解他们的需求和兴趣。

Afterward, the architect develops a list of interests and needs of the two spouses (“morning sun, open fireplace, comfortable place to read, room for a wood shop, storage for snow-blower and medium-size car,” and so on). He asks each spouse in turn to criticize the list and suggest improvements on it. It is hard to make concessions, but it is easy to criticize.

之后，建筑师列出了夫妻二人的兴趣爱好和需求清单（例如“早晨的阳光、开放式壁炉、舒适的阅读空间、木工坊、存放除雪机和中型汽车的空间”等等）。他请夫妻二人依次对清单进行评价并提出改进建议。做出让步很难，但提出批评却很容易。

A few days later the architect returns with a rough floor plan. “Personally, I am dissatisfied with it, but before working on it further I thought I would get your criticisms. What would be wrong with something like this?” The husband might say, “What’s wrong with it? Well, for one thing, the bathroom is too far from the bedroom. I don’t see enough room for my books. And where would overnight guests sleep?” The wife is similarly asked for her criticism of the first sketch.

几天后，建筑师带着一份粗略的平面图回来了。“我个人不太满意，但在进一步修改之前，我想先听听你们的意见。这样的设计有什么问题吗？”丈夫可能会说：“有什么问题？嗯，首先，浴室离卧室太远了。我觉得我的书放不下。还有，过夜的客人睡哪儿呢？”同样，妻子也会被问及对第一份草图的意见。

A short time later the architect comes back with a second sketch, again asking for criticism. “I’ve tried to deal with the bathroom problem and the book problem, and also with the idea of using the den as a spare bedroom and adding more storage space. What do you think about this?” As the plan takes shape, each spouse will tend to raise those issues most important to him or to her, not trivial details. Without conceding anything, the wife, for example, will want to make sure that the architect fully understands her major needs. No one’s ego, not even that of the architect, is committed to any draft. Inventing the best possible reconciliation of their interests within their financial constraints is separated from making decisions and is free of the fear of making an overhasty commitment. Husband and wife do not have to abandon their positions, but they now sit side by side, at least figuratively, jointly critiquing the plans as they take shape and helping the architect prepare a recommendation he may later present to them.

不久之后，建筑师带着第二张草图回来，再次征求意见。“我尝试解决了浴室和书籍摆放的问题，也考虑了将书房改造成客房并增加储物空间的想法。您觉得怎么样？”随着方案逐渐成形，夫妻双方都会倾向于提出各自最关心的问题，而不是无关紧要的细节。例如，妻子在不做出任何让步的前提下，会确保建筑师完全理解她的主要需求。没有人的自尊心，甚至建筑师的自尊心，会强加于任何一份草图之上。在经济条件允许的范围内，找到双方利益的最佳平衡点，这与做出最终决定是分开的，也避免了仓促承诺的顾虑。夫妻双方无需放弃各自的立场，但他们现在至少在精神上并肩而坐，共同审视方案的进展，并帮助建筑师准备一份他之后可能会提交给他们的建议。

And so it goes, through a third plan, a fourth, and a fifth. Finally, when he feels he can improve it no further, the architect says, “This is the best I can do. I have tried to reconcile your various interests as best I could. Many of the issues I have resolved using standard architectural and engineering solutions, precedent, and the best professional judgment I can bring to bear. Here it is. I recommend you accept this plan.”

就这样，他又修改了三个方案，第四个，第五个。最后，当他觉得方案已经无可改进时，建筑师说：“这是我能做到的最好结果了。我已经尽力协调你们各方的需求。许多问题我都运用了标准的建筑和工程解决方案、先例以及我所能运用的最佳专业判断来解决。这就是最终方案。我建议你们接受这个方案。”

Each spouse now has only one decision to make: yes or no. In making their decisions they know exactly what they are going to get. And a yes answer can be made contingent on the other side’s also saying yes. The one-text procedure not only shifts the game away from positional bargaining, it greatly simplifies the process both of inventing options and of deciding jointly on one.

现在，夫妻双方只需做出一个决定：是或否。在做出决定时，他们清楚地知道自己将得到什么。而且，一方的“是”可以附加条件，即另一方也必须说“是”。这种单条短信的流程不仅使谈判摆脱了立场博弈，还大大简化了提出方案和共同做出最终决定的过程。

In other negotiations, who could play the role of the architect? You could invite a third party in to mediate. Or, in negotiations involving more than two parties, a natural third party may be a participant whose interests on this issue lie more in effecting an agreement than in affecting the particular terms.

在其他谈判中，谁能扮演“架构师”的角色？你可以邀请第三方介入调解。或者，在涉及两方以上的谈判中，一个天然的第三方可能是那些在该问题上更注重促成协议而非影响具体条款的参与者。

In many negotiations that someone may be you. For instance, you may be a sales representative for a plastics plant negotiating a large order with an industrial customer who makes plastic bottles. The customer may want a special kind of plastic made up, but the plant you represent may be reluctant to do the retooling needed for the order. Your commission depends more on effecting an agreement between your customer and your production people than on affecting the terms. Or you may be a legislative assistant for a senator who is more concerned with getting a certain appropriations bill passed than with whether the appropriation is ten million dollars or eleven. Or you may be a manager trying to decide an issue on which each of your two subordinates favors a different course of action; you care more about making a decision both can live with than about which alternative is chosen. In each of these cases, even though you are an active participant, it may be in your best interest to behave as a mediator would and to use the one-text procedure. Mediate your own dispute.

在许多谈判中，这个人可能就是你。例如，你可能是一家塑料厂的销售代表，正在与一家生产塑料瓶的工业客户洽谈一笔大订单。客户可能需要一种特殊类型的塑料，但你所代表的工厂可能不愿意进行订单所需的设备改造。你的佣金更多地取决于促成客户和生产人员之间的协议，而不是影响条款本身。或者，你可能是一位参议员的立法助理，他更关心的是如何通过某项拨款法案，而不是拨款金额是1000万美元还是1100万美元。又或者，你可能是一位经理，正在努力解决一个问题，你的两位下属对此各执己见；你更关心的是如何做出双方都能接受的决定，而不是最终选择哪种方案。在这些情况下，即使你是积极的参与者，像调解员一样行事，并采用“一键式”程序，或许对你更有利。尝试调解你自己的纠纷。

Perhaps the most famous use of the one-text procedure was by the United States at the Camp David summit in September 1978 when mediating between Egypt and Israel. The United States listened to both sides, prepared a draft to which no one was committed, asked for criticism, and improved the draft again and again until the mediators felt they could improve it no further. After thirteen days and some twenty-three drafts, the United States had a text it was prepared to recommend. When President Jimmy Carter finally did recommend it, Israel and Egypt accepted. As a mechanical technique for limiting the number of decisions, reducing the uncertainty of each decision, and preventing the parties from getting increasingly locked into their positions, it worked remarkably well.

或许，单文本程序最著名的应用案例是美国在1978年9月戴维营峰会上调解埃及和以色列之间的争端。美国听取了双方的意见，起草了一份双方均不承担任何义务的草案，征求各方意见，并反复修改完善，直到调解员认为无法再做任何改进为止。经过十三天和大约二十三稿的修改，美国最终形成了一份可以推荐的文本。当吉米·卡特总统最终提出推荐时，以色列和埃及都接受了这份文本。作为一种限制决策次数、降低每次决策的不确定性、防止各方立场僵化的有效方法，单文本程序取得了显著成效。

The one-text procedure is a great help for two-party negotiations involving a mediator. It is almost essential for large multilateral negotiations. One hundred and fifty nations, for example, cannot constructively discuss a hundred and fifty different proposals. Nor can they make concessions contingent upon mutual concessions by everybody else. Combining parts of many different proposals is also unlikely to produce the best answer, as illustrated by the old quip that a camel is a horse designed by a committee. Multiple parties need some way to simplify the process of decision-making without diminishing the quality of the outcome. The one-text procedure serves that purpose.

单一文本程序对于有调解人的双边谈判大有裨益，对于大型多边谈判则几乎必不可少。例如，150个国家不可能建设性地讨论150个不同的提案，也不可能做出以其他所有国家做出相互让步为条件的让步。将众多不同提案的部分内容拼凑在一起也不太可能产生最佳方案，正如那句古老的谚语所说：“骆驼是委员会设计的马”。多方需要某种方法来简化决策过程，同时又不降低结果的质量。单一文本程序正是为此而设。

The Law of the Sea negotiations started making significant progress only when they began using a prototype of the one-text procedure created by veteran diplomat Tommy Koh of Singapore. The negotiators were divided into groups to work on different issues with appointed chairpersons tabling drafts, soliciting criticism, and revising drafts within each group. A similar process was used for parts of the South African constitutional negotiations that ultimately ended apartheid and created an inclusive multilateral democracy. [3]

《海洋法公约》谈判只有在采用新加坡资深外交官许通美（Tommy Koh）创建的“单一文本程序”原型后才取得显著进展。谈判代表被分成若干小组，分别处理不同的议题，每个小组都由指定的主席负责提交草案、征求意见并进行修改。类似的程序也曾用于南非宪法谈判的部分内容，最终结束了种族隔离制度，建立了一个包容性的多边民主政体。[3]

Note that in most situations you do not have to get anyone’s consent to start using the one-text procedure. Simply prepare a draft and ask for criticism. Again, you can change the game simply by starting to play the new one. Even if the other side is not willing to talk to you directly (or vice versa), a third party can take a draft around.

请注意，在大多数情况下，您无需征得任何人的同意即可开始使用单条短信沟通方式。只需准备一份草稿并征求意见即可。同样，您只需开始使用这种新方式，就能改变局面。即使对方不愿意直接与您沟通（反之亦然），也可以通过第三方传递草稿。

Getting them to play: The case of Jones Realty and Frank Turnbull

如何让他们参与：琼斯地产公司和弗兰克·特恩布尔的案例

The following real-life example of a negotiation between a landlord and tenant should give you a feel for how you might deal with a party who is reluctant to engage in principled negotiation. It illustrates what it means to change the game by starting to play a new one.

以下这个房东和租客之间的真实谈判案例，应该能让你了解如何应对不愿进行原则性谈判的一方。它说明了改变游戏规则、另辟蹊径的意义所在。

The case in brief. Frank Turnbull rented an apartment in March from Jones Realty for $1,200 a month. In July, when he and his roommate, Paul, wanted to move out, Turnbull learned that the apartment was under rent control. The maximum legal rent was $932 a month—$268 less than he had been paying.

案情简述：弗兰克·特恩布尔三月份从琼斯地产公司租了一套公寓，月租金1200美元。七月份，当他和室友保罗想搬走时，特恩布尔才知道这套公寓受租金管制。法定最高租金为每月932美元——比他之前支付的租金少了268美元。

Disturbed that he had been overcharged, Turnbull called on Mrs. Jones of Jones Realty to discuss the problem. At first, Mrs. Jones was unreceptive and hostile. She claimed to be right and accused Turnbull of ingratitude and blackmail. After several long negotiating sessions, however, Mrs. Jones agreed to reimburse Turnbull and his roommate. Her tone in the end became friendlier and apologetic.

特恩布尔对被多收费感到不满，于是打电话给琼斯地产公司的琼斯太太商讨此事。起初，琼斯太太态度冷漠且充满敌意。她坚称自己是对的，并指责特恩布尔忘恩负义、敲诈勒索。然而，经过几次长时间的协商，琼斯太太最终同意赔偿特恩布尔及其室友。她的语气也变得友好而歉意。

Throughout, Turnbull used the method of principled negotiation. Presented below is a selection of the exchanges that took place during the negotiation. Each exchange is headed by a stock phrase that a principled negotiator might use in any similar situation. Following each exchange is an analysis of the theory that lies behind it and its impact.

特恩布尔在整个谈判过程中都运用了原则性谈判法。以下摘录了谈判期间的部分对话。每段对话都以一句原则性谈判者在类似情况下可能使用的标准用语开头。每段对话之后都附有对其背后理论及其影响的分析。

“Please correct me if I’m wrong”

“如果我说错了，请纠正我。”

Turnbull: Mrs. Jones, I’ve just learned—please correct me if I’m wrong—that our apartment’s under rent control. We’ve been told that the legal maximum rent is $932 a month. Have we been misinformed?

特恩布尔：琼斯太太，我刚了解到——如果我说错了请纠正我——我们的公寓是受租金管制的。我们被告知法定最高租金是每月932美元。我们是不是被误导了？

Analysis. The essence of principled negotiation lies in remaining open to persuasion by objective facts and principles. By cautiously treating his view of the objective facts as possibly inaccurate and asking Mrs. Jones to correct it, Turnbull establishes a dialogue based on reason. He invites her to participate by either agreeing with the facts as presented or setting them right. This approach makes them two colleagues trying to establish the facts. The confrontation is defused. If Turnbull simply asserted his views of the facts as facts, Mrs. Jones would feel disrespected, threatened, and defensive. She might deny the facts, especially if she thought any aspect of Turnbull’s view was inaccurate or incomplete. The negotiation would not start off constructively.

分析。有原则的谈判的精髓在于保持开放的心态，接受客观事实和原则的说服。特恩布尔谨慎地将自己对客观事实的看法视为可能不准确，并请琼斯夫人纠正，从而建立起基于理性的对话。他邀请琼斯夫人参与，让她可以选择同意所呈现的事实，或者纠正其中的错误。这种方法使他们成为两位共同努力查明事实的同事，从而化解了冲突。如果特恩布尔只是简单地将自己的事实观点当作既定事实，琼斯夫人会感到不被尊重、受到威胁，并产生防御心理。她可能会否认这些事实，尤其当她认为特恩布尔的观点有任何不准确或不完整之处时。这样一来，谈判就不会以建设性的方式开始。

If Turnbull is genuinely mistaken, asking for corrections beforehand will make them easier to accept. To tell Mrs. Jones that these are the facts, only to learn he is wrong, would make him lose face. Worse yet, she would then doubt all the more anything else he says, making it difficult to negotiate.

如果特恩布尔确实犯了错误，事先请求对方更正会更容易被接受。如果他告诉琼斯夫人这些就是事实，结果却发现自己错了，那会让他颜面尽失。更糟糕的是，琼斯夫人会因此更加怀疑他说的其他话，使谈判更加困难。

Making yourself open to correction and persuasion is a pillar in the strategy of principled negotiation. You can convince the other side to be open to the principles and objective standards you suggest only if you show yourself open to the ones they suggest.

乐于接受批评和劝说是原则性谈判策略的基石。只有当你对对方提出的原则和客观标准持开放态度时，才能说服对方接受你提出的原则和客观标准。

“We appreciate what you’ve done for us”

“我们非常感谢您为我们所做的一切。”

Turnbull: Paul and I understand you were doing a personal favor by renting us this apartment. You were very kind to put in the time and effort, and we appreciate it.

特恩布尔：保罗和我明白您把这套公寓租给我们是帮了您一个忙。您花费了时间和精力，我们非常感激。

Analysis. Giving personal support to the person on the other side is crucial to disentangling the people from the problem—separating relationship issues from the substantive merits. By expressing his appreciation of Mrs. Jones’s good deeds, Turnbull in effect says, “We have nothing against you personally. We think you’re a generous person.” He puts himself on her side. He defuses any threat she may feel to her self-image.

分析。给予对方个人支持至关重要，这有助于将人与问题本身区分开来——将人际关系问题与实质性问题区分开来。特恩布尔通过表达对琼斯太太善行的赞赏，实际上是在说：“我们对你个人没有任何意见。我们认为你是一个慷慨的人。”他站在了她这边。他消除了她可能感受到的任何对其自我形象的威胁。

Praise and support, moreover, imply that the person will continue to deserve them. After being praised, Mrs. Jones now has a slight emotional investment in Turnbull’s approval of her. She has something to lose and as a result may act more conciliatory.

此外，赞扬和支持意味着这个人会继续配得上它们。琼斯太太受到赞扬后，对特恩布尔的认可产生了些许情感上的依恋。她有所顾虑，因此可能会表现得更加和解。

“Our concern is fairness”

“我们关注的是公平。”

Turnbull: We want to know that we didn’t pay any more than we should have. When we’re persuaded that the rent paid measures up fairly to the time spent in the apartment, we’ll call it even and move out.

特恩布尔：我们想知道我们付的钱是否多。只有当我们确信支付的租金与我们在公寓里居住的时间相符时，我们才会认为这笔交易公平合理，然后搬出去。

Analysis. Turnbull takes a basic stand on principle and announces his intention to stick to it; he must be persuaded on the basis of principle. At the same time, he lets Mrs. Jones know he is open to persuasion along the lines of this principle. She is thus left with little choice but to reason with him in pursuit of her interests.

分析。特恩布尔在原则问题上立场坚定，并宣布他将坚持这一原则；必须基于原则才能说服他。与此同时，他也让琼斯太太知道，如果按照这一原则，他愿意接受说服。因此，为了自身利益，她别无选择，只能与他讲道理。

Turnbull does not take a righteous stand on principle backed up with whatever power he possesses. Not only are his ends principled but also the means he contemplates. His ends, he claims, are a fair balance between rent paid and time spent. If convinced the rent paid is just right for the time spent, he will move out. If the rent paid is excessive, it is only fair that he remain in the apartment until the rent and the time spent are in balance.

特恩布尔并非凭借自身权力，秉持正义的原则行事。他不仅目标明确，而且所采取的手段也同样如此。他声称，他的目标是租金与居住时间之间达到公平的平衡。如果他认为租金与居住时间相符，他就会搬走。如果租金过高，那么他理应继续住在公寓里，直到租金与居住时间达到平衡为止。

“We would like to settle this on the basis of independent standards, not of who can do what to whom”

“我们希望根据独立标准来解决这个问题，而不是根据谁可以对谁做什么来解决这个问题。”

Mrs. Jones: It’s funny you should mention fairness, because what you’re really saying is that you and Paul just want money, and that you’re going to take advantage of your still being in the apartment to try and get it from us. That really makes me angry. If I had my way, you and Paul would be out of the apartment today.

琼斯太太：你居然提到了公平，真是讽刺，因为你真正的意思是，你和保罗只是想要钱，而且你们打算利用还住在公寓里的机会从我们这里骗钱。这真让我生气。如果由我做主，你和保罗今天就得搬出去。

Turnbull (barely controlling his anger): I must not be making myself clear. Of course it would be nice if Paul and I got some money. Of course we could try and stay here in the apartment until you got us evicted. But that’s not the point, Mrs. Jones.

特恩布尔（强压怒火）：我可能没说清楚。当然，如果我和保罗能拿到一些钱，那当然很好。当然，我们可以试着继续住在这间公寓里，直到你们把我们赶出去。但这并不是重点，琼斯太太。

More important to us than making a few dollars here or there is the feeling of being treated fairly. No one likes to feel cheated. And if we made this a matter of who’s got the power and refused to move, we’d have to go to court, waste a lot of time and money, and end up with a big headache. You would too. Who wants that?

对我们来说，比起赚点小钱，更重要的是感受到公平对待。没人喜欢被欺骗。如果我们把这件事变成权力之争，拒绝搬迁，那就得上法庭，浪费大量时间和金钱，最后只会徒增烦恼。你也会一样。谁想这样呢？

No, Mrs. Jones, we want to handle this problem fairly on the basis of some independent standard, rather than who can do what to whom.

不，琼斯夫人，我们希望根据一些独立的标准公平地处理这个问题，而不是根据谁可以对谁做什么来处理。

Analysis. Mrs. Jones challenges the idea of negotiating on the basis of principle, calling it a charade. It’s a matter of will and her will is to throw out Turnbull and his roommate today.

分析。琼斯夫人质疑以原则为基础的谈判理念，称其为一场闹剧。这完全是意志力的问题，而她的意志就是今天就把特恩布尔和他的室友赶出去。

At this Turnbull almost loses his temper—and with it his control over the negotiation. He feels like counterattacking: “I’d like to see you try to get us out. We’ll go to court. We’ll get your license revoked.” The negotiation would then break off, and Turnbull would lose a lot of time, effort, and peace of mind. But instead of reacting, Turnbull keeps his temper and brings the negotiation back to the merits. This is a good example of negotiation jujitsu. He deflects Mrs. Jones’s attack by taking responsibility for her mistaken perceptions, and he tries to persuade her of his sincere interest in principle. He does not hide either his selfish interests or his leverage over her; on the contrary, he makes both explicit. Once they are acknowledged, he can distinguish them from the merits and they can cease being an issue.

这时，特恩布尔几乎要发火了——谈判的主动权也随之丧失。他很想反击：“我倒要看看你怎么把我们赶出去。我们会上法庭。我们会吊销你的执照。”这样一来，谈判就会破裂，特恩布尔也会白白浪费大量时间、精力，还心烦意乱。但他并没有冲动，而是控制住了情绪，把谈判拉回到了实质性问题上。这正是谈判技巧的典范。他主动承担了琼斯太太误解的责任，以此化解了她的攻击，并试图说服她相信自己原则上的诚意。他既没有掩饰自己的私利，也没有利用对琼斯太太的影响力；相反，他把这两点都说得清清楚楚。一旦琼斯太太承认了这些，他就能将它们与实质性问题区分开来，从而不再成为争论的焦点。

Turnbull also tries to give the game of principled negotiation some weight by telling Mrs. Jones this is his basic code—the way he always plays. He attributes this not to high-minded motives—which are always suspect—but to simple self-interest.

特恩布尔还试图通过告诉琼斯夫人这是他的基本准则——他一贯的行事方式——来强调原则性谈判的重要性。他将此归因于单纯的自身利益，而非高尚的动机（这种动机总是令人怀疑）。

“Trust is a separate Issue”

“信任是另一个问题”

Mrs. Jones: You don’t trust me? After all I’ve done for you?

琼斯太太：你不信任我？我为你做了那么多，你却不信任我？

Turnbull: Mrs. Jones, we appreciate all you’ve done for us. For us, this is not a matter of trust. The issue is the principle: Did we pay more than we should have? What considerations do you think we should take into account in deciding this?

特恩布尔：琼斯夫人，我们非常感谢您为我们所做的一切。对我们来说，这不是信任问题，而是原则问题：我们是否支付了过多的费用？您认为我们在做决定时应该考虑哪些因素？

Analysis. Mrs. Jones tries to manipulate Turnbull into a corner. Either he pursues the point and looks untrusting, or he looks trusting and gives in. Turnbull slips out of the corner, however, by expressing his gratitude once more and then defining the question of trust as irrelevant. Turnbull at once reaffirms his appreciation of Mrs. Jones while he remains firm on the principle. In doing so, he avoids connecting the two thoughts with “but,” implicitly using “and” instead. “But,” sometimes called the “great eraser,” has a tendency to negate the first thing you say by implying that only one of two statements can be true, making it either/or. “And” underscores the more complex reality that both thoughts can be true at the same time. It helps ensure both that Mrs. Jones feels heard and appreciated and that she can’t frame Turnbull as wrongly untrusting.

分析。琼斯太太试图将特恩布尔逼入绝境。他要么坚持己见，显得不信任；要么表现出信任，最终妥协。然而，特恩布尔巧妙地摆脱了困境，他再次表达了感激之情，并指出信任问题无关紧要。特恩布尔既重申了他对琼斯太太的感激之情，又坚定地维护了自己的原则。他避免使用“但是”来连接这两个想法，而是巧妙地使用了“而且”。“但是”有时被称为“大橡皮擦”，它往往会否定你最初所说的内容，暗示两个陈述中只有一个是正确的，使之成为非此即彼的选择。“而且”则强调了更为复杂的现实，即这两个想法可以同时成立。这既确保了琼斯太太感到被倾听和重视，也避免了她指责特恩布尔不信任她。

Moreover, instead of just shunting aside the question of trust, Turnbull actively directs the discussion back to principle by asking Mrs. Jones what considerations she thinks are relevant.

此外，特恩布尔并没有回避信任问题，而是积极地将讨论引回原则层面，询问琼斯夫人她认为有哪些因素是相关的。

Turnbull sticks to principle without blaming Mrs. Jones. He never calls her dishonest. He does not ask, “Did you take advantage of us?” but inquires more impersonally, “Did we pay more than we should have?” Even if he does not trust her, it would be a poor strategy to tell her so. She would probably become defensive and angry and might either withdraw into a rigid position or break off the negotiation altogether.

特恩布尔坚持原则，没有指责琼斯太太。他从未指责她不诚实。他没有问“你占了我们的便宜吗？”，而是更客观地问“我们付的钱是不是太多了？”即使他不信任她，直接告诉她也不是明智之举。她可能会变得防备和愤怒，要么采取强硬立场，要么干脆终止谈判。

It helps to have stock phrases like “It’s not a question of trust” to turn aside ploys like Mrs. Jones’s plea for trust.

准备一些常用语，比如“这不是信任问题”，有助于驳斥像琼斯太太那样恳求信任的伎俩。

“Could I ask you a few questions to see whether my facts are right?”

“我可以问你几个问题，看看我的陈述是否正确吗？”

Turnbull: Could I ask you a few questions to see whether the facts I’ve been given are right?

特恩布尔：我可以问你几个问题，看看我所了解到的事实是否正确吗？

Is the apartment really under rent control?

这套公寓真的在租金管制范围内吗？

Is the legal maximum rent really $932?

法定最高租金真的是932美元吗？

Paul asked me whether this makes us parties to a violation of the law.

保罗问我，这是否使我们成为违法行为的参与者。

Did someone inform Paul at the time he signed the lease that the apartment was under rent control, and that the legal maximum was $268 lower than the rent he agreed to?

保罗在签署租约时，是否有人告知他该公寓受租金管制，且法定最高租金比他同意的租金低 268 美元？

Analysis. Statements of fact can feel lecturing or threatening. Whenever you can, ask a question instead.

分析。陈述事实可能会让人感觉像是在说教或受到威胁。尽可能地，用提问代替陈述。

Turnbull might have declared, “The legal rent is $932. You broke the law. What’s worse, you involved us in breaking the law without telling us so.” Mrs. Jones would probably have reacted strongly to these statements, dismissing them as verbal attacks intended to score points.

特恩布尔可能会宣称：“合法租金是932美元。你们违法了。更糟糕的是，你们瞒着我们一起违法。”琼斯太太很可能对这些话反应强烈，认为这是旨在博取政治资本的言语攻击。

Phrasing each piece of information as a question allows Mrs. Jones to participate, listen to the information, evaluate it, and either accept or correct it. Turnbull communicates the same information to her but in a less provocative manner. He reduces the heat still further by attributing a particularly pointed question to his absent roommate.

将每条信息都以问题的形式表达出来，可以让琼斯太太参与进来，倾听信息，评估信息，并决定接受或纠正。特恩布尔也向她传达了同样的信息，但方式更为温和。他还将一个特别尖锐的问题归咎于不在场的室友，进一步缓和了气氛。

In effect, Turnbull induces Mrs. Jones to help lay a foundation of agreed-upon facts upon which a principled solution can be built.

实际上，特恩布尔促使琼斯夫人帮助奠定了双方认可的事实基础，以便在此基础上建立一个有原则的解决方案。

“What’s the principle behind your action?”

你的行为背后的原则是什么？

Turnbull: I’m not clear why you charged us $1,200 a month. What were your reasons for charging that much?

特恩布尔：我不明白你们为什么每月向我们收取1200美元。你们收取这么多费用的理由是什么？

Analysis. A principled negotiator neither accepts nor rejects the other side’s positions. To keep the dialogue focused on the merits, Turnbull questions Mrs. Jones about the reasons for her position. He does not ask whether there were any reasons. He assumes there are good reasons. This flattering assumption leads the other side to search for reasons even if there are none, thus keeping the negotiation on the basis of principle.

分析。一位有原则的谈判者既不接受也不拒绝对方的立场。为了使对话聚焦于实质内容，特恩布尔询问琼斯夫人持此立场的理由。他并没有问她是否有理由，而是假定她有充分的理由。这种奉承式的假设促使对方即使没有理由也会去寻找理由，从而使谈判始终建立在原则之上。

“Let me see if I understand what you’re saying”

“让我看看我是否理解了你的意思。”

Turnbull: Let me see if I understand what you’re saying, Mrs. Jones. If I’ve understood you correctly, you think the rent we paid is fair because you made a lot of repairs and improvements to the apartment since the last rent control evaluation. It wasn’t worth your while to ask the Rent Control Board for an increase for the few months you rented the place to us.

特恩布尔：琼斯太太，让我看看我是否理解了您的意思。如果我理解正确的话，您认为我们支付的租金很合理，因为自上次租金管制评估以来，您对公寓进行了很多维修和改进。您觉得为了这几个月把房子租给我们，向租金管制委员会申请涨租不值得。

In fact, you rented it only as a favor to Paul. And now you’re concerned that we may take unfair advantage of you and try to get money from you as the price for moving out. Is there something I’ve missed or misunderstood?

事实上，你租这房子只是帮保罗一个忙。现在你担心我们会占你便宜，想方设法从你那里榨取搬走的费用。是不是我漏掉了什么或者理解错了？

Analysis. Principled negotiation requires good communication. Before responding to Mrs. Jones’s arguments, Turnbull restates to her in positive terms what he has heard to make sure he has indeed understood her.

分析。有原则的谈判需要良好的沟通。在回应琼斯夫人的论点之前，特恩布尔用肯定的语气复述了他听到的内容，以确保他确实理解了她的意思。

Once she feels understood, she can relax and discuss the problem constructively. She can’t dismiss his arguments on the grounds that they do not take into account what she knows. She is more likely to listen now and be more receptive. In trying to sum up her point of view, Turnbull establishes a cooperative game in which both are making sure he understands the facts.

一旦她感到被理解，她就能放松下来，以建设性的方式讨论问题。她不能再以对方的论点没有考虑到她所了解的情况为由而否定它们。现在她更愿意倾听，也更容易接受。特恩布尔试图总结她的观点，从而建立起一种合作博弈，双方都在努力确保他理解事实。

“Let me get back to you”

“我稍后回复你。”

Turnbull: Now that I think I understand your point of view, let me talk with my roommate and explain it to him. Can I get back to you tomorrow sometime?

特恩布尔：现在我想我明白你的意思了，让我跟我的室友谈谈，跟他解释一下。我明天某个时候能再联系你吗？

Analysis. A good negotiator rarely makes an important decision on the spot. The psychological pressure to be nice and to give in is too great. A little time and distance help disentangle the people from the problem.

分析：优秀的谈判者很少当场做出重要决定。因为出于礼貌和妥协的心理压力太大。给人们一些时间和空间，有助于他们从问题中抽身而出。

A good negotiator comes to the table with a credible reason in his pocket for leaving when he wants. Such a reason should not indicate passivity or inability to make a decision. Here, Turnbull sounds as if he knows exactly what he is doing, and he arranges to resume the negotiation at a given time. He shows not only decisiveness but also control over the course of the negotiation.

一位优秀的谈判者会带着令人信服的理由来到谈判桌前，以便在需要时离开。这样的理由不应表明其消极被动或缺乏决策能力。特恩布尔的表态听起来像是胸有成竹，他安排在某个特定时间恢复谈判。他不仅展现了果断，也体现了对谈判进程的掌控。

Once away from the table, Turnbull can check on points of information and consult his “constituency,” Paul. He can think about the decision and make sure he has not lost perspective.

离开谈判桌后，特恩布尔可以查阅相关信息，并咨询他的“选民”保罗的意见。他可以仔细思考这项决定，确保自己没有失去客观的视角。

Too much time at the table may wear down one’s commitment to principled negotiation. Returning to the table with renewed resolve, Turnbull can be soft on the person without being soft on the problem.

在谈判桌上待的时间过长可能会削弱一个人坚持原则谈判的决心。特恩布尔重拾决心回到谈判桌前，既能对人保持温和，又能直面问题。

“Let me show you where I have trouble following some of your reasoning”

“让我来指出我难以理解你的某些推理之处。”

Turnbull: Let me show you where I have trouble following some of your reasons for the extra $268 a month. One reason was the repairs and improvements on the apartment. The Rent Control Examiner said it would take about $30,000 in improvements to justify an increase of $268 a month. How much money was spent on improvements?

特恩布尔：让我指出我难以理解的几个关于每月额外增加268美元的理由。其中一个理由是公寓的维修和改造。租金管制审查员表示，大约需要3万美元的改造费用才能证明每月增加268美元的合理性。那么，究竟花了多少钱进行改造呢？

I must admit it didn’t seem like $30,000 worth to Paul and me. The hole in the linoleum you promised to repair was never fixed, neither was the hole in the living room floor. The toilet broke down repeatedly. These are just some of the defects and malfunctions we experienced.

我必须承认，我和保罗都觉得这房子不值三万美元。你承诺修好的油毡地板上的洞一直没修，客厅地板上的洞也没修。马桶也经常坏。这些只是我们遇到的部分缺陷和故障。

Analysis. In principled negotiation you present your reasons first before offering a proposal. If principles come afterward, they appear not as the objective criteria that any proposal should satisfy but as mere justifications for an arbitrary position.

分析。在有原则的谈判中，你应该先阐明理由，然后再提出方案。如果原则是后加的，它们就不是任何方案都应满足的客观标准，而仅仅是对某种武断立场的辩解。

For Turnbull to explain his reasons first shows his openness to persuasion and his awareness of the need to convince Mrs. Jones. If he announced his proposal first, Mrs. Jones probably would not bother to listen to the reasons that followed. Her mind would be elsewhere, considering what objections and counterproposals she could make.

特恩布尔先解释原因，表明他愿意接受劝说，也意识到需要说服琼斯太太。如果他先宣布自己的提议，琼斯太太可能根本不会听他解释。她会心不在焉地想着该如何反对，提出反建议。

Turnbull has also sought out objective standards to support his concerns. He has called the Rent Control Board to quantify a correlation between improvements and a $268 per month rent increase. In preparing for your negotiation, it helps to think about what standards would be useful, who might be able to provide them, and how to frame your questions to elicit the most relevant information.

特恩布尔也一直在寻求客观标准来佐证他的担忧。他已致电租金管制委员会，要求量化房屋改善与每月268美元租金上涨之间的相关性。在准备谈判时，思考哪些标准会有帮助、谁可以提供这些标准，以及如何措辞才能获得最相关的信息，这些都将有所裨益。

“One fair solution might be . . .”

“一个公平的解决方案可能是……”

Turnbull: Given all the considerations we’ve discussed, one fair solution seems to be for Paul and me to be reimbursed for the amount of rent we paid in excess of the legal maximum. Does that sound fair to you?

特恩布尔：考虑到我们讨论的所有因素，一个公平的解决方案似乎是，我和保罗应该获得超出法定最高限额的租金补偿。您觉得这公平吗？
