Analysis. Turnbull presents a proposal not as his, but as a fair option that deserves their joint consideration. He does not claim it is the only fair solution, but one fair solution. He is specific without digging himself into a position and inviting rejection.

分析。特恩布尔提出的方案并非他个人的主张，而是值得双方共同考虑的公平选择。他并未声称这是唯一公平的解决方案，而只是众多公平方案之一。他的方案具体明确，既没有固守己见，也没有招致反对。

“If we agree . . . if we disagree . . . ”

“如果我们意见一致……如果我们意见不一致……”

Turnbull: If you and I could reach agreement now, Paul and I would move out immediately. If we can’t reach an agreement, the hearing examiner at the Rent Control Board suggested that we stay in the apartment and withhold rent and/or sue you for reimbursement, treble damages, and legal fees . Paul and I are extremely reluctant to take either of these courses. We feel confident we can settle this matter fairly with you to your satisfaction and ours.

特恩布尔：如果我们现在能达成协议，我和保罗会立即搬出去。如果无法达成协议，租金管制委员会的听证官建议我们继续住在公寓里，拒付房租，或者起诉您要求赔偿、三倍赔偿金和诉讼费。我和保罗非常不愿意采取这两种做法。我们相信，我们可以与您公平地解决此事，让您和我们都满意。

Analysis. Turnbull is trying to make it easy for Mrs. Jones to say yes to his proposal. So he starts by making it clear that all it takes for the problem to go away is Mrs. Jones’s agreement.

分析。特恩布尔试图让琼斯太太更容易接受他的提议。因此，他首先明确表示，只要琼斯太太同意，问题就能迎刃而解。

The trickiest part of the message to communicate is the alternative if no agreement is reached. How can Turnbull get this across—he wants her to take it into account in her decision—without upsetting the negotiations? He bases the alternative on objective principle by attributing it to a legal authority—the hearing examiner. He distances himself personally from the suggestion. Nor does he say he will definitely take action. Instead, he leaves it as a possibility and emphasizes his reluctance to do anything drastic. Finally, he closes by affirming his confidence that a mutually satisfactory agreement will be reached.

信息中最难传达的部分是如果无法达成协议的替代方案。特恩布尔该如何传达这一点——他希望她将此纳入决策考量——同时又不破坏谈判？他将替代方案建立在客观原则之上，并援引法律权威——听证官——的说法。他刻意与这一建议保持距离，也没有明确表示一定会采取行动。相反，他将其视为一种可能性，并强调自己不愿采取任何激烈的措施。最后，他重申自己相信最终会达成双方都满意的协议。

Turnbull’s BATNA—his best alternative to a negotiated agreement—is probably neither staying in the apartment nor going to court. He and Paul have already rented another apartment and would greatly prefer to move out now. A lawsuit would be difficult, given their busy schedules, and even if they won, they might never be able to collect. Turnbull’s BATNA is probably just to move out and stop worrying about the $1,340 overpayment. Since his BATNA is probably less attractive than Mrs. Jones thinks, Turnbull does not disclose it.

特恩布尔的替代方案（BATNA，即他达成协议之外的最佳选择）可能既不是继续住在公寓里，也不是上法庭。他和保罗已经租了另一套公寓，现在非常希望搬出去。考虑到他们繁忙的日程安排，打官司会很困难，即使胜诉，他们也可能永远无法收回欠款。特恩布尔的替代方案很可能就是搬出去，不再为那1340美元的超额付款而烦恼。由于他的替代方案可能不像琼斯太太想象的那样有吸引力，所以特恩布尔并没有透露。

“We’d be happy to see if we can leave when it’s most convenient for you”

“我们很乐意看看能否在您最方便的时候离开。”

Mrs. Jones: When do you plan to move out?

琼斯太太：你打算什么时候搬出去？

Turnbull: As long as we’ve agreed on the appropriate rent for our time in the apartment, we’d be happy to see if we can leave when it’s most convenient for you. When would you prefer?

特恩布尔：只要我们双方就公寓的租金达成一致，我们很乐意看看能否在您最方便的时候搬走。您希望什么时候搬？

Analysis. Sensing the possibility of a joint gain, Turnbull indicates his willingness to discuss ways of meeting Mrs. Jones’s interest. As it turns out, Turnbull and Mrs. Jones have a shared interest in Turnbull moving out as soon as possible.

分析。特恩布尔察觉到双方都有利的可能性，表示愿意探讨如何满足琼斯太太的利益。事实证明，特恩布尔和琼斯太太的共同利益在于，特恩布尔希望他尽快搬出去。

Incorporating her interests into the agreement not only gives her more of a stake in it but also allows Mrs. Jones to save face. On the one hand, she can feel good about agreeing to a fair solution even though it costs her money. On the other, she can say that she got the tenants out of the apartment early.

将她的利益纳入协议，不仅让她更有发言权，也让琼斯太太保住了面子。一方面，即使要付出金钱代价，她也能因同意一个公平的解决方案而感到欣慰。另一方面，她可以说自己让租户提前搬出了公寓。

“It’s been a pleasure dealing with you”

“与您合作非常愉快。”

Turnbull: Paul and I do appreciate, Mrs. Jones, all that you’ve done for us, and I’m pleased that we’ve settled this last problem fairly and amicably.

特恩布尔：琼斯夫人，我和保罗非常感谢您为我们所做的一切，我很高兴我们公平友好地解决了最后一个问题。

Mrs. Jones: Thank you, Mr. Turnbull. Have a nice summer.

琼斯太太：谢谢你，特恩布尔先生。祝你暑假愉快。

Analysis. Turnbull ends the negotiation on a final conciliatory note toward Mrs. Jones. Because they successfully dealt with the problem independently of the relationship, neither party feels cheated or angry, and neither is likely to try to sabotage or ignore their agreement. A working relationship is maintained for the future.

分析。特恩布尔以对琼斯夫人较为和解的语气结束了谈判。由于双方成功地独立于彼此关系解决了问题，因此双方均未感到被欺骗或愤怒，也都不太可能试图破坏或无视他们的协议。双方将维持未来的工作关系。

Whether you use principled negotiation and negotiation jujitsu, as Frank Turnbull did, or a third party with the one-text procedure, the conclusion remains the same: you can usually get the other side to play the game of principled negotiation with you, even if at first they appear unwilling.

无论你是像弗兰克·特恩布尔那样运用原则性谈判和谈判技巧，还是通过第三方进行单文本程序，结论都是一样的：你通常可以让对方和你一起玩原则性谈判的游戏，即使他们一开始看起来不愿意。

# ↩

8 What If They Use Dirty Tricks?

8 如果他们使用卑鄙的手段呢？

(Taming the Hard Bargainer)

（驯服难缠的谈判者）

P rincipled negotiation is all very well, but what if the other negotiator deceives you or tries to throw you off balance? Or what if they escalate their demands just when you are on the verge of agreement?

坚持原则的谈判固然很好，但如果对方谈判者欺骗你或试图扰乱你的节奏怎么办？或者，如果他们在你即将达成协议时突然提高要求怎么办？

There are many tactics and tricks people can use to try to take advantage of you. Everyone knows some of them. They range from lies and psychological abuse to various forms of pressure tactics. They may be illegal, unethical, or simply unpleasant. Their purpose is to help the user “win” some substantive gain in an unprincipled contest of will. Such tactics may be called tricky bargaining.

人们会使用许多伎俩和手段来占你便宜。每个人都知道其中的一些。这些伎俩包括谎言、心理虐待以及各种形式的施压。它们可能违法、不道德，或者仅仅是令人不快。其目的在于帮助使用者在一场毫无原则的意志较量中“赢得”一些实质性的利益。这类伎俩可以被称为“狡猾的谈判”。

If they recognize that a tricky bargaining tactic is being used against them, most people respond in one of two ways. The first standard response is to put up with it. It is unpleasant to rock the boat. You may give the other side the benefit of the doubt or get angry and promise yourself never to deal with them again. For now, you hope for the best and keep quiet. Most people respond this way. They hope that if they give in this time, the other side will be appeased and will not ask for more. Sometimes this works, more often it fails. This is how Neville Chamberlain, the British Prime Minister, responded in 1938 to Hitler’s negotiating tactics. After Chamberlain thought he had an agreement, Hitler raised his demands. At Munich, Chamberlain, hoping to avoid war, went along. A year later, World War II started.

如果人们意识到对方正在使用狡猾的谈判策略，大多数人会采取以下两种应对方式之一。第一种常见的做法是忍气吞声。打破僵局令人不快。你可能会选择相信对方，或者勃然大怒，发誓再也不跟他们打交道。眼下，你只能祈祷一切顺利，保持沉默。大多数人都会这样做。他们希望这次让步能平息对方的怒火，让他们不再提出更多要求。有时这种方法奏效，但更多时候却以失败告终。英国首相内维尔·张伯伦在1938年就是这样应对希特勒的谈判策略的。张伯伦以为已经达成协议后，希特勒却提高了要求。在慕尼黑，为了避免战争，张伯伦选择了妥协。一年后，第二次世界大战爆发了。

The second common response is to respond in kind. If they start outrageously high, you start outrageously low. If they are deceptive, so are you. If they make threats, you make counter-threats. If they lock themselves into their position, you lock yourself even more tightly into yours. In the end either one party yields or, all too often, negotiation breaks off.

第二种常见的应对方式是以其人之道还治其人之身。如果他们一开始就开出天价，你就开出天价。如果他们耍花招，你也一样。如果他们威胁你，你就以牙还牙。如果他们固执己见，你就更加坚定自己的立场。最终，要么一方让步，要么——这种情况屡见不鲜——谈判破裂。

Such tricky tactics are illegitimate because they fail the test of reciprocity. They are designed to be used by only one side; the other side is not supposed to know the tactics or is expected to tolerate them knowingly. Earlier we argued that an effective counter to a one-sided substantive proposal is to examine the legitimacy of the principle that the proposal reflects. Tricky bargaining tactics are in effect one-sided proposals about negotiating procedure, about the negotiating game that the parties are going to play. To counter them, you will want to engage in principled negotiation about the negotiating process.

这种狡猾的策略是不合法的，因为它违背了互惠原则。这些策略的设计初衷只是为了让一方使用；另一方要么不应该知晓这些策略，要么应该明知故犯地容忍它们。我们之前已经论证过，应对片面的实质性提议的有效方法是检验该提议所体现的原则是否合法。狡猾的谈判策略实际上是关于谈判程序、关于双方将要进行的谈判游戏的片面提议。为了应对这些策略，你需要就谈判过程展开有原则的谈判。

How do you negotiate about the rules of the game?

如何就游戏规则进行谈判？

There are three steps in negotiating the rules of the negotiating game where the other side seems to be using a tricky tactic: recognize the tactic, raise the issue explicitly, and question the tactic’s legitimacy and desirability—negotiate over it.

在谈判中，如果对方似乎使用了狡猾的策略，那么在谈判规则的协商过程中，有三个步骤：识别策略、明确提出问题、质疑策略的合法性和合理性——并就此进行谈判。

You have to know what is going on to be able to do something about it. Learn to spot particular ploys that indicate deception, those designed to make you uncomfortable, and those that lock the other side into their position. Often just recognizing a tactic will neutralize it. Realizing, for example, that the other side is attacking you personally to impair your judgment may well frustrate the effort.

你必须了解事情的来龙去脉才能有所作为。学会识别那些表明欺骗的伎俩、那些旨在让你感到不舒服的伎俩，以及那些让对方陷入被动局面的伎俩。通常，仅仅识别出某种策略就能化解它。例如，意识到对方正在对你进行人身攻击以削弱你的判断力，很可能就会挫败他们的阴谋。

After recognizing the tactic, consider bringing it up with the other side. “Say, Joe, I may be totally mistaken, but I’m getting the feeling that you and Ted here are playing a good-guy/bad-guy routine. If you two want a recess any time to straighten out differences between you, just ask.” Discussing the tactic not only makes it less effective, it also may cause the other side to worry about alienating you completely. Simply raising a question about a tactic may be enough to get them to stop using it.

识别出对方的策略后，不妨和对方谈谈。“乔，我可能完全搞错了，但我感觉你和泰德好像在玩正邪对立的游戏。如果你们俩想找个时间解决一下分歧，尽管开口。” 讨论这种策略不仅能降低其效果，还能让对方担心彻底疏远你。仅仅提出一个关于这种策略的问题，就足以让他们停止使用。

The most important purpose of bringing the tactic up explicitly, however, is to give you an opportunity to negotiate about the rules of the game. This is the third step. This negotiation focuses on procedure instead of substance, but the goal remains to produce a wise agreement (this time about procedure) efficiently and amicably. Not surprisingly, the method remains the same.

然而，明确提出这一策略最重要的目的在于，让你有机会就游戏规则进行谈判。这是第三步。此次谈判的重点在于程序而非实质内容，但目标仍然是高效友好地达成一项明智的协议（这次是关于程序的协议）。不出所料，方法依然不变。

Separate the people from the problem. Don’t attack people personally for using a tactic you consider illegitimate. If they get defensive it may be more difficult for them to give up the tactic, and they may be left with a residue of anger that will fester and interfere with other issues. Question the tactic, not their personal integrity. Rather than saying, “You deliberately put me here facing the sun,” attack the problem: “I am finding the sun in my eyes quite distracting. Unless we can solve the problem, I may have to leave early to get some rest. Shall we revise the schedule?” It will be easier to reform the negotiating process than to reform those with whom you are dealing. Don’t be diverted from the negotiation by the urge to teach them a lesson.

将人与问题分开来看。不要因为对方使用了你认为不正当的策略而进行人身攻击。如果他们采取防御姿态，就更难放弃这种策略，而且他们心中可能还会残留愤怒，这种愤怒会不断滋生，影响到其他问题。质疑的是策略本身，而不是他们的人格。与其说“你故意让我面对着太阳”，不如针对问题本身展开讨论：“阳光刺眼，让我很分心。如果我们不能解决这个问题，我可能得提前离开休息一下。我们修改一下日程安排好吗？” 改革谈判流程远比改变谈判对象容易得多。不要因为想要教训对方而偏离谈判的重点。

Focus on interests, not positions. “Why are you committing yourself in the press to an extreme position? Are you trying to protect yourself from criticism? Or are you protecting yourself from changing your position? Is it in our mutual interest to have both of us use this tactic?”

关注利益，而非立场。“你为什么要在媒体上公开表明极端立场？你是想保护自己免受批评吗？还是想阻止自己改变立场？我们双方都采取这种策略，对我们双方都有利吗？”

Invent options for mutual gain. Suggest alternative games to play. “How about our undertaking to make no statements to the press until we reach agreement or break off the talks?”

寻找互利共赢的方案。提出其他可行的谈判策略。“我们不妨承诺，在达成协议或中止谈判之前，不向媒体发表任何声明？”

Insist on using objective criteria. Above all, be hard on principle. “Is there a theory behind having me sit in the low chair with my back to the open door?” Try out the principle of reciprocity on them. “I assume that you will sit in this chair tomorrow morning?” Frame the principle behind each tactic as a proposed “rule” for the game. “Shall we alternate spilling coffee on one another day by day?”

坚持使用客观标准。最重要的是，要严格遵守原则。“让我背对着敞开的门坐在矮椅上，这背后有什么理论依据吗？” 试试用互惠原则来反驳他们。“我假设你明天早上也会坐在这把椅子上？” 将每项策略背后的原则包装成游戏的“规则”。“我们是不是应该每天轮流把咖啡洒在对方身上？”

As a last resort, turn to your BATNA (your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement) and walk out. “It’s my impression that you’re not interested in negotiating in a way that we both think will produce results. Here’s my phone number. If I’m mistaken, I’m ready any time you are. Until then, we’ll pursue the court option.” If you are walking out on clearly legitimate grounds, as when they have deliberately deceived you about facts or their authority, and if they are genuinely interested in an agreement, they are likely to call you back to the table.

如果以上方法都行不通，那就采取你的BATNA（最佳替代方案），直接离开。“我的感觉是，你们似乎对以我们双方都认为能达成协议的方式进行谈判没有兴趣。这是我的电话号码。如果我弄错了，我随时准备接听。在此之前，我们将诉诸法律途径。” 如果你离开的理由非常正当，例如对方故意隐瞒事实或篡改权限，而且对方真心想要达成协议，他们很可能会邀请你回到谈判桌前。

Some common tricky tactics

一些常见的狡猾伎俩

Tricky tactics can be divided into three categories: deliberate deception, psychological warfare, and positional pressure tactics. You should be prepared to deal with all three. Below are a number of common examples of each type; for each in turn, we show how principled negotiation might be applied to counter it.

狡猾的策略可以分为三类：蓄意欺骗、心理战和立场施压策略。你应该做好应对这三种策略的准备。以下列举了每种策略的一些常见例子；我们将逐一说明如何运用原则性谈判来应对。

Deliberate deception

蓄意欺骗

Perhaps the most common form of dirty trick is misrepresentation about facts, authority, or intentions.

最常见的卑鄙伎俩或许就是歪曲事实、权威或意图。

Phony facts. The oldest form of negotiating trickery is to make some knowingly false statement: “This car was driven only 5,000 miles by a little old lady from Pasadena who never went over 35 miles per hour.” The dangers of being taken in by false statements are great. What can you do?

虚假事实。谈判中最古老的伎俩之一就是故意捏造事实：“这辆车只开了5000英里，是一位来自帕萨迪纳的老太太开的，而且她开车从没超过每小时35英里。” 被虚假陈述蒙蔽的危险性极大。那么，我们该如何防范呢？

Disentangle the people from the problem. Unless you have good reason to trust somebody, don’t. This does not mean calling him a liar; rather it means making the negotiation proceed independent of trust. Do not let someone treat your doubts as a personal attack. No seller is likely to give you a watch or a car simply in exchange for your statement that you have money in the bank. Just as a seller will routinely check on your credit (“because there are so many other people around that can’t be trusted”), you can do the same for statements of the other side. A practice of verifying factual assertions reduces the incentive for deception, and your risk of being cheated.

将人与问题区分开来。除非你有充分的理由信任某人，否则不要轻易相信。这并非意味着指责对方撒谎，而是意味着谈判应独立于信任之外进行。不要让任何人将你的疑虑视为人身攻击。没有哪个卖家会仅仅因为你声称自己银行账户里有存款就给你一块手表或一辆车。正如卖家会例行检查你的信用记录（“因为周围有太多不可信的人”），你也可以对对方的说法进行同样的核实。核实事实陈述的做法可以降低对方欺骗的动机，也能降低你被骗的风险。

Ambiguous authority. The other side may allow you to believe that they, like you, have full authority to compromise when they don’t. After they have pressed you as hard as they can and you have worked out what you believe to be a firm agreement, they announce that they must take it to someone else for approval. This technique is designed to give them a “second bite at the apple.”

权限模糊。对方可能会让你误以为他们和你一样拥有完全的妥协权限，而实际上并非如此。在他们竭尽全力向你施压，而你也达成了你认为已经稳妥的协议之后，他们会突然宣布必须提交给其他人审批。这种伎俩旨在让他们有机会“再试一次”。

This is a bad situation to fall into. If only you have authority to make concessions, only you will make concessions.

这是一种糟糕的处境。如果只有你拥有做出让步的权力，那么也只有你会做出让步。

Do not assume that the other side has full authority just because they are there negotiating with you. An insurance adjuster, a lawyer, or a salesperson may allow you to think that your flexibility is being matched by flexibility on their side. You may later find that what you thought was an agreement will be treated by the other side as simply a floor for further negotiation.

不要因为对方在场与你谈判就想当然地认为他们拥有绝对的权威。保险理赔员、律师或销售人员可能会让你误以为他们的灵活性与你的灵活性相匹配。但你之后可能会发现，你以为达成的协议，在对方看来仅仅是进一步谈判的底线。

Before starting on any give-and-take, find out about the authority on the other side. It is perfectly legitimate to inquire, “Just how much authority do you have in this particular negotiation?” If the answer is ambiguous, you may wish to talk to someone with real authority or to make clear that you on your side are reserving equal freedom to reconsider any point.

在开始任何谈判之前，务必先了解对方的权限。完全可以询问：“在这次谈判中，你们究竟拥有多大的权限？”如果答案含糊不清，你可能需要与真正有权限的人沟通，或者明确表示你方也保留重新考虑任何要点的同等权利。

If they do announce unexpectedly that they are treating what you thought was an agreement as a basis for further negotiation, insist on reciprocity. “All right. We will treat it as a joint draft to which neither side is committed. You check with your boss and I’ll sleep on it and see if I come up with any changes I want to suggest tomorrow.” Or you might say, “If your boss approves this draft tomorrow, I’ll stick by it. Otherwise each of us should feel free to propose changes.”

如果他们出人意料地宣布，他们要将你以为已经达成的协议作为进一步谈判的基础，那就坚持对等原则。“好的。我们就把它当作一份双方共同起草的草案，双方都不承担任何义务。你跟你的老板确认一下，我考虑一下，看看明天有没有什么修改意见。”或者你可以说：“如果你的老板明天批准了这个草案，我就坚持执行。否则，我们双方都可以自由地提出修改意见。”

One way to try to head off this problem is to clarify early in the negotiation that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed,” so that any effort to reopen one issue automatically reopens all issues.

避免出现此问题的一个方法是在谈判初期就明确“所有问题都必须达成一致才能算达成一致”，这样任何重新讨论一个问题的努力都会自动重新讨论所有问题。

Dubious intentions. Where the issue is one of possible misrepresentation of their intention to comply with the agreement, it is often possible to build compliance features into the agreement itself.

动机可疑。如果问题在于对方可能虚假陈述其遵守协议的意图，通常可以在协议本身中加入合规条款。

Suppose you are a lawyer representing the wife in a divorce negotiation. Your client does not believe her husband will pay child support even though he may agree to do so. The time and energy spent in going to court every month may lead her to give up the effort. What can you do? Make the problem explicit and use their protestations to get a guarantee. You could say to the husband’s lawyer, “Look, my client is afraid those child support payments simply aren’t going to be made. Rather than monthly payments, how about giving her equity in the house?” The husband’s lawyer may say, “My client is perfectly trustworthy. We’ll put it in writing that he will pay child support regularly.” To which you might respond, “It’s not a matter of trust. Are you certain that your client will pay?”

假设您是一位律师，代表妻子进行离婚谈判。您的委托人并不相信她的丈夫会支付子女抚养费，即使他可能同意支付。每月出庭耗费的时间和精力可能会让她放弃。您该怎么办？明确指出问题所在，并利用对方的辩解来争取保证。您可以对丈夫的律师说：“我的委托人担心这些子女抚养费根本不会支付。与其每月支付，不如把房子的一部分给她？”丈夫的律师可能会说：“我的委托人绝对值得信赖。我们会以书面形式保证他会定期支付子女抚养费。”对此，您可以回应道：“这不是信任的问题。您确定您的委托人会支付吗？”

“Of course.”

“当然。”

“A hundred percent certain?”

“百分之百确定吗？”

“Yes, I’m a hundred percent certain.”

“是的，我百分之百确定。”

“Then you won’t mind a contingent agreement. Your client will agree to make child support payments. We’ll provide that if, for some inexplicable reason that you estimate at zero percent probability, he misses two payments, my client will get the equity in the house (minus, of course, the amount your client has already paid out in child support) and your client will no longer be liable for child support.” It is not easy for the husband’s lawyer to object.

“那么您应该不介意附带条件的协议。您的委托人同意支付子女抚养费。我们则规定，如果由于某种您认为概率为零的不可解释的原因，他拖欠了两次抚养费，那么我的委托人将获得房屋的净值（当然，要扣除您的委托人已经支付的子女抚养费），而您的委托人将不再承担子女抚养费的支付义务。” 丈夫的律师很难提出异议。

Less than full disclosure is not the same as deception. Deliberate deception as to facts or one’s intentions is quite different from not fully disclosing one’s present thinking. Good faith negotiation does not require total disclosure. Perhaps the best answer to questions such as “What is the most you would pay if you had to?” would be along the following lines: “Let’s not put ourselves under such a strong temptation to mislead. If you think no agreement is possible, and that we may be wasting our time, perhaps we could disclose our thinking to some trustworthy third party, who can then tell us whether there is a zone of potential agreement.” In this way it is possible to behave with full candor about information that is not being disclosed.

信息披露不完全并不等同于欺骗。故意隐瞒事实或意图与不完全披露当前想法截然不同。真诚的谈判并不要求完全披露。对于诸如“如果必须的话，你最多愿意支付多少钱？”这类问题，或许最好的回答是这样的：“我们不要让自己陷入误导的强烈诱惑。如果你认为无法达成协议，我们可能是在浪费时间，或许我们可以将我们的想法告知一位值得信赖的第三方，让他/她告诉我们是否存在达成协议的可能性。” 这样，即使有些信息没有披露，我们也能坦诚相待。

Psychological warfare

心理战

These tactics are designed to make you feel uncomfortable, so that you will have a subconscious desire to end the negotiation as soon as possible.

这些策略旨在让你感到不舒服，从而让你在潜意识里想要尽快结束谈判。

Stressful situations. Much has been written about the physical circumstances in which negotiations take place. You should be sensitive to such modest questions as whether a meeting takes place at your place or theirs, or on neutral territory. Contrary to the accepted wisdom, it is sometimes advantageous to accept an offer to meet on the other side’s turf. It may put them at ease, making them more open to your suggestions. If necessary, it will be easier for you to walk out. If, however, you do allow the other side to choose the physical environment, be aware of what that choice is and what effects it may have.

压力情境。关于谈判的实际环境，已有大量著述。你应该关注一些看似无关紧要的问题，例如会面是在你方、对方还是中立场地进行。与普遍认知相反，有时接受对方提出的在对方地盘会面的提议反而更有利。这或许能让对方感到放松，更容易接受你的建议。如有必要，你也能更轻松地退出谈判。但是，如果你允许对方选择会面地点，务必了解对方的选择及其可能带来的影响。

Ask yourself if you feel under stress, and if so, why. If the room is too noisy, if the temperature is too hot or cold, if there is no place for a private caucus with a colleague, be aware that the setting might have been deliberately designed to make you want to conclude negotiations promptly and, if necessary, to yield points to do so.

问问自己是否感到压力，如果有，原因是什么。如果房间太吵闹，温度太高或太低，或者没有地方可以和同事进行私下会谈，那么就要意识到，这种环境可能是故意设计的，目的是让你想要尽快结束谈判，必要时甚至做出让步。

If you find the physical surroundings prejudicial, do not hesitate to say so. You can suggest changing chairs, taking a break, or adjourning to a different location or another time. In every case your job is to identify the problem, be willing to raise it with the other side, and then negotiate better physical circumstances in an objective and principled fashion.

如果您觉得周围环境不理想，请毫不犹豫地提出。您可以建议换个座位、休息一下，或者改期到其他地点进行。无论如何，您的任务都是找出问题所在，主动与对方沟通，然后以客观、有原则的方式协商改善环境。

Personal attacks. In addition to manipulating the physical environment, there are also ways for the other side to use verbal and nonverbal communication to make you feel uncomfortable. They can comment on your clothes or your appearance. “Looks like you were up all night. Things not going well at the office?” They can attack your status by making you wait for them or by interrupting the negotiations to deal with other people. They can imply that you are ignorant. They can refuse to listen to you and make you repeat yourself. They can deliberately refuse to make eye contact with you. (Simple experiments with students have confirmed the malaise many feel when this tactic is used, and they are unable to identify the cause of the problem.) In each case recognizing the tactic will help nullify its effect; bringing it up explicitly will probably prevent a recurrence.

人身攻击。除了操纵物理环境外，对方还会利用言语和非言语沟通方式让你感到不舒服。他们会评论你的衣着或外貌。“你看起来熬了一整夜。办公室里是不是出了什么事？”他们可能会让你等他们，或者打断谈判去和其他人交谈，以此来贬低你的地位。他们会暗示你无知。他们会拒绝倾听你的话，让你重复。他们甚至会故意回避与你的眼神交流。（针对学生的简单实验证实，许多人在使用这种策略时都会感到不适，但他们却无法找到问题的根源。）无论哪种情况，识别出这种策略都有助于消除其影响；明确地指出问题所在，则很可能防止其再次发生。

The good-guy/bad-guy routine. One form of psychological pressure that also involves deception is the good-guy/bad-guy routine. This technique appears in its starkest form in old police movies. The first policeman threatens the suspect with prosecution for numerous crimes, puts him under a bright light, pushes him around, then finally takes a break and leaves. The good guy then turns off the light, offers the suspect a cigarette, and apologizes for the tough policeman. He says he’d like to control the tough guy, but he can’t unless the suspect cooperates. The result: the suspect tells all he knows.

正邪对立的套路。一种涉及欺骗的心理施压手段就是正邪对立的套路。这种技巧在老式警匪片中表现得最为典型。第一个警察威胁嫌疑人要以多项罪名起诉，把他放在强光下，推搡他，最后休息片刻后离开。这时，好人关掉灯，递给嫌疑人一支烟，并为刚才那个严厉的警察道歉。他说他想控制住那个“狠角色”，但除非嫌疑人配合，否则他做不到。结果：嫌疑人供出了他所知道的一切。

Similarly in a negotiation, two people on the same side will stage a quarrel. One will take a tough stand: “This business is worth $80,000 and I won’t accept a penny less.” His partner looks pained and a little embarrassed. Finally he breaks in: “Frank, you are being unreasonable. After all, cash flow is a little down, even if receivables are strong.” Turning to the other side, he says reasonably, “Could you pay $76,000?” The concession isn’t large, but it almost seems like a favor.

同样，在谈判中，同一方的两个人也会争吵。其中一人会态度强硬：“这笔生意值8万美元，我一分钱都不会少。”他的同伴看起来很痛苦，也有些尴尬。最后，他插话道：“弗兰克，你太不讲理了。毕竟，即使应收账款充足，现金流也有些紧张。”他转向对方，理智地问道：“你能出7.6万美元吗？”这个让步虽然不大，但几乎就像是帮了对方一个忙。

The good-guy/bad-guy routine is a form of psychological manipulation. If you recognize it, you won’t be taken in. When the good guy makes his pitch, just ask him the same question you asked the bad guy: “I appreciate that you are trying to be reasonable, and I still want to know why you think that’s a fair price. What is your principle? I am prepared to pay $80,000 if you can persuade me it’s the fairest price.”

正邪对立是一种心理操纵手段。如果你能识破这种伎俩，就不会上当。当“好人”提出条件时，你只需问他和“坏人”一样的问题：“我很欣赏你试图讲道理，但我还是想知道你为什么认为这个价格合理。你的原则是什么？如果你能说服我这是最公平的价格，我愿意支付8万美元。”

Threats. Threats are one of the most abused tactics in negotiation. A threat seems easy to make—much easier than an offer. All it takes is a few words, and if it works, you never have to carry it out. But threats can lead to counterthreats in an escalating spiral that can unhinge a negotiation and even destroy a relationship.

威胁。威胁是谈判中最常被滥用的策略之一。发出威胁似乎很容易——远比提出报价容易得多。只需几句话，如果奏效，你甚至不必真的去兑现。但威胁会引发反威胁，形成恶性循环，最终可能导致谈判破裂，甚至摧毁彼此的关系。

Threats are pressure. Pressure often accomplishes just the opposite of what it is intended to do; it builds up pressure the other way. Instead of making a decision easier for the other side, it often makes it more difficult. In response to outside pressure, a union, a committee, a company, or a government may close ranks. Moderates and hawks join together to resist what they may perceive as an illegitimate attempt to coerce them. The question changes from “Should we make this decision?” to “Shall we cave in to outside pressure?”

威胁即压力。压力往往适得其反，反而会加剧对方的压力。它非但不会让对方更容易做出决定，反而常常使之更加困难。面对外部压力，工会、委员会、公司或政府可能会团结一致。温和派和鹰派会联合起来，抵制他们认为的非法胁迫。问题也从“我们是否应该做出这个决定？”变成了“我们是否应该屈服于外部压力？”

Good negotiators rarely resort to threats. They do not need to; there are other ways to communicate the same information. If it seems appropriate to outline the consequences of the other side’s action, suggest those that will occur independently of your will rather than those you could choose to bring about. Warnings are much more legitimate than threats and are not vulnerable to counterthreats: “Should we fail to reach agreement, it seems highly probable to me that the news media would insist on publishing the whole sordid story. In a matter of this much public interest, I don’t see how we could legitimately or realistically suppress information. Do you?”

优秀的谈判者很少诉诸威胁。他们无需如此；还有其他方法可以传达相同的信息。如果认为有必要阐明对方行为的后果，应强调那些并非出于你的意愿而发生的后果，而不是那些你可以选择促成的后果。警告远比威胁更合理，也不容易被反威胁所抵消：“如果我们未能达成协议，我认为新闻媒体很可能会坚持报道整个丑闻。在如此重大的公共利益事件上，我看不出我们如何才能合法或现实地压制信息。您觉得呢？”

You can also warn the other side about your likely actions in the event of no agreement, so long as you can show how those actions are intended to safeguard your interests, not to coerce or punish the other side. “So you are not surprised, here is a draft of the press release we plan to issue if our contract is not renewed.” If the other side finds this prospect unpleasant, they may react by asking, “Are you threatening me?” Provided your plans are a true warning, you should be able to reply confidently, “Absolutely not. In our shoes, would you recommend a better way to safeguard our interests?”

只要你能证明这些行动是为了维护自身利益，而非胁迫或惩罚对方，你还可以提前告知对方在无法达成协议的情况下你可能采取的行动。“为了避免你感到意外，这是我们计划在合同未续签的情况下发布的新闻稿草稿。”如果对方对此感到不适，可能会问：“你是在威胁我吗？”只要你的计划确实是在发出警告，你就可以自信地回答：“绝对不是。如果你处在我们的位置，你会建议我们采取更好的方式来维护自身利益吗？”

For threats to be effective they must be credibly communicated. Sometimes you can interfere with the communication process. You can ignore threats; you can take them as unauthorized, spoken in haste, or simply irrelevant. You can also make it risky to communicate them. At a coal mine where one of the authors was recently mediating, a large number of false but costly bomb threats were being received. These dropped off dramatically when the company’s receptionist began answering all phone calls with “Your voice is being recorded. What number are you calling?”

威胁要想奏效，必须以可信的方式传达。有时，你可以干扰沟通过程。你可以忽略威胁；你可以认为威胁未经授权、仓促说出，或者根本无关紧要。你也可以让传达威胁变得危险。最近，一位作者曾调解过一个煤矿的纠纷，那里收到了大量虚假但代价高昂的炸弹威胁。当公司前台开始用“您的声音正在被录音。请问您要拨打哪个号码？”来接听所有电话后，这些威胁的数量急剧下降。

Sometimes threats can be turned to your political advantage. A union could announce to the press: “Management has such a weak case that they are resorting to threats.” Perhaps the best response to a threat, however, is to be principled. “We have prepared a sequence of countermoves for each of management’s customary threats. However, we have delayed taking action until we see whether we can agree that making threats is not the most constructive activity we could engage in just now.” Or “I only negotiate on the merits. My reputation is built on not responding to threats.”

有时，威胁可以转化为政治优势。工会可以向媒体宣布：“资方的论点如此站不住脚，以至于他们诉诸威胁。”然而，应对威胁的最佳方式或许是坚持原则。“我们针对资方惯用的威胁，已经制定了一系列反制措施。但是，我们暂缓采取行动，直到我们达成共识：发出威胁并非目前最具建设性的做法。”或者，“我只就事论事地进行谈判。我的声誉建立在不回应威胁的基础之上。”

Positional pressure tactics

位置压力战术

This kind of bargaining tactic is designed to structure the situation so that only one side can effectively make concessions.

这种谈判策略旨在构建一种局面，使只有一方能够有效地做出让步。

Refusal to negotiate. When the American diplomats and embassy personnel were taken hostage in Tehran in November 1979, the Iranian government announced its demands and refused to negotiate. A lawyer will often do the same, simply telling opposing counsel, “I’ll see you in court.” What can you do when the other side refuses to negotiate altogether?

拒绝谈判。1979年11月，美国外交官和使馆人员在德黑兰被扣为人质时，伊朗政府宣布了其要求并拒绝谈判。律师通常也会这样做，只是简单地告诉对方律师：“法庭见。” 如果对方完全拒绝谈判，你该怎么办？

First, recognize the tactic as a possible negotiating ploy: an attempt to use their entry into negotiation as a bargaining chip to obtain some concession on substance. A variant on this ploy is to set preconditions for negotiations.

首先，要认识到这种策略可能是一种谈判伎俩：他们试图利用参与谈判作为筹码，以期在实质性问题上获得一些让步。这种伎俩的一种变体是为谈判设定前提条件。

Second, talk about their refusal to negotiate. Communicate either directly or through third parties. Don’t attack them for refusing to negotiate, but rather find out their interests in not negotiating. Are they worried about giving you status by talking to you? Will those who talk with you be criticized for being “soft”? Do they think negotiation will destroy their precarious internal unity? Or do they simply not believe that an agreement is possible?

其次，谈谈他们拒绝谈判的原因。可以直接沟通，也可以通过第三方沟通。不要攻击他们拒绝谈判，而是要弄清楚他们不愿谈判的原因。他们是否担心与你谈判会提升你的地位？与你谈判的人是否会被批评为“软弱”？他们是否认为谈判会破坏他们岌岌可危的内部团结？或者他们根本不相信能够达成协议？

Suggest some options, such as negotiating through third parties, sending letters, or encouraging private individuals like journalists to discuss the issues (as happened in the Iranian case).

建议采取一些措施，例如通过第三方进行谈判、发送信件，或者鼓励记者等私人人士讨论这些问题（就像伊朗案例中发生的那样）。

Finally, insist on using principles. Is this the way they would want you to play? Do they want you to set preconditions as well? Will they want others to refuse to negotiate with them? What are the principles they think should apply to this situation?

最后，坚持运用原则。他们希望你这样做吗？他们是否也希望你设定前提条件？他们是否希望其他人拒绝与他们谈判？他们认为哪些原则应该适用于这种情况？

Extreme demands. Negotiators will frequently start with extreme proposals like offering $175,000 for your house that is apparently worth $300,000. The goal is to lower your expectations. They also figure that an extreme initial position will give them a better end result, on the theory that the parties will ultimately end up splitting the difference between their positions. There are drawbacks to this approach, even for tricky bargainers. Making an extreme demand that both you and they know will be abandoned undermines their credibility. Such an opening may also kill the deal; if they offer too little, you may think they are not worth bothering with.

极端要求。谈判者经常会提出一些极端的报价，比如他们可能只出价17.5万美元购买你那套价值30万美元的房子。他们的目的是降低你的预期。他们认为，一开始就提出极端的条件，最终会让他们获得更好的结果，因为他们相信双方最终会各让一步。然而，即使对于老练的谈判者来说，这种方法也有弊端。提出一个双方都知道最终会被放弃的极端要求，会损害他们的信誉。这样的开场白甚至可能导致交易失败；如果他们给出的报价太低，你可能会觉得他们根本不值得你费心。

Bringing the tactic to their attention works well here. Ask for principled justification of their position until it looks ridiculous even to them.

把这种策略摆在他们面前很有效。要求他们从原则上证明自己的立场，直到连他们自己都觉得荒谬可笑为止。

Escalating demands. A negotiator may raise one of his demands for every concession he makes on another. He may also reopen issues you thought had been settled. The benefits of this tactic lie in decreasing the overall concession, and in the psychological effect of making you want to agree quickly before he raises any more of his demands.

不断升级的要求。谈判者可能会为了在某一方面做出让步而提高另一项要求。他甚至可能重新提出你认为已经解决的问题。这种策略的好处在于减少整体让步幅度，以及通过心理战让你在他提出更多要求之前尽快同意。

The Prime Minister of Malta used this tactic in negotiating with Great Britain in 1971 over the price of naval and air base rights. Each time the British thought they had an agreement, he would say, “Yes, agreed, but there is still one small problem.” And the small problem would turn out to be a £10 million cash advance or guaranteed jobs for dockyard and base workers for the life of the contract.

马耳他总理在1971年与英国就海军和空军基地使用权价格进行谈判时就使用了这种策略。每次英国人以为达成协议时，他都会说：“是的，同意了，但还有一个小问题。”而这个小问题最终往往是1000万英镑的预付款，或者是在合同有效期内保证船坞和基地工人的就业。

When you recognize this, call it to their attention and then perhaps take a break while you consider whether and on what basis you want to continue negotiations. This avoids an impulsive reaction while indicating the seriousness of their conduct. And again, insist on principle. When you come back, anyone interested in settlement will be more serious.

当你意识到这一点时，要提醒对方，然后或许可以暂停一下，思考是否以及在什么基础上继续谈判。这样做既能避免冲动行事，又能表明对方行为的严重性。再次强调，要坚持原则。当你回来时，任何真心想解决问题的人都会更加认真。

Lock-in tactics. This tactic is illustrated by Thomas Schelling’s well-known example of two dynamite trucks barreling toward each other on a single-lane road. The question becomes which truck goes off the road to avoid an accident. As the trucks near each other, one driver in full view of the other pulls off his steering wheel and throws it out the window. Seeing this, the other driver has a choice between an explosive crash or driving his truck off the road into a ditch. This is an example of an extreme commitment tactic designed to make it impossible to yield. Paradoxically, you strengthen your bargaining position by weakening your control over the situation.

锁定策略。托马斯·谢林著名的例子生动地阐释了这种策略：两辆装满炸药的卡车在一条单行道上疾驰而来。问题在于，哪辆卡车会驶离道路以避免碰撞。当两辆卡车接近时，其中一辆卡车的司机在另一辆卡车的众目睽睽之下，扯下方向盘扔出窗外。看到这一幕，另一辆卡车的司机面临着两个选择：要么发生爆炸性的碰撞，要么将卡车开到路边的沟里。这是一个极端承诺策略的例子，旨在使对方无法做出让步。矛盾的是，你通过削弱自己对局势的控制，反而增强了自身的谈判地位。

In labor-management and international negotiations this tactic is common. A union president makes a rousing speech to her constituency pledging that she will never accept less than a 15 percent salary increase. Since she stands to lose face and credibility if she does agree to anything less, she can more convincingly persuade management the union must have 15 percent.

在劳资谈判和国际谈判中，这种策略很常见。工会主席会向其成员发表慷慨激昂的演讲，承诺绝不接受低于15%的加薪幅度。由于如果她同意低于这个幅度，就会颜面尽失，信誉扫地，因此她可以更有力地说服管理层，工会必须争取15%的加薪。

But lock-in tactics are gambles. You may call the other side’s bluff and force them to make a concession, which they will then have to explain to their constituency.

但这种锁定策略是赌博。你可能会识破对方的虚张声势，迫使他们做出让步，而他们之后就不得不向自己的支持者解释。

Like threats, lock-in tactics depend on communication. If the other truck driver does not see the steering wheel fly out the window, or if he thinks the truck has an emergency steering mechanism, the act of throwing the steering wheel out the window will not have its intended effect. The pressure to avoid a collision will be felt equally by both drivers.

与威胁一样，锁定战术也依赖于沟通。如果另一位卡车司机没有看到方向盘飞出车窗，或者他认为卡车配备了紧急转向装置，那么将方向盘扔出车窗的行为就不会达到预期效果。避免碰撞的压力将由双方司机共同承担。

In response to a commitment tactic, therefore, you may be able to interrupt the communication. You can so interpret the commitment as to weaken it. “Oh, I see. You told the papers your goal was to settle for $400,000. Well, we all have our aspirations, I guess. Do you want to know what mine are?” Alternatively, you can crack a joke and not take the lock-in seriously.

因此，面对对方的承诺策略，你可以尝试打断对方的沟通。你可以对承诺进行解读，从而削弱其效力。“哦，我明白了。你告诉媒体你的目标是40万美元和解。好吧，我想我们每个人都有自己的目标。你想知道我的目标是什么吗？”或者，你也可以开个玩笑，不要把对方的承诺当回事。

You can also resist lock-ins on principle: “Fine, Bob, I understand you made that statement publicly. But my practice is never to yield to pressure, only to reason. Now let’s talk about the merits of the problem.” Whatever you do, avoid making the commitment a central question. Deemphasize it so that the other side can more gracefully back down.

你也可以从原则上抵制这种僵局：“好的，鲍勃，我知道你公开发表了那份声明。但我的原则是绝不屈服于压力，只讲道理。现在我们来谈谈问题的实质。”无论如何，都要避免把承诺作为核心问题。淡化它的重要性，这样对方才能更体面地让步。

Hardhearted partner. Perhaps the most common negotiating tactic used to justify not yielding to your requests is for the other negotiator to say that he personally would have no objection, but his hardhearted partner will not let him. “It’s a perfectly reasonable request, I agree. But my boss absolutely refuses to hear of it.”

铁石心肠的伙伴。谈判中最常见的拒绝你要求的策略或许就是，对方会说他个人并不反对，但他铁石心肠的伙伴绝不让他妥协。“我承认，这完全合情合理。但我老板坚决不肯接受。”

Recognize the tactic. Rather than discussing it with the other negotiator, you may want to get his agreement to the principle involved—perhaps in writing—and then if possible speak directly with the “hardhearted partner.”

要认清这种策略。与其与对方谈判者讨论，不如先让他同意所涉及的原则——最好以书面形式——然后如果可能的话，直接与这位“铁石心肠的伙伴”交谈。

A calculated delay. Frequently one side will try to postpone coming to a decision until a time they think favorable. Labor negotiators will often delay until the last few hours before a strike deadline, relying on the psychological pressure of the deadline to make management more malleable. Unfortunately, they often miscalculate and the strike deadline passes. Once the strike begins, management, in turn, may decide to wait for a more favorable time, such as when the union’s strike fund has run out. Waiting for the right time is a high-cost game.

精心策划的拖延。通常情况下，一方会试图推迟做出决定，直到他们认为有利的时机。劳资谈判代表常常拖到罢工截止日期前的最后几个小时，指望利用截止日期带来的心理压力迫使管理层妥协。然而，他们往往判断失误，罢工截止日期最终还是过去了。一旦罢工开始，管理层反过来可能会选择等待更有利的时机，例如工会的罢工资金耗尽之时。等待所谓的“最佳时机”代价高昂。

In addition to making delaying tactics explicit and negotiating about them, consider creating a fading opportunity for the other side. If you represent one company negotiating a merger with another, start talks with a third company, exploring the possibility of merging with them instead. Look for objective conditions that can be used to establish credible deadlines, such as the date on which taxes are due, the annual trustees meeting, the end of the contract, or the end of the legislative session.

除了明确拖延战术并就此进行谈判之外，还可以考虑为对方创造机会，但这种机会正在逐渐消失。例如，如果您代表一家公司与另一家公司进行合并谈判，不妨先与第三家公司展开对话，探讨与其合并的可能性。寻找可以用来设定可信截止日期的客观条件，例如税款缴纳截止日期、年度董事会会议日期、合同到期日或立法会议结束日期。

“Take it or leave it.” There is nothing inherently wrong with confronting the other side with a firm choice. In fact, most American business is conducted this way. If you go into a supermarket and see a can of beans marked $1.50, you don’t normally try to negotiate with the supermarket manager. This is an efficient method of conducting business, but it is not negotiation. It is not interactive decision-making. Nor is there anything wrong after long negotiations to conclude them when you mean to do so by saying, “Take it or leave it,” except that you should probably phrase it more politely.

“要么接受，要么放弃。” 用坚定的立场面对对方，这本身并没有错。事实上，大多数美国商业活动都是这样进行的。如果你走进超市，看到一罐豆子标价1.5美元，你通常不会试图和超市经理讨价还价。这是一种高效的商业模式，但这并非谈判，也并非互动式决策。同样，在漫长的谈判结束后，如果你想结束谈判，用“要么接受，要么放弃”来表达也无可厚非，只是措辞可能要更礼貌一些。

As an alternative to explicitly recognizing the “Take it or leave it” tactic and negotiating about it, consider ignoring it at first. Keep talking as if you didn’t hear it, or change the subject, perhaps by introducing other solutions. If you do bring up the tactic specifically, let them know what they have to lose if no agreement is reached and look for a face-saving way, such as a change in circumstances, for them to get out of the situation. After management has announced its final offer, the union could tell them, “A $3.69 per hour raise was your final offer before we discussed our cooperative efforts to make the plant more productive.”

与其直接指出对方的“要么接受要么放弃”的策略并就此展开谈判，不如先忽略它。继续交谈，假装没听到，或者转移话题，比如提出其他解决方案。如果你确实要提及这种策略，要让他们明白如果无法达成协议，他们会损失什么，并寻找一种体面的解决办法，例如情况发生变化，让他们能够脱身。在管理层宣布最终报价后，工会可以告诉他们：“每小时加薪3.69美元是你们的最终报价，之后我们再讨论如何合作提高工厂的生产效率。”

Don’t be a victim

不要成为受害者

It is often hard to decide what it means to negotiate in “good faith.” People draw the line in different places. It may help to ask yourself such questions as: Is this an approach I would use in dealing with a good friend or a member of my family? If a full account of what I said and did appeared in the media, would I be embarrassed? In literature, would such conduct be more appropriate for a hero or a villain? These questions are not intended to bring external opinion to bear so much as to shed light on your own internal values. You must decide on your own whether you want to use tactics you would consider improper and in bad faith if used against you.

很多时候，很难界定“诚信谈判”的含义。每个人的底线都不尽相同。不妨问问自己以下问题：我会用这种方式对待好友或家人吗？如果我的言行被媒体全盘报道，我会感到尴尬吗？在文学作品中，这种行为更适合英雄还是反派？这些问题并非意在引入外界意见，而是为了帮助你审视自身的价值观。你必须自己决定，是否愿意使用那些如果被对方用来对付自己，你会认为不恰当甚至不诚信的策略。

It may be useful at the beginning of the negotiation to say, “Look, I know this may be unusual, but I want to know the rules of the game we’re going to play. Are we both trying to reach a wise agreement as quickly and with as little effort as possible? Or are we going to play ‘hard bargaining’ where the more stubborn fellow wins?” Whatever you do, be prepared to fight tricky bargaining tactics. You can be just as firm as they can, even firmer. It is easier to defend principle than an illegitimate tactic. Don’t be a victim.

在谈判之初，不妨这样说：“我知道这可能有点不寻常，但我希望先了解一下我们即将玩的游戏规则。我们是想尽快达成一个明智的协议，并且尽可能减少双方的付出？还是要玩‘硬碰硬’的游戏，让更固执的一方最终获胜？”无论如何，都要做好应对各种狡猾谈判策略的准备。你可以像他们一样坚定，甚至更加坚定。捍卫原则远比对抗不正当的策略容易得多。不要让自己成为受害者。

# ↩

IV IN CONCLUSION

第四部分 结论

# ↩

In Conclusion

综上所述

T hree points.

三分。

You knew it all the time

你一直都知道。

There is probably nothing in this book that you did not already know at some level of your experience. What we have tried to do is to organize common sense and common experience in a way that provides a usable framework for thinking and acting. The more consistent these ideas are with your knowledge and intuition the better. In teaching this method to skilled lawyers and businesspeople with years of experience, we have been told, “Now I know what I have been doing, and why it sometimes works” and “I knew what you were saying was right because I knew it already.”

这本书里的内容，或许你早已在某种程度上有所了解。我们尝试做的，是将常识和经验整理成一个实用的思考和行动框架。这些理念与你的知识和直觉越契合，效果就越好。在向经验丰富的律师和商界人士传授这种方法时，我们曾听到这样的反馈：“现在我明白自己一直在做什么，以及为什么有时候会奏效了”以及“我知道你说的是对的，因为我早就知道了”。

Learn from doing

从实践中学习

A book can point you in a promising direction. By making you aware of ideas and aware of what you are doing, it can help you learn.

一本书可以为你指明一条充满希望的方向。它能让你了解各种想法，并意识到自己正在做的事情，从而帮助你学习。

No one, however, can make you skillful but yourself. Reading a pamphlet on the Royal Canadian Air Force fitness program will not make you physically fit. Studying books on tennis, swimming, riding a bicycle, or riding a horse will not make you an expert. Negotiation is no different.

然而，除了你自己，没有人能让你变得技艺精湛。阅读加拿大皇家空军体能训练计划的小册子并不会让你拥有强健的体魄。学习网球、游泳、骑自行车或骑马的书籍也不会让你成为专家。谈判也是如此。

“Winning”

“胜利”

In 1964 an American father and his twelve-year-old son were enjoying a beautiful Saturday in Hyde Park, London, playing catch with a Frisbee. Few in England had seen a Frisbee at that time and a small group of strollers gathered to watch this strange sport. Finally, one homburg-clad Englishman came over to the father: “Sorry to bother you. Been watching you a quarter of an hour. Who’s winning? ”

1964年，一个美国父亲带着他十二岁的儿子在伦敦海德公园享受着美好的周六时光，玩着飞盘。当时英国很少有人见过飞盘，一群散步的人围观着这项奇特的运动。最后，一位头戴软呢帽的英国人走到父亲面前问道：“不好意思打扰您了。我已经看了您一刻钟了。谁赢了？”

In most instances to ask a negotiator “Who’s winning?” is as inappropriate as to ask who’s winning a marriage. If you ask that question about your marriage, you have already lost the more important negotiation—the one about what kind of game to play, about the way you deal with each other and your shared and differing interests.

在大多数情况下，问谈判者“谁赢了？”就像问谁在婚姻中占上风一样不合适。如果你问这个问题，说明你已经输掉了更重要的谈判——关于该如何博弈、如何处理彼此的利益以及你们的共同点和分歧的谈判。

This book is about how to “win” that important game—how to achieve a better process for dealing with your differences. To be better, the process must, of course, produce good substantive results; winning on the merits may not be the only goal, but certainly losing is not the answer. Both theory and experience suggest that the method of principled negotiation will produce over the long run substantive outcomes as good as or better than you are likely to obtain using any other negotiation strategy. In addition, it should prove more efficient and less costly to human relationships. We find the method comfortable to use and hope you will too.

本书探讨的是如何“赢得”这场重要的博弈——如何找到更有效的化解分歧的方法。当然，要达到“更有效”的程度，这个方法必须能够产生实质性的成果；取得实质性的胜利或许并非唯一目标，但失败也绝非良策。理论和经验都表明，从长远来看，遵循原则的谈判方法能够取得与其他任何谈判策略一样好甚至更好的实质性成果。此外，这种方法也更加高效，并且对人际关系的损害更小。我们发现这种方法使用起来非常舒适，也希望您能有同样的感受。

That does not mean it is easy to change habits, to disentangle emotions from the merits, or to enlist others in the task of working out a wise solution to a shared problem. From time to time you may want to remind yourself that the first thing you are trying to win is a better way to negotiate—a way that avoids your having to choose between the satisfactions of getting what you deserve and of being decent. You can have both.

但这并不意味着改变习惯、将情绪与利弊剥离开来，或者让其他人参与到共同问题的明智解决方案的制定中来很容易。你或许需要时不时地提醒自己，你首先要争取的是更好的谈判方式——一种让你不必在获得应得之物和保持体面之间做出选择的谈判方式。你可以两者兼得。

V TEN QUESTIONS PEOPLE ASK ABOUT GETTING TO YES

关于如何达成协议，人们常问的十个问题

Questions About Fairness and “Principled” Negotiation

关于公平性和“有原则的”谈判的问题

1. “Does positional bargaining ever make sense?”

1.“立场谈判真的有意义吗？”

2. “What if the other side believes in a different standard of fairness?”

2.“如果对方信奉不同的公平标准呢？”

3. “Should I be fair if I don’t have to be?”

3.“如果我不必做到公平，我应该做到公平吗？”

Questions About Dealing with People

关于与人相处的问题

4. “What do I do if the people are the problem?”

4.“如果问题出在人身上，我该怎么办？”

5. “Should I negotiate even with terrorists or someone like Hitler? When does it make sense not to negotiate?”

5.“我是否应该与恐怖分子或像希特勒这样的人谈判？什么时候不应该谈判？”

6. “How should I adjust my negotiating approach to account for differences of personality, gender, culture, and so on?”

6.“我应该如何调整我的谈判方式以适应性格、性别、文化等方面的差异？”

关于战术的问题

7. “How do I decide things like ‘Where should we meet?’ ‘How should we communicate?’ ‘Who should make the first offer?’ and ‘How high should I start?’”

7. “我该如何决定诸如‘我们应该在哪里见面？’‘我们应该如何沟通？’‘谁应该先出价？’以及‘我应该开价多高？’之类的事情呢？”

8. “Concretely, how do I move from inventing options to making commitments?”

8. “具体来说，我该如何从提出方案过渡到做出承诺？”

# ↩

Ten Questions People Ask About Getting to YES

人们常问的关于如何获得“是”的十个问题

QUESTIONS ABOUT FAIRNESS AND “PRINCIPLED” NEGOTIATION

关于公平性和“有原则的”谈判的问题

Question 1: “Does positional bargaining ever make sense?”

问题 1：“立场谈判真的有意义吗？”

Positional bargaining is easy, so it is not surprising that people often do it. It requires no preparation, it is universally understood (sometimes you can even do it with fingers when you and the other side do not share a common language), and in some contexts it is entrenched and expected. In contrast, looking behind positions for interests, inventing options for mutual gain, and finding and using objective criteria take hard work and, when the other side seems recalcitrant, emotional restraint and maturity.

立场谈判很容易，所以人们经常这样做也就不足为奇了。它无需任何准备，几乎人人都能理解（有时甚至在双方语言不通的情况下，用手指就能表达清楚），而且在某些情况下，这种谈判方式根深蒂固，是人们所期望的。相比之下，探究立场背后的真正利益，创造互利共赢的方案，以及寻找并运用客观标准，都需要付出艰辛的努力；当对方态度强硬时，更需要情绪上的克制和成熟的思考。

In virtually every case, the outcome will be better for both sides with principled negotiation. The issue is whether it is worth the extra effort. Here are some questions to consider:

几乎在所有情况下，秉持原则的谈判都会对双方都有利。问题在于，这种额外的努力是否值得。以下是一些值得思考的问题：

How important is it to avoid an arbitrary outcome? If, like the house builder in Chapter 5, you are negotiating over how deep to build your home’s foundations, you will not want to haggle over arbitrary positions no matter how much easier it might be to reach agreement. Even if you are negotiating for a one-of-a-kind antique chamber pot, where objective standards will be hard to find, exploring the dealer’s interests and looking for creative options is probably a good idea. Still, one factor to consider in choosing a negotiating approach is how much you care about finding an answer to the problem that makes sense on the merits. The stakes would be much higher if you were negotiating over the foundations for an office building than those for a tool shed. They will also be higher if this transaction will set a precedent for future transactions.

避免达成武断的结果有多重要？如果你像第五章中的房屋建造商一样，正在协商房屋地基的深度，那么无论达成协议多么容易，你都不想在武断的立场上讨价还价。即使你是在为一件独一无二的古董便壶谈判，客观标准很难找到，但了解卖家的利益并寻找有创意的方案或许也是个好主意。不过，选择谈判策略时需要考虑的一个因素是，你有多在意找到一个切实可行的解决方案。如果你正在为办公楼的地基谈判，那么风险肯定比为工具棚的地基谈判高得多。如果这笔交易会为未来的交易树立先例，那么风险也会更高。

How complex are the issues? The more complex the subject matter, the more unwise it is to engage in positional bargaining. Complexity calls for careful analysis of interests that are shared or that can be creatively dovetailed, and then for brainstorming. Both will be easier to the extent the parties see themselves as engaged in joint problem-solving.

问题有多复杂？议题越复杂，采取立场谈判就越不明智。复杂性要求我们仔细分析共同利益或可以创造性地结合起来的利益，然后进行头脑风暴。如果各方都认为自己是在共同解决问题，那么这两方面都会更容易。

How important is it to maintain a good working relationship? If the other side is a valued customer or client, maintaining your ongoing relationship may be more important to you than the outcome of any one deal. This does not mean you should be less persistent in pursuing your interests, but it does suggest avoiding tactics such as threats or ultimatums that involve a high risk of damage to the relationship. Negotiation on the merits helps avoid a choice between giving in or angering the other side.

维持良好的工作关系有多重要？如果对方是您的重要客户，那么维护长期合作关系可能比任何一笔交易的结果都更重要。这并不意味着您应该在追求自身利益时有所懈怠，而是建议您避免使用威胁或最后通牒等可能严重损害关系的策略。基于事实进行谈判有助于避免在妥协和激怒对方之间做出艰难抉择。

In single-issue negotiations among strangers where the transaction costs of exploring interests would be high and where each side is protected by competitive opportunities, simple haggling over positions may work fine. But if the discussion starts to bog down, be prepared to change gears. Start clarifying the underlying interests.

在陌生人之间就单一议题进行的谈判中，如果双方利益探索的成本很高，且各自都受到竞争机会的保护，那么简单的立场讨价还价或许可行。但如果讨论开始陷入僵局，就要做好转换策略的准备。首先要明确双方的根本利益。

You should also consider the effect of this negotiation on your relationship with others. Is this negotiation likely to affect your reputation as a negotiator and, consequently, how others approach negotiating with you? If so, what effect would you like it to have?

你还应该考虑这次谈判对你与他人关系的影响。这次谈判是否可能影响你作为谈判者的声誉，进而影响他人与你谈判的方式？如果会，你希望它产生什么样的影响？

What are the other side’s expectations, and how hard would they be to change? In many labor-management and other contexts, the parties have a long history of hard-fought and almost ritualistic positional bargaining. Each side sees the other as “the enemy” and the situation as zero-sum, ignoring the enormous shared costs of strikes, lockouts, and bad feelings. In these situations it is not easy to establish joint problem-solving, yet it may be correspondingly more important. Even parties that would like to change often find it hard in practice to shed old habits: to listen instead of attacking, to brainstorm instead of quarreling, and to explore interests before making a commitment. Some parties locked into adversarial ruts seem unable to consider alternative approaches until they reach the brink of mutual annihilation, and some not even then. In such contexts you will want to set a realistic timetable for change that may span several complete negotiations. It took General Motors and the United Auto Workers four contracts to change the fundamental structure of their negotiations, and there remain constituents on each side who are not yet comfortable with the new regime.

对方的期望是什么？改变这些期望有多难？在许多劳资关系和其他情境中，双方长期以来都进行着艰苦卓绝、近乎仪式化的立场谈判。双方都将对方视为“敌人”，并将局势视为零和博弈，忽略了罢工、停工和彼此敌对情绪带来的巨大共同成本。在这种情况下，建立共同解决问题的机制并非易事，但其重要性也因此可能更高。即使是那些想要改变的各方，在实践中也常常发现很难摆脱旧习：倾听而非攻击，集思广益而非争吵，以及在做出承诺前先了解彼此的利益。一些陷入对抗僵局的各方似乎只有在濒临毁灭的边缘才会考虑其他方案，甚至有些一方即便到了那时也依然如此。在这种情况下，你需要制定一个切实可行的变革时间表，这可能需要经过多次完整的谈判。通用汽车和美国汽车工人联合会用了四份合同才改变了谈判的基本结构，但双方仍然有一些成员对新的制度感到不适应。

Where are you in the negotiation? Bargaining over positions tends to inhibit looking for joint gains. In many negotiations, the parties end up with outcomes that “leave a lot of gold on the table.” Bargaining over positions does the least harm if it comes after you have identified each other’s interests, invented options for mutual gain, and discussed relevant standards of fairness.

谈判进行到什么阶段了？纠结于立场往往会阻碍双方寻求共同利益。很多谈判最终的结果都是“拱手让出很多好处”。如果双方在明确彼此利益、探索互利共赢的方案并讨论相关的公平标准之后再进行立场谈判，那么这种谈判的危害最小。

Question 2: “What if the other side believes in a different standard of fairness?”

问题 2：“如果对方信奉不同的公平标准呢？”

In most negotiations there will be no one “right” or “fairest” answer; people will advance different standards by which to judge what is fair. Yet using external standards improves on haggling in three ways: An outcome informed even by conflicting standards of fairness and community practice is likely to be wiser than an arbitrary result. Using standards reduces the costs of “backing down”—it is easier to agree to follow a principle or independent standard than to give in to the other side’s positional demand. And finally, unlike arbitrary positions, some standards are more persuasive than others.

大多数谈判中不会存在唯一的“正确”或“最公平”答案；人们会提出不同的标准来判断何为公平。然而，运用外部标准可以从三个方面改进讨价还价：即使公平标准和社区惯例存在冲突，最终结果也可能比任意的结果更明智。运用标准可以降低“让步”的成本——遵守原则或独立标准比屈服于对方的立场要求要容易得多。最后，与任意立场不同，某些标准比其他标准更具说服力。

In a negotiation between a young lawyer and a Wall Street law firm over salary, for example, it would be absurd for the hiring partner to say, “I don’t suppose you think you are any smarter than I am, so we’ll offer you the same salary I made when I started out forty years ago—$24,000.” The young lawyer would point out the impact of inflation over the intervening years and suggest using current salaries. If the partner proposed using the current salaries for young lawyers in Dayton or Des Moines, the young lawyer would point out that the average salary for young lawyers in similarly prestigious Manhattan firms was a more appropriate standard.

例如，在一位年轻律师与华尔街律师事务所就薪资进行谈判时，如果聘用他的合伙人说：“我想你大概觉得自己并不比我聪明，所以我们给你开的薪水和我四十年前刚入行时一样——24000美元。” 这位年轻律师会指出这些年来通货膨胀的影响，并建议采用当前的薪资水平。如果合伙人提议采用代顿或得梅因等地年轻律师的当前薪资水平，这位年轻律师会指出，曼哈顿同等声望的律师事务所年轻律师的平均薪资才是更合适的标准。

Explore how conflicting standards have developed . Usually one standard will be more persuasive than another to the extent that it is more directly on point, more widely accepted, and more immediately relevant in terms of time, place, and circumstance. When that isn’t obvious, it is helpful to ask why and how conflicting standards have developed. Is the market in transition, for example, in the midst of evolving to a new structure with different expectations and standards? Or are two traditions converging? By understanding the logic and history of how standards have developed, you can better argue which are more appropriate in your situation. In many industries, for example, the advent of the Internet has undercut the traditional role of local distributors, with many buyers wanting to buy online or direct from manufacturers. Traditional standards of a reasonable distributor profit margin are in sharp conflict with competitive market prices, leading to new conversations about the value of service and local access. Over time, distributors evolve their business models or go out of business.

探究相互冲突的标准是如何形成的。通常，如果某个标准更切中要害、更广为接受，并且在时间、地点和具体情况下更具相关性，那么它就比其他标准更具说服力。如果这一点并不明显，那么探究相互冲突的标准是如何形成的就很有帮助。例如，市场是否正处于转型期，正在向具有不同预期和标准的新结构演进？或者，两种传统是否正在融合？通过理解标准发展的逻辑和历史，您可以更好地论证哪些标准更适合您的具体情况。例如，在许多行业，互联网的出现削弱了本地分销商的传统作用，许多买家希望在线购买或直接从制造商处购买。合理的经销商利润率这一传统标准与竞争激烈的市场价格之间存在着尖锐的冲突，从而引发了关于服务价值和本地化渠道的新讨论。随着时间的推移，分销商要么改进其商业模式，要么退出市场。

Agreement on the “best” standard is not necessary. Differences in values, culture, experience, and perceptions may well lead parties to disagree about the relative merits of different standards. If it were necessary to agree on which standard was “best,” settling a negotiation might not be possible. But agreement on criteria is not necessary. Criteria are just one tool that may help the parties find an agreement better for both than no agreement. Using external standards often helps narrow the range of disagreement and may help expand the area of potential agreement. When standards have been refined to the point that it is difficult to argue persuasively that one standard is more applicable than another, the parties can explore trade-offs or resort to fair procedures to settle the remaining differences. They can flip a coin, use an arbitrator, or even split the difference.

无需就“最佳”标准达成一致。价值观、文化、经验和认知上的差异很可能导致各方对不同标准的相对优劣产生分歧。如果必须就哪个标准“最佳”达成一致，谈判可能根本无法进行。但无需就标准达成一致。标准只是众多工具之一，可以帮助各方找到比无协议更好的方案。使用外部标准通常有助于缩小分歧范围，并可能有助于扩大潜在共识的领域。当标准经过完善，难以令人信服地论证某个标准比其他标准更适用时，各方可以探讨权衡取舍，或诉诸公平的程序来解决剩余的分歧。他们可以掷硬币、使用仲裁程序，甚至折中解决分歧。

Question 3: “Should I be fair if I don’t have to be?”

问题 3：“如果我不必做到公平，我应该做到公平吗？”

Getting to YES is not a sermon on the morality of right and wrong; it is a book on how to do well in a negotiation. We do not suggest that you should be good for the sake of being good (nor do we discourage it). [4] We do not suggest that you give in to the first offer that is arguably within the realm of fairness. Nor do we suggest that you never ask for more than what a judge or jury might think is fair. We argue only that using independent standards to discuss the fairness of a proposal is an idea that can help you get what you deserve and protect you from getting taken.

《谈判技巧》并非对是非对错的道德说教，而是一本关于如何在谈判中取得成功的指南。我们并非建议你为了做好人而做好人（当然，我们也不反对这样做）。[4] 我们并非建议你接受第一个看似合理的报价。我们也并非建议你永远不要索要超出法官或陪审团认为公平范围的金额。我们只是认为，运用独立的标准来评估一项提议的公平性，可以帮助你获得应得的利益，并保护你免受欺骗。

If you want more than you can justify as fair and find that you are regularly able to persuade others to give it to you, you may not find some of the suggestions in this book all that useful. But the negotiators we meet more often fear getting less than they should in a negotiation, or damaging a relationship if they press firmly for what they do deserve. The ideas in this book are meant to show you how to get what you are entitled to while still getting along with the other side.

如果你想要的东西超过了你认为合理的范围，而且你发现自己经常能够说服别人满足你，那么这本书中的一些建议可能对你来说用处不大。但我们更常遇到的谈判者担心在谈判中得不到应得的，或者担心如果坚持争取自己应得的东西会损害彼此的关系。本书旨在向你展示如何在与对方保持良好关系的同时，获得你应得的东西。

Nevertheless, sometimes you may have an opportunity to get more than you think would be fair. Should you take it? In our opinion, not without careful thought. More is at stake than just a choice about your moral self-definition. (That too probably deserves careful thought, but advising in that realm is not our purpose here.) Presented with the opportunity to get more than you think is fair, you should weigh the possible benefits against the potential costs of accepting the windfall:

然而，有时你可能会遇到一个机会，获得超出你认为公平的回报。你应该接受吗？我们认为，不经深思熟虑是不可取的。这不仅仅关乎你对自身道德的认知。（当然，道德认知也值得深思，但我们在此并非意在就此提供建议。）当你有机会获得超出你认为公平的回报时，你应该权衡接受这份意外之财的潜在收益和代价：

How much is the difference worth to you? What is the most that you could justify to yourself as fair? Just how important to you is the excess above that standard? Weigh this benefit against the risk of incurring some of the costs listed below, and then consider whether there might not be better options. (For example, could the proposed transaction be structured so that the other side sees themselves as doing you a favor rather than getting ripped off?)

对你来说，这其中的差价价值几何？你认为合理的最高标准是多少？超出这个标准的额外部分对你来说究竟有多重要？权衡一下这项收益与承担以下列出的某些成本的风险，然后考虑是否有更好的选择。（例如，能否对拟议的交易进行结构调整，使对方觉得是在帮你，而不是被你占便宜？）

It would also be wise to consider how certain you are of these potential benefits. Might you be overlooking something? Is the other side really so blind? Many negotiators are overly optimistic in assuming that they are more clever than their counterparts.

此外，明智的做法是考虑一下你对这些潜在好处的把握有多大。你是否忽略了什么？对方真的如此盲目吗？许多谈判者过于乐观，认为自己比对方更聪明。

Will the unfair result be durable? If the other side later concludes that an agreement is unfair, they may be unwilling to carry it out. What would it cost to try to enforce the agreement or to replace it? Courts may refuse to enforce an agreement found to be “unconscionable.”

这种不公平的结果会持续下去吗？如果对方日后认为协议不公平，他们可能不愿意履行。强制执行协议或更换协议的成本是多少？法院可能会拒绝执行被认定为“显失公平”的协议。

You should also consider where you are in the negotiation. There is no value in a super-favorable tentative agreement if the other side wakes up and repudiates it before it becomes final. And if the other side concludes from the incident that you are an untrustworthy lout out to take advantage of them, the cost may not be limited to this provision of this agreement.

你还应该考虑谈判的进展情况。如果对方在协议最终生效前突然反悔，那么即使达成了非常有利的初步协议也毫无价值。而且，如果对方因此认为你是个不可信赖、一心想占他们便宜的无赖，那么损失可能远不止协议中的这一条款。

What damage might the unfair result cause to this or other relationships? How likely is it that you will find yourself negotiating with this same party again? If you did, what might be the risks for you if they were “out for revenge”? How about your reputation with other people, especially your reputation for fair dealing? Might it be adversely affected more than would offset your immediate gain?

不公平的结果可能会对这段关系或其他关系造成哪些损害？你再次与同一方谈判的可能性有多大？如果再次谈判，而对方“伺机报复”，你可能会面临哪些风险？你在他人眼中的声誉，尤其是你公平交易的声誉，会受到怎样的影响？这种负面影响是否会超过你眼前的利益？

A well-established reputation for fair dealing can be an extraordinary asset. It opens up a large realm of creative agreements that would be impossible if others did not trust you. Such a reputation is much easier to destroy than to build.

建立起公平交易的良好声誉是一项非凡的资产。它能为你开启许多富有创意的合作协议，而如果没有他人的信任，这些协议是不可能实现的。这样的声誉远比建立起来容易得多，也更容易被摧毁。

Will your conscience bother you? Are you likely later to regret the agreement, believing that you took unfair advantage of someone? Consider the tourist who bought a beautiful Kashmir rug from the family who had labored for a full year to make it. He cleverly offered to pay in German currency, then offered worthless bills from the inflationary pre-WWII Weimar period. Only when he told the story to shocked friends back home did he begin to think about what he had done to this family. In time, the very sight of his beautiful rug turned his stomach. Like this tourist, many people find that they care about more in life than money and “beating” the other side.

你的良心会受到谴责吗？你日后是否会后悔当初的约定，觉得自己占了别人的便宜？想想那位游客，他从一个辛勤劳作了一整年才织成精美克什米尔地毯的家庭手中买下了它。他先是狡猾地提出用德国货币付款，然后又拿出二战前魏玛共和国时期那些贬值严重的钞票。直到他把这件事告诉了家乡震惊的朋友们，他才开始反思自己对这个家庭所做的一切。久而久之，他甚至连看到那张漂亮的地毯都感到恶心。就像这位游客一样，许多人发现，生活中除了金钱和“占便宜”之外，还有更重要的东西。

QUESTIONS ABOUT DEALING WITH PEOPLE

关于与人相处的问题

Question 4: ‘‘What do I do if the people are the problem?”

问题 4：“如果问题出在人身上，我该怎么办？”

Some people have interpreted the admonition “Separate the people from the problem” to mean sweep people problems under the rug. This is emphatically not what we mean. People problems often require more attention than substantive ones. The human propensity for defensive and reactive behavior is one reason so many negotiations fail when agreement would otherwise make sense. In negotiation you ignore people issues—how you are treating the other side—at your peril. Our basic advice is the same whether people problems are one concern or the main focus of your negotiation:

有些人将“将人与问题分开”的告诫解读为对人际问题视而不见。这绝非我们的本意。人际问题往往比实质性问题更需要关注。人类天生具有防御性和反应性，这正是许多谈判失败的原因之一，即便这些谈判原本可以达成一致。在谈判中，忽视人际问题——即你如何对待对方——将会带来严重后果。无论人际问题只是谈判中的一个考量因素还是主要焦点，我们的基本建议都是一样的：

Build a working relationship independent of agreement or disagreement. The more seriously you disagree with someone, the more important it is that you be able to deal well with that disagreement. A good working relationship is one that can cope with differences. Such a relationship cannot be bought by making substantive concessions or by pretending that disagreements do not exist. Experience suggests that appeasement does not often work. Making an unjustified concession now is unlikely to make it easier to deal with future differences. You may think that next time it is their turn to make a concession; they are likely to believe that if they are stubborn enough, you will again give in. (Neville Chamberlain’s agreement to German occupation of the Sudetenland and the lack of military response to Hitler’s subsequent occupation of all of Czechoslovakia probably encouraged the Nazis to believe that an invasion of Poland would also not lead to war.)

建立一种不因意见一致或分歧而改变的工作关系。你与某人的分歧越严重，就越需要妥善处理分歧。良好的工作关系能够应对分歧。这种关系并非通过做出实质性让步或假装分歧不存在就能建立的。经验表明，绥靖政策往往行不通。现在做出不合理的让步不太可能让未来的分歧更容易处理。你或许认为下次轮到他们做出让步；但他们很可能认为，只要他们足够固执，你就会再次让步。（内维尔·张伯伦同意德国占领苏台德地区，以及对希特勒随后占领整个捷克斯洛伐克缺乏军事反应，可能使纳粹相信入侵波兰也不会引发战争。）

Nor should you try to coerce a substantive concession by threatening the relationship. (“If you really cared for me, you would give in.” “Unless you agree with me, our relationship is through.”) Whether or not such a ploy succeeds for the moment in obtaining a concession, it will damage the relationship. It will tend to make it more difficult for the two sides to deal well with future differences.

你也不应该试图通过威胁关系来强迫对方做出实质性让步。（“如果你真的在乎我，你就会妥协。”“除非你同意我的观点，否则我们的关系就结束了。”）无论这种策略能否暂时迫使对方做出让步，它都会损害彼此的关系。这会让双方在未来处理分歧时更加困难。

Rather, substantive issues need to be disentangled from relationship and process issues. The content of a possible agreement needs to be separated from questions of how you talk about it and how you deal with the other side. Each set of issues needs to be negotiated on its own merits. The following list illustrates the distinction:

相反，实质性问题需要与关系和流程问题区分开来。可能达成的协议内容需要与如何讨论以及如何与对方沟通等问题分开。每组问题都需要根据其自身情况进行谈判。以下列表说明了这种区别：

Substantive Issues

实质性问题

  • Terms
    条款
  • Conditions
    状况
  • Prices
    价格
  • Dates
    日期
  • Numbers
    数字
  • Liabilities
    负债

Relationship Issues

人际关系问题

  • Balance of emotion and reason
    情感与理性的平衡
  • Ease of communication
    沟通便利性
  • Degree of trust and reliability
    信任度和可靠性
  • Attitude of acceptance (or rejection)
    接受（或拒绝）的态度
  • Relative emphasis on persuasion (or coercion)
    相对侧重于说服（或胁迫）
  • Degree of mutual understanding
    相互理解程度

People often assume that there is a trade-off between pursuing a good substantive outcome and pursuing a good relationship. We disagree. A good working relationship tends to make it easier to get good substantive outcomes (for both sides). Good substantive outcomes tend to make a good relationship even better.

人们常常认为，追求良好的实质性成果和建立良好的人际关系之间存在权衡取舍。我们并不认同这种观点。良好的工作关系往往有助于双方取得良好的实质性成果。而良好的实质性成果反过来又能进一步巩固良好的人际关系。

Sometimes there may be good reasons to agree, even when you believe fairness would dictate otherwise. For example, if you already have an excellent working relationship, you may well decide to give in on an issue, confident that on some future occasion the other person will recognize that they “owe you one” and reciprocate the favor. (But make sure they also see what you are doing as a favor.) Or you may reasonably decide that one or more issues are not worth fighting over, all things considered. Our point is that you should not give in for the purpose of trying to improve a relationship.

有时，即使你认为公平起见应该做出相反的决定，也可能存在合理的理由让你同意。例如，如果你和对方已经建立了良好的工作关系，你或许会决定在某个问题上做出让步，因为你相信在未来的某个时候，对方会意识到“欠你一个人情”，并会回报你的恩情。（但要确保对方也明白你这样做是在帮你。）或者，考虑到各种因素，你也可能合理地认为某些问题不值得争论。我们的观点是，你不应该为了改善关系而做出让步。

Negotiate the relationship. If, despite your efforts to establish a working relationship and to negotiate substantive differences on their merits, people problems still stand in the way, negotiate them—on their merits. Raise your concerns about the other side’s behavior and discuss them as you would a substantive difference. Avoid judging them or impugning their motivations. Rather, explain your perceptions and feelings and inquire into theirs. Propose external standards or fair principles to determine how you should deal with each other and decline to give in to pressure tactics. Frame your discussion as looking forward, not back, and operate on the assumptions that the other side may not intend all the consequences you experience and that they can change their approach if they see the need.

协商关系。如果尽管你努力建立工作关系并就实质性分歧进行协商，但人际关系问题仍然存在，那就就事论事地协商这些问题。提出你对对方行为的担忧，并像讨论实质性分歧一样讨论这些问题。避免评判对方或质疑其动机。相反，解释你的看法和感受，并询问对方的看法和感受。提出外部标准或公平原则来决定你们应该如何相处，并拒绝屈服于压力策略。将你的讨论定位为展望未来，而不是回顾过去，并假设对方可能并非有意造成你所经历的所有后果，而且如果他们认为有必要，他们可以改变做法。

As always in negotiation, you need to have thought through your BATNA. In some cases the other side may come to appreciate that your concerns are a shared problem only when they realize that your BATNA, in the event you fail to reach a solution satisfactory to you, is not very good for them.

谈判中，一如既往，你需要仔细考虑你的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。在某些情况下，只有当对方意识到，如果你们无法达成令你满意的解决方案，而你的最佳替代方案对他们来说并不理想时，他们才会理解你的担忧是双方共同面临的问题。

Distinguish how you treat them from how they treat you. There is no need to emulate unconstructive behavior. Doing so may indeed “teach them a lesson,” though often not the lesson we would like. In most cases responding in kind reinforces the behavior we dislike. It encourages the other side to feel that everyone behaves that way and that it is the only way to protect themselves. Our behavior should be designed to model and encourage the behavior we would prefer and to avoid any reward for the behavior we dislike, both without compromising our substantive interests.

区分你如何对待他人和他们如何对待你。没有必要效仿那些不具建设性的行为。这样做或许确实能“给他们一个教训”，但往往并非我们所希望的教训。在大多数情况下，以牙还牙只会强化我们反感的行为。这会让对方觉得每个人都这样行事，而且这是保护自己的唯一方法。我们的行为应该旨在树立和鼓励我们更倾向的行为，避免对我们反感的行为给予任何奖励，同时又不损害我们自身的实质性利益。

Deal rationally with apparent irrationality. Much—perhaps most—behavior in the world is not very rational. As we say in Chapter 2, negotiators are people first. We often act impulsively or react without careful thought, especially when we are angry, afraid, or frustrated. And we all know people who seem just plain irrational no matter the situation. How do you cope with such behavior?

理性应对看似不理性的行为。世界上很多行为——或许绝大多数——都并非完全理性。正如我们在第二章中所说，谈判者首先是人。我们常常会冲动行事，或者不经深思熟虑就做出反应，尤其是在愤怒、恐惧或沮丧的时候。而且，我们都认识一些人，无论在什么情况下，他们看起来都完全不理性。你该如何应对这种行为呢？

First, recognize that, while people often do not negotiate rationally, it is worth trying to yourself. In a mental hospital, we do not want psychotic doctors. Likewise, in coping with the irrationality of other negotiators, you would like to be as purposive as possible.

首先，要认识到，虽然人们在谈判中常常缺乏理性，但尝试理性谈判仍然值得。精神病院里不需要精神错乱的医生。同样，在应对其他谈判者的非理性行为时，你也应该尽可能地保持目标明确。

Second, question your assumption that others are acting irrationally. Perhaps they see the situation differently. In most conflicts, each side believes that they are reasonably saying “no” to what they hear the other demanding. Perhaps they hear your well-padded opening position as unjustifiable on the merits; perhaps they value things differently; or there may be a communication failure.

其次，质疑一下你认为他人行为不理智的假设。或许他们对情况的看法与你不同。在大多数冲突中，双方都认为自己对对方的要求说“不”是合情合理的。或许他们认为你精心准备的开场白缺乏实质依据；或许他们的价值观与你不同；又或许是沟通出现了问题。

Sometimes people do hold views that many of us think are objectively “irrational,” such as people who fear flying. Internally, however, these people are reacting rationally to the world as they see it. At some level, they believe that this plane will crash. If we believed that, we would not fly either. It is the perception that is skewed, not the response to that perception. Neither telling such people that they are wrong (with however many scientific studies) nor punishing them for their beliefs is likely to change how they feel. On the other hand, if you inquire empathetically, taking their feelings seriously and trying to trace their reasoning to its roots, it is sometimes possible to effect change. Working with them, you may discover a logical leap, a factual misperception, or a traumatic association from an earlier time that, once brought to light, can be examined and modified by the people themselves. In essence, you are looking for the psychological interests behind their position, to help them find a way to meet more of their interests more effectively.

有时，人们会持有我们许多人认为客观上“不理性”的观点，例如害怕坐飞机的人。然而，从内心深处来看，这些人对他们所看到的世界做出了理性的反应。在某种程度上，他们相信这架飞机将会坠毁。如果我们也这样认为，我们也不会坐飞机。问题在于认知本身，而非对认知的反应。无论用多少科学研究来证明他们的想法是错误的，或者惩罚他们的信念，都不太可能改变他们的感受。另一方面，如果你以同理心去询问，认真对待他们的感受，并尝试追溯他们推理的根源，有时就有可能促成改变。与他们合作，你可能会发现逻辑上的跳跃、对事实的误解，或者早年经历的创伤性联想。一旦这些因素被揭示出来，他们就可以审视并修正这些认知。本质上，你是在寻找他们立场背后的心理动机，帮助他们找到一种更有效的方式来满足自身更多的利益。

Question 5: “Should I negotiate even with terrorists or someone like Hitler? When does it make sense not to negotiate?”

问题 5：“我应该与恐怖分子或像希特勒这样的人谈判吗？什么时候不应该谈判？”

However unsavory the other side, unless you have a better BATNA, the question you face is not whether to negotiate, but how.

然而，无论对方多么令人厌恶，除非你有更好的替代方案（BATNA），否则你面临的问题不是是否谈判，而是如何谈判。

Negotiate with terrorists? Yes. In fact, in the sense that you are trying to influence their decisions—and they are trying to influence yours—you are negotiating with them even if you are not talking with them. The question is whether to do so at a distance by actions and words (such as “We will never negotiate with terrorists!”) or whether to do so more directly. In general, the better the communication, the better your chance to exert influence. If questions of personal safety can be resolved, it might make sense to establish a dialogue with terrorists, whether they are holding hostages or threatening some act of violence. If you have a good case, you are more likely to influence them than they are to influence you. (The same arguments apply to dealing with negotiation “terrorists,” who try to use dirty tricks.)

与恐怖分子谈判？可以。事实上，从某种意义上说，你试图影响他们的决定——他们也试图影响你的决定——即使你不与他们直接对话，你也在与他们谈判。问题在于，你是应该通过言行（例如“我们绝不与恐怖分子谈判！”）来保持距离，还是应该更直接地进行谈判。一般来说，沟通越顺畅，你施加影响的机会就越大。如果人身安全问题能够得到解决，那么与恐怖分子建立对话或许是有意义的，无论他们是劫持人质还是威胁实施暴力行为。如果你有充分的理由，你更有可能影响他们，而不是他们影响你。（同样的道理也适用于应对那些试图使用卑鄙手段的谈判“恐怖分子”。）

Negotiation does not mean giving in. There are high costs in paying ransom or blackmail. Rewarding kidnapping encourages more kidnapping. Through communication it may be possible to convince terrorists (and possible future terrorists) that they will not receive a ransom. It may also be possible to learn of some legitimate interests they have and to work out an arrangement in which neither side gives in.

谈判并不意味着妥协。支付赎金或敲诈勒索的代价高昂。奖励绑架只会助长更多绑架行为。通过沟通，或许可以说服恐怖分子（以及潜在的未来恐怖分子）他们不会收到赎金。此外，或许还可以了解他们的一些合法利益，并达成双方都能接受的协议。

With the help of Algerian mediators, the United States and Iran were able to negotiate the release in January 1981 of the American diplomats who had been held for more than a year in the U.S. embassy in Tehran. The basis of the settlement was that each side got no more than that to which they were entitled: The hostages would be released; Iran would pay its debts; when those amounts were settled, the balance of the funds seized by the United States would be returned to Iran; the United States would recognize the government of Iran and would not interfere in its internal affairs; and so on. It would have been difficult if not impossible to work out a settlement without negotiation. And despite the gross illegality of the seizure of the U.S. embassy, both sides benefited from the negotiations that finally took place in the fall of 1980.

在阿尔及利亚调解人的帮助下，美国和伊朗于1981年1月达成协议，释放了被扣押在德黑兰美国大使馆一年多的美国外交官。和解的基础是双方各自获得应得的：人质获释；伊朗偿还债务；债务偿清后，美国扣押的剩余资金将归还伊朗；美国承认伊朗政府，不再干涉其内政；等等。如果没有谈判，达成和解几乎是不可能的。尽管扣押美国大使馆的行为极其非法，但双方都从1980年秋季最终进行的谈判中获益。

It is sometimes said that officials should refuse to talk with political terrorists because to do so would confer status and reward their illegal action. It is true that for a high government official to meet with terrorists might well appear to enhance the terrorists’ importance to an extent that outweighs the potential gain. But contact at a professional level may be quite different. Urban police negotiators have learned that direct personal dialogue with criminals who are holding hostages frequently results in the hostages being released and the criminals being taken into custody.

有人认为，官员应该拒绝与政治恐怖分子对话，因为这样做会提升他们的地位，并奖励他们的非法行为。的确，高级政府官员与恐怖分子会面，很可能会显著提升恐怖分子的地位，使其得不偿失。但专业层面的接触则截然不同。城市警察谈判专家发现，与劫持人质的罪犯进行直接的个人对话，往往能促成人质获释，罪犯被抓获。

During the 1988 hijacking of Kuwait Airways Flight 422, extensive negotiations occurred with the hijackers but over increasingly small issues. The government of Kuwait said flatly at the beginning of the incident that they would not release the hijackers’ comrades, who were in jail in Kuwait after having been convicted of terrorist acts, and the government never retreated from that fundamental principle. But local authorities in Cyprus and Algeria negotiated incessantly over things like permission for the plane to land, requests for additional fuel, access to news media, and deliveries of food. For each transaction these authorities successfully obtained the release of more hostages. At the same time, they appealed—as fellow Muslims—to Islamic ideals of mercy and the Prophet Muhammed’s admonitions against the taking of hostages. Eventually all the hostages were released. The hijackers were also allowed to leave Algeria, but their prolonged and embarrassing failure to achieve any of their announced goals no doubt contributed to a subsequent reduction in terrorist hijackings.

1988年科威特航空422号航班劫机事件期间，当局与劫机者进行了广泛的谈判，但谈判的焦点却越来越分散，最终沦为一些细枝末节的问题。科威特政府在事件伊始便明确表示，不会释放劫机者的同伙——他们此前因恐怖主义行为被定罪，目前在科威特监狱服刑——并且政府始终坚持这一基本原则。然而，塞浦路斯和阿尔及利亚的地方当局却就飞机降落许可、额外燃料请求、新闻媒体采访以及食品供应等问题与劫机者进行了不懈的谈判。每一次谈判，这些地方当局都成功地促成了更多人质的获释。与此同时，他们以穆斯林的身份，呼吁人们遵循伊斯兰教的仁慈理念，并援引先知穆罕默德反对劫持人质的训诫。最终，所有人质都获释了。劫机者也被允许离开阿尔及利亚，但他们长期未能实现任何既定目标，这无疑导致了随后恐怖劫机事件的减少。

Negotiate with someone like Hitler? It depends on the alternative. Some interests you have may be worth fighting and even dying for. Many of us feel that ridding the world of fascism, standing up to territorial aggression, and putting a stop to genocide fall into that category. If such interests are at stake and cannot be met by less costly means, you should be prepared to fight if that will help, and—some will say—sometimes even if it won’t.

与希特勒这样的人谈判？这取决于你的选择。有些利益值得你为之奋斗，甚至牺牲生命。我们许多人认为，清除世界上的法西斯主义、抵制领土侵略、制止种族灭绝都属于此类。如果这些利益受到威胁，且无法通过代价较低的手段实现，那么你就应该做好战斗的准备，只要战斗能够有所帮助；有些人甚至会说，即使战斗无济于事，有时也应该战斗。

On the other hand, war is a nasty business, too often romanticized. If you can achieve a substantial measure of your interests through nonviolent means, you should give that option serious consideration. Few wars are as one-sided as the United Nations liberation of Kuwait. Even there, a negotiated withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait might have avoided the oil fires in Kuwait, the environmental damage to the Persian Gulf, and the enormous human suffering caused by the war.

另一方面，战争是一件残酷的事情，却常常被浪漫化。如果你能通过非暴力手段实现大部分自身利益，就应该认真考虑这种选择。很少有战争像联合国解放科威特那样一边倒。即便如此，如果伊拉克军队通过谈判从科威特撤军，或许就能避免科威特的油田大火、波斯湾的环境破坏以及战争造成的巨大人道主义灾难。

Most important, war offers no guarantee of results better than could be achieved by other means.
