As premier of the Soviet Union, Joseph Stalin was in many ways as objectionable to the world as Hitler had been. He committed a variety of territorial aggressions, engaged in genocide, and promoted a state-centered ideology that in practice looked a lot like National Socialism. But in an age of hydrogen bombs, conquering the Soviet Union as the Allies had conquered Germany in World War II was no longer a viable option. Nor did the principles at stake seem to justify mutual annihilation. Instead, the West waited, patient and steadfast in its moral opposition to Soviet communism, until it collapsed of its own accord.

最重要的是，战争并不能保证取得比其他手段更好的结果。作为苏联最高领导人，约瑟夫·斯大林在许多方面与希特勒一样令世人憎恶。他发动了各种领土侵略，实施了种族灭绝，并推行了一种以国家为中心的意识形态，这种意识形态在实践中与国家社会主义极为相似。但在氢弹时代，像盟军在二战中征服德国那样征服苏联已不再可行。而且，双方所面临的原则问题似乎也不足以成为相互毁灭的理由。因此，西方国家保持耐心，坚定地在道德上反对苏联共产主义，直到它自行崩溃。

Even with someone like Hitler or Stalin, we should consider negotiating if negotiation holds the promise of achieving an outcome that, all things considered, meets our interests better than our BATNA. [5] When a war does occur, in many cases it is actually a move within a negotiation. The violence is intended to change the other side’s BATNA, or their perception of it, so that they will more readily agree to our terms for peace. In such cases thinking in negotiation terms is vital so that we do not neglect to craft and communicate our offer in ways that we can reasonably expect will be persuasive to the other side.

即使面对希特勒或斯大林这样的人物，如果谈判有望达成一个综合所有因素后比我们的最佳替代方案（BATNA）更符合我们利益的结果，我们也应该考虑谈判。[5] 战争爆发时，在很多情况下，它实际上是谈判进程中的一个环节。暴力的目的是改变对方的最佳替代方案（BATNA），或者改变他们对最佳替代方案（BATNA）的认知，从而使他们更容易接受我们提出的和平条件。在这种情况下，运用谈判思维至关重要，这样我们才不会忽略精心设计并以我们认为能够说服对方的方式提出我们的方案。

Negotiate when people are acting out of religious conviction? Yes. Although people’s religious convictions are unlikely to be changed through negotiation, the actions they take, even those based on their convictions, may be subject to influence. Such was the case with the Kuwait Airways hijacking. A key point, worth repeating, is that negotiating does not require compromising your principles. More often success is achieved by finding a solution that is arguably consistent with each side’s principles.

当人们出于宗教信仰而采取行动时，是否应该进行谈判？答案是肯定的。虽然人们的宗教信仰不太可能通过谈判改变，但他们采取的行动，即使是基于信仰的行动，也可能受到谈判的影响。科威特航空劫机事件就是一个例证。一个值得重申的关键点是：谈判并不意味着要妥协你的原则。通常情况下，成功是通过找到一个双方原则都相对一致的解决方案来实现的。

Many situations only appear to be “religious” conflicts. The conflict in Northern Ireland between Protestants and Catholics, like the conflict in Lebanon between Christians and Muslims, is not over religion. In each case, religion serves as a handy boundary line for dividing one group from another. That cleavage is reinforced as it is used to divide where people live, where they work, who their friends are, and for whom they vote. Negotiation between such groups is highly desirable, as it improves the chance that they will be able to reach pragmatic accommodations that are to their mutual interest.

许多冲突表面上看似“宗教”冲突。北爱尔兰新教徒和天主教徒之间的冲突，如同黎巴嫩基督徒和穆斯林之间的冲突，并非源于宗教。在这两种情况下，宗教都只是划分群体的便捷分界线。这种分裂随着人们居住地、工作地点、朋友圈和投票意向的划分而不断强化。因此，这些群体之间的谈判至关重要，因为它能提高双方达成务实妥协、实现共同利益的可能性。

When does it make sense not to negotiate? Whether it makes sense to negotiate and how much effort to put into it depends on how satisfactory you find your BATNA and how likely you think it is that negotiation will produce better results. If your BATNA is fine and negotiation looks unpromising, there is no reason to invest much time in negotiation. On the other hand, if your BATNA is awful, you should be willing to invest a little more time—even where negotiation looks unpromising—to test whether something more satisfactory might be worked out.

什么情况下不谈判才是明智之举？是否应该谈判以及投入多少精力，取决于你对最佳替代方案（BATNA）的满意度，以及你认为谈判能带来更好结果的可能性有多大。如果你的最佳替代方案令人满意，而谈判前景黯淡，那么就没有理由在谈判上投入太多时间。另一方面，如果你的最佳替代方案非常糟糕，即使谈判前景黯淡，你也应该愿意投入更多时间，看看能否找到更令人满意的方案。

To do this analysis, you need to have thought carefully about your BATNA and the other side’s. You should not make the mistake of the bank that was negotiating with a bankrupt energy company. Legally, the bank was entitled to take over ownership of the entire company, but the judge in the case said that he wanted the parties to settle. The bank offered to take 51 percent of the stock and reduce the interest on the loan, but the company (owned by management) stonewalled. Frustrated, the bank spent months trying to get the company to show an interest in negotiating. Understandably, the company refused—the company saw their BATNA as merely waiting for oil prices to rise. At that point they could pay off their loan and they would still own 100 percent of their company. The bank had failed to think clearly either about their own BATNA or the company’s. The bank should have been negotiating with the judge, explaining how this situation was unfair and appealable. (Indeed, once the bank successfully enlisted the judge’s help—appealing to his interest in not having to hear the case—the company settled within twenty-four hours.) But the bank thought negotiating with the company was its only choice.

要进行这项分析，你需要仔细考虑你和对方的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。你不应该犯那家与破产能源公司谈判的银行的错误。从法律上讲，银行有权接管整个公司的所有权，但该案法官表示希望双方和解。银行提出收购51%的股份并降低贷款利息，但这家公司（由管理层所有）却百般阻挠。银行感到沮丧，花了几个月的时间试图让该公司表现出谈判的意愿。可以理解的是，该公司拒绝了——他们认为自己的最佳替代方案仅仅是等待油价上涨。届时，他们就可以偿还贷款，并且仍然拥有公司100%的股份。银行既没有认真考虑自己的最佳替代方案，也没有考虑公司的。银行本应与法官协商，解释这种情况的不公平之处以及可以上诉的理由。 （事实上，一旦银行成功争取到法官的帮助——利用他不想审理此案的利益——该公司在24小时内就达成了和解。）但银行认为与该公司谈判是其唯一的选择。

Governments often make the mistake of assuming that they have a better BATNA than they do—for example, when they imply that if “political” and “economic” means fail in a given situation, then there is always “the military option.” There is not always a viable military option. (Consider most hostage situations, in which there is no military option that can realistically promise the hostages’ safe retrieval. Successful rescue raids like that of the Israeli military on the Ugandan airport at Entebbe—an airport designed and built by Israeli engineers—are exceptional and become more difficult with each success, as terrorists adapt to new tactics.) Whether or not we have a self-help option depends on the situation: Can the objective be achieved solely through our own efforts, or will someone on the other side have to make a decision? If the latter, then whose decision will we have to influence, what decision do we want, and how, if at all, could military force help influence that decision?’

政府常常犯一个错误，那就是高估了自身拥有的最佳替代方案（BATNA）——例如，他们暗示，如果“政治”和“经济”手段在特定情况下失效，那么总有“军事选项”。然而，并非总有可行的军事选项。（想想大多数人质危机，在这些危机中，没有任何军事选项能够真正保证人质安全获救。像以色列军队在恩德培机场（由以色列工程师设计建造）的营救行动那样成功的营救行动实属例外，而且随着恐怖分子不断调整战术，营救难度也会随之增加。）我们是否有自助选项取决于具体情况：目标能否仅靠我们自身的努力实现？或者对方必须做出决定？如果是后者，那么我们需要影响谁的决定？我们希望对方做出怎样的决定？军事力量又该如何（如果有的话）才能影响这一决定？

Don’t assume that you have a BATNA better than negotiating or that you don’t. Think it through. Then decide whether negotiating makes sense.

不要想当然地认为你一定有比谈判更好的替代方案（BATNA），或者根本没有。仔细考虑一下。然后再决定谈判是否明智。

Question 6: “How should I adjust my negotiating approach to account for differences of personality, gender, culture, and so on?”

问题 6：“我应该如何调整我的谈判方式以适应性格、性别、文化等方面的差异？”

In some ways people everywhere are similar to one another. We want to be loved, we care about the respect of other people and of ourselves, and we do not like to feel taken advantage of. In other ways, people—even those of similar background—are quite different. Some of us are outgoing, others shy; some verbal and logic-chopping, others more physical and emotive; some people are blunt, others more indirect and tactful; some relish conflict, others will do almost anything to avoid it. As negotiators, different people will have different interests and styles of communication. Different things may be persuasive to them, and they may have different ways of making decisions. How should we accommodate such similarities and differences in negotiating with different people? Here are some suggested guidelines:

在某些方面，世界各地的人们彼此相似。我们渴望被爱，重视他人和自身的尊重，也不喜欢被人占便宜。但在其他方面，人们——即使是背景相似的人——也截然不同。有些人外向，有些人内向；有些人善于言辞、逻辑清晰，有些人则更注重肢体语言和情感表达；有些人直率，有些人则更委婉、更讲究技巧；有些人乐于冲突，有些人则会竭尽全力避免冲突。作为谈判者，不同的人会有不同的兴趣和沟通风格。不同的事物可能对他们更有说服力，他们做决定的方式也可能不同。在与不同的人谈判时，我们应该如何兼顾这些相似之处和差异呢？以下是一些建议的指导原则：

Get in step. In any negotiation it is highly desirable to be sensitive to the values, perceptions, concerns, norms of behavior, and mood of those with whom you are dealing. Adapt your behavior accordingly. If you are negotiating with someone, it is that person whom you are trying to affect. The more successfully you can get in step with that person’s way of thinking, the more likely you are to be able to work out an agreement. Some common differences that can make a difference in negotiation include the following:

步调一致。在任何谈判中，对谈判对象的价值观、认知、顾虑、行为规范和情绪保持敏感至关重要。相应地调整你的行为。如果你正在与某人谈判，那么你试图影响的就是对方。你越能与对方的思维方式保持一致，就越有可能达成协议。以下是一些可能影响谈判结果的常见差异：

  • Pacing: fast or slow?
    节奏：快还是慢？
  • Formality: high or low?
    正式程度：高还是低？
  • Physical proximity while talking: close or distant?
    交谈时的身体距离：近还是远？
  • Oral or written agreements: which are more binding and inclusive?
    口头协议还是书面协议：哪种更具约束力和包容性？
  • Bluntness of communication: direct or indirect?
    沟通方式的直率程度：直接还是间接？
  • Time frame: short-term or longer?
    时间范围：短期还是长期？
  • Scope of relationship: business-only or all-encompassing?
    合作关系范围：仅限于业务往来还是涵盖所有方面？
  • The expected place of doing business: private or public?
    预期开展业务的地点：私营还是公共？
  • Who negotiates: equals in status or the most competent people for the task?
    谁来谈判：地位相当的人还是最适合这项任务的人？
  • Rigidity of commitments: written in stone or meant to be flexible?
    承诺的僵化程度：是铁律式的还是可以灵活变通的？

Adapt our general advice to the specific situation. This is a book of general advice. It will not apply in the same way in every circumstance with every person. But the basic propositions are generally applicable. Absent a compelling reason to do otherwise, we advise crafting your specific approach to every negotiation around them. The best way to implement these general principles will depend on the specific context. Consider where you are, with whom you are dealing, customs of the industry, past experience with this negotiator, and so on, in crafting an approach to fit the situation.

根据具体情况调整我们的通用建议。本书提供的是通用建议，并非适用于所有人和所有情况。但基本原则具有普遍适用性。除非有充分的理由，否则我们建议您围绕这些原则制定针对每次谈判的具体策略。实施这些通用原则的最佳方式取决于具体情况。在制定适合当前情况的策略时，请考虑您所处的环境、谈判对象、行业惯例、与该谈判者的过往经验等等。

Pay attention to differences of belief and custom, but avoid stereotyping individuals. Different groups and places have different customs and beliefs. Know and respect them, but beware of making assumptions about individuals.

尊重信仰和习俗的差异，但避免对个人抱有刻板印象。不同的群体和地区有着不同的习俗和信仰。了解并尊重它们，但切勿妄下断言。

The attitudes, interests, and other characteristics of an individual are often quite different from those of a group to which they may belong. For example, the “average” Japanese tends to favor more indirect methods of communication and negotiation, but individual Japanese span the full gamut of negotiating styles. One prominent, long-time minister in the Japanese government was famous for his brash “American-style” negotiating—which is not at all typical of many Americans. Some research suggests that women are more likely than men to gather information in a more open and less structured way, to be more sensitive to relationships, and to operate on a morality that is based proportionately more on caring and obligation to others and less on rules and individual rights. These same data, however, suggest that there are a great many individuals of each sex who tend the other way. [6]

个人的态度、兴趣和其他特征往往与他们所属群体截然不同。例如，“普通”日本人倾向于使用较为间接的沟通和谈判方式，但日本人个体的谈判风格却涵盖了所有类型。一位在日本政府中身居要职的资深大臣就以其大胆的“美式”谈判风格而闻名——这与大多数美国人的风格截然不同。一些研究表明，女性比男性更倾向于以更开放、更少结构化的方式收集信息，更注重人际关系，并且她们的道德观更多地基于对他人的关怀和义务，而非规则和个人权利。然而，同样的数据也表明，男女中都有相当一部分人倾向于相反的风格。[6]

Making assumptions about someone based on their group characteristics is insulting, as well as factually risky. It denies that person his or her individuality. We do not assume that our beliefs and habits are dictated by the groups in which we happen to fit; to imply as much of others is demeaning. Each of us is affected by myriad aspects of our environment and upbringing, our culture and group identity, but in no individually predictable way.

基于群体特征对他人妄下断言既是一种侮辱，也存在事实风险。这种做法否定了个人的个性。我们不会认为自己的信仰和习惯是由我们恰好所属的群体决定的；暗示他人也受其影响是一种贬低。我们每个人都受到环境、成长经历、文化和群体认同等诸多因素的影响，但这些影响的方式并非个人可以预测的。

Question your assumptions; listen actively. Whatever assumption you make about others—whether you assume they are just like you or totally different—question it. Be open to learning that they are quite unlike what you expected. The wide variations among cultures provide clues as to the kind of differences for which you should be looking, but remember that all of us have special interests and qualities that do not fit any standard mold.

质疑你的假设；积极倾听。无论你对他人抱有怎样的假设——无论你认为他们和你一样还是截然不同——都要质疑它。要乐于接受他们可能与你预期大相径庭的事实。不同文化之间的巨大差异为我们提供了线索，让我们知道应该关注哪些方面的差异，但请记住，我们每个人都有独特的兴趣和特质，无法被任何标准模式所束缚。

QUESTIONS ABOUT TACTICS

关于战术的问题

Question 7: “How do I decide things like ‘Where should we meet?’ ‘How should we communicate?’ ‘Who should make the first offer?’ and ‘How high should I start?’”

问题 7：“我该如何决定诸如‘我们应该在哪里见面？’‘我们应该如何沟通？’‘谁应该先报价？’以及‘我应该开出多高的价位？’之类的事情？”

Before a doctor can answer such questions as what pill to take and what food to avoid, he or she will want to learn about the patient’s symptoms and diagnose possible causes. Only then can the doctor develop a general strategy for better health. The same is true for specialists in negotiation. We have no all-purpose patent medicines. Good tactical advice requires knowledge of specific circumstances.

医生在回答诸如服用什么药、避免食用什么食物等问题之前，需要了解患者的症状并诊断可能的病因。只有这样，医生才能制定出改善健康的总体策略。谈判专家也是如此。我们没有万能的专利药。好的策略建议需要了解具体情况。

This can be illustrated by considering four specific examples:

我们可以通过以下四个具体例子来说明这一点：

Where should we meet? What are we worried about? If both parties tend to be extremely busy and subject to constant interruptions, seclusion may be the most important consideration. If the other person tends to feel insecure or in need of staff support, perhaps they would be more comfortable meeting in their office. You may also want to meet in the other party’s office if you would like to feel free to walk away. Are there charts, files, or technical experts that you might want to be able to consult during the negotiation? If you want to be free to use flip charts, a whiteboard, or an overhead projector, you may want to meet in a conference room that has such facilities.

我们应该在哪里见面？我们都担心什么？如果双方都非常忙碌且经常被打断，那么私密性可能是最重要的考虑因素。如果对方容易感到不安全或需要工作人员的支持，他们或许会更愿意在自己的办公室见面。如果您希望可以随时离开，也可以选择在对方的办公室见面。谈判过程中，您是否需要查阅图表、文件或咨询技术专家？如果您希望能够自由使用挂图、白板或投影仪，那么最好选择配备这些设备的会议室。

How should we communicate? Today many negotiations are conducted by phone, email, or text, and the interaction can be quite different than meeting face-to-face. The short length and abbreviations used in texting greatly increase the likelihood of unintended misunderstandings. The lack of audio and visual cues in texts and email make it much harder to hear or interpret the emotional undertones of communication, which can feed our tendency to hear the worst. Furthermore, not having another person in front of us reduces or eliminates the impact of “mirror neurons” in our brain, which normally increase our empathy and sense of human connection with our counterpart.

我们应该如何沟通？如今，许多谈判都是通过电话、电子邮件或短信进行的，这种互动方式与面对面交流截然不同。短信中常用的简短文字和缩写大大增加了产生误解的可能性。短信和电子邮件缺乏音频和视觉线索，使得我们更难听懂或解读沟通中的情感弦外之音，这容易导致我们倾向于往坏处想。此外，由于没有面对面的人，大脑中“镜像神经元”的作用会减弱甚至消失，而镜像神经元通常会增强我们的同理心和与对方的情感联系。

One study suggests the potential impact of these differences: In a negotiation where only sellers knew what an item was worth, the results varied dramatically based on the mode of communication. In face-to-face interactions, only a small minority of sellers lied and took advantage. But in written interactions a third did and in phone negotiations more than half did. Meanwhile, buyers were appropriately wary in written interactions, but generally trusting in face-to-face and phone negotiations, leading many telephone buyers to be seriously disadvantaged. Almost 60 percent of face-to-face negotiations resulted in mutually beneficial agreements, while only 22 percent did in written interactions and 38 percent in telephone negotiations. Meanwhile, more than half of the written interactions resulted in impasse, while only 19 percent of the face-to-face talks and 14 percent of the telephone negotiations did. [7]

一项研究表明了这些差异的潜在影响：在只有卖方知道商品价值的谈判中，结果会因沟通方式的不同而产生显著差异。在面对面交流中，只有极少数卖方撒谎或占买方便宜。但在书面交流中，三分之一的卖方会这样做，而在电话谈判中，超过一半的卖方会这样做。与此同时，买方在书面交流中保持了应有的谨慎，但在面对面和电话谈判中则普遍信任卖方，这导致许多电话买家处于严重不利地位。近60%的面对面谈判达成了互惠互利的协议，而书面交流中只有22%达成了互惠互利的协议，电话谈判中也只有38%达成了互惠互利的协议。此外，超过一半的书面交流以僵局告终，而面对面谈判和电话谈判中分别只有19%和14%陷入僵局。[7]

What are the implications of such differences for strategy? First, difficult conversations involving emotions or relationship issues are best pursued face-to-face, if at all possible, and definitely not by email or text. If a phone call is the only option, consider using a Webcam and an Internet service to make it a video call.

这些差异对策略有何影响？首先，涉及情绪或人际关系问题的棘手对话最好尽可能面对面进行，绝对不要通过电子邮件或短信。如果只能打电话，可以考虑使用网络摄像头和网络服务进行视频通话。

When you are on the phone, and especially when you are using email or texts, make an effort to create some personal connection before diving into substance. Studies show that a little effort up front to schmooze—to learn and share something personal, to evoke an existing relationship or shared identity, or to find a shared connection—helps promote cooperation and increases the chances of agreement. With email or a text, reread your message one or more times before sending. Put in a little extra effort to make the context and your reasoning transparent. Look for ambiguities and ask yourself how the other party could hear something different from what you intend. Then, if a reply suggests that your message has possibly generated a bad or unexpected reaction, consider changing your mode of communication before continuing. Walk down the hall, or pick up the phone.

打电话时，尤其是在使用电子邮件或短信时，在深入讨论实质内容之前，务必努力建立一些个人联系。研究表明，事先花点心思进行寒暄——了解并分享一些个人信息、唤起现有的关系或共同身份认同，或者寻找共同点——有助于促进合作，并提高达成共识的可能性。使用电子邮件或短信时，发送前请反复阅读一遍或几遍。多花些心思，使上下文和你的逻辑清晰明了。注意是否存在歧义，并问问自己对方可能如何理解与你本意不同的内容。如果对方的回复表明你的信息可能引发了不良或意想不到的反应，请考虑在继续之前改变沟通方式。可以走到走廊尽头，或者拿起电话。

Even if the bulk of your communication needs to be on email, try to have an initial meeting in person or on the phone, and schedule periodic check-ins in the same mode, to create and maintain a level of human connection. It also helps to make some procedural agreements that anticipate possible difficulties. For example, you may want to make a mutual promise to raise even tentative concerns early, in person or by phone, and to raise them as fears, fantasies, or hypotheses, rather than as accusations.

即使大部分沟通需要通过电子邮件进行，也尽量安排一次初次会面（无论是当面还是电话），并定期以同样的方式进行沟通，以建立和维持人与人之间的联系。事先达成一些程序性协议，预先应对可能出现的困难也很有帮助。例如，你们可以共同承诺，尽早当面或通过电话提出哪怕是初步的担忧，并且要以恐惧、设想或假设的形式提出，而不是以指责的形式。

Of course, there are occasions where using the phone, email, or texting may be advantageous. Many people find it easier to be less accommodating on the phone, for example, and to ask tougher questions. Research suggests that people pay closer attention to content in the absence of other interpersonal information, and that strong arguments may have more effect by email than face-to-face. Email also allows time for reflection and research before answering, which can help you avoid making unwise decisions under pressure. (Texting, in contrast, tends to move faster and can give “fast talkers” an undeserved edge.)

当然，有些情况下，使用电话、电子邮件或短信可能更有优势。例如，许多人发现，在电话里更容易不那么迁就对方，也更容易提出更尖锐的问题。研究表明，在缺乏其他人际信息的情况下，人们会更加关注邮件内容，而且强有力的论点通过电子邮件可能比面对面交流更有说服力。电子邮件还允许你在回复之前进行思考和研究，这有助于你避免在压力下做出不明智的决定。（相比之下，短信交流节奏更快，可能会让“语速快”的人获得不应有的优势。）

As always, the choice of how to communicate is something that should emerge from careful preparation, taking into account these kinds of considerations.

一如既往，沟通方式的选择应该经过仔细准备，并考虑到这些因素。

Who should make the first offer? It would be a mistake to assume that making an offer is always the best way to put a figure on the table. Usually you will want to explore interests, options, and criteria for a while before making an offer. Making an offer too soon can make the other side feel railroaded. Once both sides have a sense of the problem, an offer that makes an effort to reconcile the interests and standards that have been advanced is more likely to be received as a constructive step forward. (Without that groundwork, even a generous offer may be seen suspiciously as a result of what social psychologists call “reactive devaluation”: If you are offering it, it must not be good for me. [8] )

谁应该先提出报价？认为报价总是提出价格的最佳方式是错误的。通常情况下，在提出报价之前，你需要先了解对方的兴趣、选择和标准一段时间。过早报价会让对方感到被迫。一旦双方都对问题有了大致的了解，一个努力调和双方已提出的利益和标准的报价更有可能被视为建设性的进步。（如果没有这些铺垫，即使是慷慨的报价也可能因为社会心理学家所说的“反应性贬值”而受到怀疑：既然你提出了这个报价，那它肯定对我没好处。[8]）

Whether or not you make an offer, you may want to try to “anchor” the discussion early around an approach or standard favorable to you. On the other hand, if you are ill prepared and have no idea what would be reasonable, you will probably be reluctant to put an idea or an offer on the table, perhaps hoping that the other side will go first and offer something generous. But you should be careful. It is extremely risky to measure the value of an item by the other side’s first proposal or figure. If you know that little about an item’s value, you should probably engage in more research before starting the negotiation.

无论你是否主动出价，你都可以尝试在谈判初期就将讨论“锚定”在你认为有利的方案或标准上。另一方面，如果你准备不足，对合理的条件一无所知，你可能不愿提出任何想法或报价，或许希望对方先出价，给出更慷慨的条件。但你务必谨慎。根据对方的第一个报价或数字来衡量物品的价值是极其冒险的。如果你对物品的价值知之甚少，那么在开始谈判之前，你最好进行更多调查研究。

The better prepared both parties are in a negotiation over price, the less difference it makes who makes the first offer. Rather than learning rules about who should make the first offer, it would be better to learn the rule of being well prepared with external measures of value.

双方在价格谈判中准备越充分，谁先出价的影响就越小。与其纠结于谁应该先出价，不如学习如何充分准备外部价值衡量标准。

How high should I start? Many people tend to measure success by how far the other party has moved. Even if the first figure is a wholly arbitrary assertion of “sticker price” or “retail value,” buyers will often feel happy about getting something for less. They have not checked the market. They do not know what their best alternative would cost, so they derive satisfaction from paying less than the first “asking price.”

我应该一开始就出价多少？很多人倾向于以对方出价的幅度来衡量成功与否。即使第一个数字完全是随意设定的“标价”或“零售价”，买家通常也会因为能以更低的价格买到东西而感到高兴。他们没有考察过市场行情，也不知道最佳替代方案的价格是多少，所以他们会因为支付的价格低于最初的“要价”而感到满足。

Under these circumstances, if you are selling, you would ordinarily start with the highest figure that you could justify without embarrassment. Another way to think of it is to start with the highest figure that you would try to persuade a neutral third party was fair. In putting forth such a figure you would first explain the reasoning and then give the number. (If they hear a number they don’t like, they may not listen to the reasoning.)

在这种情况下，如果你是销售人员，通常会先报出你能坦然接受的最高价格。换句话说，先报出你能说服中立的第三方认为合理的最高价格。在提出这个价格时，你应该先解释原因，然后再给出具体数字。（如果他们听到一个不喜欢的数字，可能就不会听你解释。）

Such an opening figure need not be advanced as a firm position. Indeed, the firmer you suggest early figures to be, the greater you damage your credibility as you move off them. It is safer and at least as effective to say something like “Well, one factor to consider would be what others are paying for comparable work. In New York, for example, they pay $58 an hour. How does that sound?” Here you have put out a standard and a figure without committing to it at all.

这样的初步报价不必作为最终定论。事实上，你提出的数字越是坚定，当你偏离这些数字时，你的信誉就越容易受损。更稳妥也至少同样有效的做法是这样说：“嗯，需要考虑的一个因素是其他人对类似工作的收费标准。例如，在纽约，他们支付每小时 58 美元。您觉得怎么样？” 这样，你就提出了一个标准和一个具体的数字，而没有做出任何承诺。

Strategy depends on preparation. There are two generalizations about strategy worth passing along. First, in almost all cases, strategy is a function of preparation. If you are well prepared, a strategy will suggest itself. If you are well versed in the standards relevant to your negotiation, it will be obvious which ones to discuss and which ones the other side might raise. If you have thoroughly considered your interests, it will be clear which ones to mention early on and which ones to bring up later or not at all. And if you have formulated your BATNA in advance, you’ll know when it’s time to walk.

策略取决于准备。关于策略，有两点值得一提。首先，几乎在所有情况下，策略都取决于准备。如果你准备充分，策略自然会水到渠成。如果你熟知与谈判相关的标准，哪些标准需要讨论，哪些标准对方可能会提出，就会一目了然。如果你已经充分考虑过自身利益，就会清楚地知道哪些利益应该尽早提及，哪些利益应该稍后再提，甚至完全不提。如果你事先制定了最佳替代方案（BATNA），你就会知道何时应该放弃谈判。

Second, a clever strategy cannot make up for lack of preparation. If you formulate a step-by-step strategy that is sure to knock their socks off, you will run into trouble when they come into the negotiation wearing sandals. Your strategy might depend on discussing relationship issues at the beginning, but they might want to talk about BATNAs. Because you can never be sure what their strategy will be, it is far better to know the terrain than to plan on taking one particular path through the woods.

其次，再巧妙的策略也无法弥补准备不足。如果你制定了一套万无一失的策略，确保对方会感到惊艳，但当他们穿着凉鞋走进谈判桌时，你就会陷入困境。你的策略可能依赖于一开始就讨论关系问题，但他们可能更想讨论最佳替代方案（BATNA）。因为你永远无法确定他们的策略是什么，所以了解谈判的整体情况远比计划走一条特定的路径要好得多。

Question 8: “Concretely, how do I move from inventing options to making commitments?”

问题 8：“具体来说，我该如何从提出方案过渡到做出承诺？”

We have offered a great deal of advice on how to develop wise, mutually satisfying options in negotiation and how to avoid or overcome a variety of people problems. The question remains, how do you reach closure on issues? We don’t believe that there is any one best process, but here are some general principles worth considering:

我们已经就如何在谈判中制定明智且双方都能接受的方案，以及如何避免或克服各种人际关系问题提供了大量建议。但问题依然存在：如何才能最终解决问题？我们认为并不存在最佳方案，但以下是一些值得考虑的一般原则：

Think about closure from the beginning. Before you even begin to negotiate, it makes sense to envision what a successful agreement might look like. This will help you figure out what issues will need to be dealt with in the negotiation and what it might take to resolve them. Imagine what it might be like to implement an agreement. What issues would need to be resolved? Then work backward. Ask yourself how the other side might successfully explain and justify an agreement to their constituents. (“We will be in the top 10 percent of all electrical workers in Ontario.” “We are paying less than the value given by two out of three appraisers.”) Think about what it will take for you to do the same. Then ask yourself what kind of an agreement would allow you both to say such things. Finally, think about what it might take to persuade the other side—and you—to accept a proposed agreement, rather than continuing to negotiate.

从一开始就考虑达成最终协议。在开始谈判之前，最好先设想一下成功的协议会是什么样子。这将有助于你弄清楚谈判中需要处理哪些问题，以及解决这些问题可能需要哪些措施。想象一下执行协议会是什么样子。需要解决哪些问题？然后反向思考。问问自己，对方会如何成功地向他们的支持者解释和证明协议的合理性。（例如，“我们将跻身安大略省所有电工的前10%。”“我们支付的工资低于三位评估师中两位给出的估值。”）想想你需要做些什么才能做到这一点。然后问问自己，什么样的协议才能让双方都这么说。最后，想想如何才能说服对方——以及你自己——接受拟议的协议，而不是继续谈判。

Keep these questions in mind as your negotiation progresses, reshaping and filling in your vision as more information becomes available. Focusing on your goal in this way will help to keep your negotiation on a productive track.

在谈判过程中，请始终牢记这些问题，并随着更多信息的获取不断调整和完善您的方案。这样专注于您的目标将有助于确保谈判朝着富有成效的方向发展。

Consider crafting a framework agreement. In negotiations that will produce a written agreement, it is usually a good idea to sketch the outlines of what an agreement might look like as part of your preparation. Such a “framework agreement” is a document in the form of an agreement, but with blank spaces for each term to be resolved by negotiation. The standard purchase-and-sale form that is available from any real-estate broker is an example of a detailed framework agreement. In other cases nothing more than a list of headings may be appropriate. Working out a framework agreement, however detailed, will help ensure that important issues are not overlooked during the negotiation. Such an agreement can serve as a starting point and an agenda for the negotiation, helping you to use your time efficiently.

考虑拟定一份框架协议。在需要达成书面协议的谈判中，通常最好在准备阶段就勾勒出协议的框架。这种“框架协议”的形式与正式协议类似，但会留出空白处，以便通过谈判解决具体条款。任何房地产经纪人提供的标准买卖合同就是一个详细的框架协议示例。在其他情况下，可能只需列出一些标题即可。无论框架协议多么详细，制定一份框架协议都能确保在谈判过程中不会遗漏重要问题。这样的协议可以作为谈判的起点和议程，帮助您高效利用时间。

Whether or not you start your negotiation with a framework agreement, it makes sense to draft possible terms of an agreement as you go. Working on a draft helps to keep discussions focused, tends to surface important issues that might otherwise be overlooked, and gives a sense of progress. Drafting as you go also provides a record of discussions, reducing the chance of later misunderstanding. If you are working with a framework agreement, drafting may involve no more than filling in the blanks as you discuss each term; or, if you have yet to reach consensus, it may involve drafting alternative provisions.

无论谈判是否从框架协议开始，边谈判边拟定可能的协议条款都是明智之举。拟定草案有助于保持讨论的重点，往往能发现一些容易被忽略的重要问题，并带来进展感。边谈判边拟定还能记录讨论内容，减少日后产生误解的可能性。如果采用框架协议，拟定工作可能只是在讨论每个条款时填写空白；如果尚未达成共识，则可能需要拟定备选条款。

Move toward commitment gradually. As the negotiation proceeds and you discuss options and standards for each issue, you should be seeking a consensus proposal that reflects all the points made and meets each side’s interests on that issue as well as possible. If you are as yet unable to reach consensus on a single option, try at least to narrow the range of options under consideration and then go on to another issue. Perhaps a better option or a trade-off possibility will occur later. (“All right. So perhaps something like $68,000 or $70,000 might make sense on salary. What about starting date?”)

逐步达成承诺。随着谈判的进行，在讨论每个问题的选项和标准时，你们应该寻求一个能够反映所有观点并尽可能满足各方利益的共识方案。如果你们目前还无法就任何单一选项达成共识，至少要尝试缩小考虑范围，然后再讨论其他问题。或许之后会出现更好的选项或折衷方案。（“好的。那么，或许6.8万美元或7万美元的薪资比较合理。那么，入职日期呢？”）

To encourage brainstorming, it is a good idea to agree explicitly that all commitments are tentative. This will allow you to have some sense of progress during your discussions, while avoiding the inhibiting effect of worrying that every option discussed may be heard as a commitment. Tentative commitments are fine and should not be changed without reason. But make clear that you are not firmly committing yourself to anything until you see the final package. At the top of a framework agreement, for example, you might write: “Tentative Draft—No Commitments.”

为了鼓励集思广益，最好明确约定所有承诺均为暂定。这样既能让你在讨论过程中感受到进展，又能避免因担心每个讨论的选项都可能被视为承诺而产生的顾虑。暂定承诺是可以接受的，不应无故更改。但务必明确表示，在看到最终方案之前，你不会对任何事情做出正式承诺。例如，在框架协议的开头，你可以写上：“暂定草案——不作任何承诺。”

The process of moving toward agreement is seldom linear. Be prepared to move through the list of issues several times, going back and forth between looking at particular issues and the total package. Difficult issues may be revisited frequently or set aside until the end, depending on whether incremental progress seems possible. Along the way, avoid demands or locking in. Instead, offer options and ask for criticism. (“What would you think of an agreement along the lines of this draft? I am not sure I could sell it to my people, but it might be in the ballpark. Could something like this work for you? If not, what would be wrong with it?”)

达成协议的过程很少是线性的。要做好准备，反复审视问题清单，在具体问题和整体方案之间来回切换。棘手的问题可能需要频繁讨论，或者暂时搁置到最后，这取决于能否逐步取得进展。在此过程中，避免提出要求或固守成规。相反，要提供多种选择并征求意见。（例如：“您觉得这份草案的协议怎么样？我不确定能否说服我的团队，但或许可以接受。您觉得这样的方案可行吗？如果不行，问题出在哪里？”）

Be persistent in pursuing your interests but not rigid in pursuing any particular solution. One way to be firm without being positional is to separate your interests from ways to meet them. When a proposal is challenged, don’t defend the proposal; rather explain again your underlying interests. Ask if the other side can think of a better way to meet those interests, as well as their own. If there appears to be an irresolvable conflict, ask if there is any reason why one side’s interests should have priority over the other’s.

坚持己见，但不要固执己见，执着于任何特定的解决方案。一种既能坚定立场又不显得立场强硬的方法是，将自身利益与实现利益的方式区分开来。当某个提议受到质疑时，不要为其辩护，而是再次阐明你的根本利益。询问对方是否能想到更好的方法来兼顾你的利益以及他们自身的利益。如果存在无法解决的冲突，询问是否存在任何理由，使得一方的利益优先于另一方。

Unless the other side makes a persuasive case for why your thinking is incomplete and should be changed, stick to your analysis. When and if you are persuaded, modify your thinking accordingly, presenting the logic first. (“Well, that’s a good point. One way to measure that factor would be to . . . .”) If you have prepared well, you should have anticipated most arguments the other side might raise and thought through how you think they should affect the result.

除非对方提出令人信服的理由，证明你的想法不完整且需要改变，否则就坚持你的分析。当你被说服时，根据对方的论点调整你的想法，但首先要阐明逻辑。（“嗯，这是一个很好的观点。衡量这一因素的一种方法是……”）如果你准备充分，就应该预料到对方可能提出的大部分论点，并思考这些论点会如何影响最终结果。

Throughout, the goal is to avoid useless quarreling. Where disagreements persist, seek second-order agreement—agreement on where you disagree. Make sure that each side’s interests and reasoning are clear. Seek differing assumptions and ways to test them. As always seek to reconcile conflicting interests with external standards or creative options. Seek to reconcile conflicting standards with criteria for evaluating which is more appropriate or with creative trade-offs. Be persistent.

始终以避免无谓的争吵为目标。如果分歧持续存在，则寻求达成第二层共识——即就分歧所在达成共识。确保双方的利益和理由都清晰明确。寻找不同的假设以及检验这些假设的方法。一如既往，尝试用外部标准或创造性方案来调和冲突的利益。尝试用评估哪种标准更合适的标准或创造性的权衡方案来调和冲突的标准。坚持不懈。

Make an offer. At some point clarifying interests, inventing options, and analyzing standards produce diminishing returns. Once an issue or group of issues is well explored, you should be prepared to make an offer. An early offer might be limited to the pairing of a couple of key issues. (“I would agree to a June 30 closing if the down payment were not more than $50,000.”) Later, such partial offers can be combined into a more comprehensive proposal.

提出报价。在某个阶段，澄清利益、提出方案和分析标准所带来的收益会递减。一旦某个或一组问题得到充分探讨，就应该准备提出报价。早期报价可能仅限于几个关键问题的组合。（例如：“如果首付不超过5万美元，我同意在6月30日完成交易。”）之后，可以将这些部分报价合并成一个更全面的方案。

Usually an offer should not come as a surprise. It should be a natural outgrowth of the discussion so far. It need not be a “take-it-or-leave-it” proposal, but neither should it be an opening position. It should be an offer that you think would make sense for both sides, given what has gone before. Many negotiations settle when a complete offer is made.

通常情况下，报价不应该让人感到意外，而应该是目前为止讨论的自然结果。它不必是“要么接受，要么放弃”的方案，但也不应该是一个开场白。报价应该是基于之前的讨论，你认为对双方都有利的。很多谈判都是在提出完整报价后达成的。

You should give some thought to how and where you convey an offer. If discussions have been carried on publicly or in large groups, you may want to seek a more private occasion for exploring final commitments. Most agreements are made in one-on-one meetings between the top negotiators for each side, although formal closure may come later in a more public forum.

您应该仔细考虑如何以及在何处提出报价。如果双方此前已公开或在大型会议上进行过讨论，您不妨寻找一个更私密的场合来探讨最终承诺。大多数协议都是在双方首席谈判代表的单独会谈中达成的，尽管正式的最终敲定可能会在之后的公开场合进行。

If agreement makes sense but some issues remain stubbornly in dispute, look for fair procedures to facilitate closure. Splitting the difference between arbitrary figures produces an arbitrary result. But splitting the difference between figures that are each backed by legitimate and persuasive independent standards is one way to find a fair result. Another approach, where differences persist, is for one or both parties to invite a third party to talk with each side and, perhaps after repeated consultations, produce a final “last chance” recommendation.

如果双方达成协议合情合理，但仍有一些问题顽固地存在争议，则应寻求公平的程序来促成最终解决。随意取个价只会得到一个随意的结果。但如果双方都以合法且令人信服的独立标准为依据，那么取个价则是找到公平结果的途径之一。另一种方法是，如果分歧依然存在，则由一方或双方邀请第三方分别与双方进行磋商，并在多次协商后，提出最终的“最后机会”建议。

Be generous at the end. When you sense you are finally close to an agreement, consider giving the other side something you know to be of value to them and still consistent with the basic logic of your proposal. Make clear that this is a final gesture; you do not want to raise expectations of further concessions. Such an improved offer can sometimes break through any last-minute doubts and clinch the deal.

最后阶段要慷慨一些。当你感觉双方即将达成协议时，可以考虑给予对方一些你认为对他们有价值的东西，并且这些东西仍然要符合你提议的基本逻辑。要明确表示这是最后的姿态；你不想让对方对进一步的让步抱有期待。这样一份改进后的提议有时可以消除对方在最后时刻的疑虑，最终促成交易。

You want the other side to leave the negotiation feeling satisfied and fairly treated. That feeling can pay off handsomely in the implementation of an agreement as well as in future negotiations.

你希望对方在谈判结束后感到满意，并认为自己受到了公平对待。这种感觉对于协议的执行以及未来的谈判都大有裨益。

Question 9: “How do I try out these ideas without taking too much risk?”

问题 9：“如何在不冒太大风险的情况下尝试这些想法？”

Perhaps you are persuaded that this approach makes sense but are worried that you will not be able to execute it well enough to better the results of your current approach. What can you do to try out these ideas without taking too much risk?

或许您认为这种方法有道理，但又担心自己无法将其有效执行，从而无法超越当前方法的效果。那么，如何在不承担过大风险的情况下尝试这些想法呢？

Start small. Experiment in negotiations where the stakes are small, where you have a good BATNA, where favorable objective standards are available and seem relevant, and where the other side is likely to be amenable to this approach. Start with ideas that build on your current skills, then try out new ideas one at a time. As you gain experience and confidence, slowly raise the stakes by trying new techniques in more significant and challenging contexts. You don’t have to try everything at once.

从小处着手。先在风险较小、有最佳替代方案（BATNA）、有有利且相关的客观标准、对方可能接受这种方法的谈判中进行尝试。从那些能够提升你现有技能的想法入手，然后一次尝试一种新方法。随着经验和信心的积累，逐渐提高风险，在更重要、更具挑战性的情境中尝试新的技巧。不必一次性尝试所有方法。

Make an investment. Some people play tennis all their lives but never get better. Those people are not willing to take a fresh look at what they do or to consider changing it. Good players recognize that getting better often means making an investment in new approaches. For a while they may get worse as they wrestle with new and unfamiliar techniques, but eventually they surpass their old plateau. The new techniques offer more long-term potential. You need to do the same with negotiation.

进行投资。有些人一辈子都在打网球，却始终无法进步。这些人不愿意重新审视自己的打法，也不愿意考虑改变。优秀的球员明白，进步往往意味着投资于新的方法。在学习新的、不熟悉的技巧时，他们可能会暂时退步，但最终他们会突破之前的瓶颈。新的技巧蕴含着更大的长期潜力。谈判也是如此。

Review your performance. Schedule time to think about how you did after each significant negotiation. What worked? What did not? What might you have done differently? Consider keeping a negotiation journal or diary, which you can reread periodically.

回顾你的表现。每次重要谈判结束后，都要安排时间思考自己的表现。哪些方面做得好？哪些方面做得不好？你本可以采取哪些不同的做法？不妨考虑记录谈判日志或日记，以便定期回顾。

Prepare! Negotiation power, as discussed below, is not something of which you have a certain quantity that can be applied anywhere for any purpose. It requires hard work in advance to bring your resources to bear on being persuasive in a particular situation. In other words, it requires preparation. There is no risk in being well prepared. It simply takes time. The better prepared you are, the more likely you are to use these ideas and to find them of value.

做好准备！如下文所述，谈判能力并非与生俱来，可以随意运用。它需要事先付出大量努力，才能在特定情况下有效地运用自身资源，从而达到说服对方的目的。换句话说，谈判需要充分的准备。做好充分的准备并无风险，只是需要时间。准备越充分，就越有可能运用这些技巧，并从中发现它们的价值。

Plan how to build and maintain a good working relationship with the other side. Write out a list of your interests and the other side’s. Then invent a list of options that might satisfy as many of these interests as possible. Look for a variety of external benchmarks or criteria that might persuade a reasonable third party of what should be done. Ask yourself what arguments you would like to be able to make, and then see if you can’t find the facts and information you would need to make them. Also consider what benchmarks your counterpart might find persuasive in justifying an agreement to his or her constituents. If negotiators for the other side would find it difficult to justify terms to their constituents, agreement on those terms is unlikely. And consider what commitments you would like each side to make. Sketch out a possible framework agreement.

计划如何与对方建立并维护良好的工作关系。列出你和对方的利益点。然后，拟定一系列可能满足尽可能多的利益点的方案。寻找各种外部基准或标准，以说服理性的第三方接受应该采取的行动。问问自己你想提出哪些论点，然后看看能否找到所需的论据和信息。同时，考虑对方在向其支持者解释协议时，可能会认为哪些基准比较有说服力。如果对方的谈判代表难以向其支持者解释协议条款，那么双方就很难达成一致。此外，还要考虑你希望双方各自做出哪些承诺。最后，拟定一个可能的框架协议。

In some cases you may want to ask a friend to help you role-play an upcoming negotiation, either by playing the other side or by playing you (after coaching) while you play the other side. (Assuming the role of the other side and listening from the receiving end to your own arguments is a powerful technique for testing your case.) You may also want to seek coaching from friends, more experienced negotiators, or professional negotiation consultants.

在某些情况下，你可能需要请朋友帮忙进行即将到来的谈判角色扮演，他可以扮演对方，也可以在你扮演对方时，由他扮演你（经过指导）。（扮演对方的角色，从接受方的角度聆听自己的论点，是检验你论点的有效方法。）你也可以向朋友、经验丰富的谈判者或专业谈判顾问寻求指导。

In many ways, negotiation is like athletics: Some people have more natural talent, and like the best athletes, they may gain the most from preparation, practice, and coaching. Yet those with less natural talent have more need for preparation, practice, and feedback, and much to gain by it. Whichever you are, there is much to learn, and hard work will pay off. It is up to you.

谈判在很多方面都像体育运动：有些人天赋异禀，就像最优秀的运动员一样，他们能从充分的准备、练习和指导中获益最多。而那些天赋稍逊的人则更需要准备、练习和反馈，也能从中获益良多。无论你是哪一种，都需要学习很多东西，努力终会有回报。一切都取决于你。

QUESTIONS ABOUT POWER

关于权力的问题

Question 10: “Can the way I negotiate really make a difference if the other side is more powerful?” And “How do I enhance my negotiating power?”

问题 10：“如果对方实力更强，我的谈判方式真的能起到作用吗？”以及“我该如何增强我的谈判能力？”

How you negotiate (and how you prepare to negotiate) can make an enormous difference, whatever the relative strengths of each party.

无论双方实力如何，谈判方式（以及谈判准备）都会产生巨大的影响。

Some things you can’t get

有些东西你得不到

Of course, no matter how skilled you are, there are limits to what you can get through negotiation. The best negotiator in the world will not be able to buy the White House. You should not expect success in negotiation unless you are able to make the other side an offer they find more attractive than their BATNA—their Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. If that seems impossible, then negotiation doesn’t make sense. Concentrate instead on improving your BATNA and perhaps changing theirs.

当然，无论你的谈判技巧多么高超，谈判所能达到的程度也是有限的。世界上最好的谈判者也无法买下白宫。除非你能向对方提出比他们的最佳替代方案（BATNA）更具吸引力的方案，否则你不应该指望谈判成功。如果这看起来不可能，那么谈判就毫无意义。你应该专注于改进自己的最佳替代方案，并尝试改变对方的方案。

How you negotiate makes a big difference

你的谈判方式至关重要。

In a situation where there is a chance for agreement, the way you negotiate can make the difference between coming to terms and not, or between an outcome that you find favorable and one that is merely acceptable. How you negotiate may determine whether the pie is expanded or merely divided, and whether you have a good relationship with the other side or a strained one. When the other side seems to hold all the cards, how you negotiate is absolutely critical. Suppose, for example, that you are negotiating for an exception to a rule or a job offer. Realistically, you may have little recourse if the other side denies your request and little to offer if they grant it. In this situation, your negotiation skill is everything. However small the opportunity for success, the way in which you negotiate will determine whether you are able to take advantage of it.

在存在达成协议可能性的情况下，你的谈判方式决定了最终能否达成协议，以及最终结果是否令你满意。你的谈判方式可能决定了利益蛋糕是扩大还是缩小，也可能决定了你与对方的关系是良好还是紧张。当对方似乎掌握所有主动权时，你的谈判方式就显得至关重要。例如，假设你正在争取对某项规则的例外处理或一份工作机会。实际上，如果对方拒绝你的请求，你可能几乎没有退路；即使对方同意，你也几乎没有什么可以争取的。在这种情况下，你的谈判技巧至关重要。无论成功的机会多么渺茫，你的谈判方式都将决定你是否能够抓住它。

“Resources” are not the same as “negotiation power”

“资源”并不等同于“谈判能力”。

Negotiation power is the ability to persuade someone to do something. The United States is rich and has lots of nuclear bombs, but neither has been of much help in deterring terrorist actions or freeing hostages when they have been held in places like Beirut. Whether your resources give you negotiating power will depend on the context—on whom you are trying to persuade and what you want them to do.

谈判能力是指说服他人做某事的能力。美国财力雄厚，拥有大量核武器，但这两项都未能有效阻止恐怖袭击或解救在贝鲁特等地被劫持的人质。你的资源能否转化为谈判优势，取决于具体情况——你试图说服的对象以及你希望他们做什么。

Don’t ask “Who’s more powerful?”

不要问“谁更强大？”

Trying to estimate whether you or your counterparts are more “powerful” is risky. If you conclude that you are more powerful, you may relax and not prepare as well as you should. On the other hand, if you conclude that you are weaker than the other side, there is a risk that you will be discouraged and again not devote sufficient attention to how you might persuade them. Whatever you conclude will not help you figure out how best to proceed.

试图评估自己和对方谁更“强大”是件冒险的事。如果你认为自己更强大，你可能会放松警惕，准备不足。反之，如果你认为自己不如对方，你可能会灰心丧气，同样无法充分思考如何说服对方。无论你得出什么结论，都无助于你找到最佳的应对策略。

In fact, a great deal can be done to enhance your negotiation power even when the resource balance is one-sided. Of course, there will be negotiations where, at least in the short term, the best cards are held by the other side. But in this increasingly interdependent world, there are almost always resources and potential allies that a skilled and persistent negotiator can exploit, at least to move the fulcrum, if not ultimately to tip the balance of power the other way. You won’t find out what’s possible unless you try.

事实上，即使资源处于一边倒的局面，你仍然可以采取很多措施来增强谈判实力。当然，有些谈判中，至少在短期内，对方会占据优势。但在当今这个日益相互依存的世界里，一位技巧娴熟且坚持不懈的谈判者几乎总能找到可以利用的资源和潜在盟友，至少可以改变局势，甚至最终扭转力量平衡。不尝试，就永远不会知道有哪些可能性。

Sometimes people seem to prefer feeling powerless and believing that there is nothing they can do to affect a situation. That belief helps them avoid feeling responsible or guilty about inaction. It also avoids the costs of trying to change the situation—making an effort and risking failure, which might cause the person embarrassment. But while this feeling is understandable, it does not affect the reality of what the person might accomplish by effective negotiation. It is a self-defeating and self-fulfilling attitude.

有时人们似乎宁愿感到无力，相信自己对现状无能为力。这种想法让他们可以避免因不作为而感到内疚或愧疚。它也让他们避免了尝试改变现状的代价——付出努力并承担失败的风险，而失败可能会让他们感到尴尬。虽然这种感觉可以理解，但它并不能改变人们通过有效谈判所能取得的成就。这是一种自我挫败且自我实现的心态。

The best rule of thumb is to be optimistic—to let your reach exceed your grasp. Without wasting a lot of resources on hopeless causes, recognize that many things are worth trying for even if you may not succeed. The more you try for, the more you are likely to get. Studies of negotiation consistently show a strong correlation between aspiration and result. Within reason, it pays to think positively.

最好的经验法则是保持乐观——让你的目标超越你的能力范围。不要把大量资源浪费在毫无希望的事情上，要认识到即使可能失败，很多事情也值得尝试。你尝试的越多，得到的可能性就越大。谈判研究始终表明，抱负与结果之间存在很强的相关性。在合理的范围内，积极思考是有益的。

There are many sources of negotiation power

谈判权力的来源有很多。

How do you enhance your negotiating power? This whole book is an attempt to answer that question. Negotiation power has many sources. One is having a good BATNA. Provided they believe you, it is persuasive to tell the other side that you have a better alternative. But each of the four elements of the method outlined in Part II of this book—people (the relationship), interests, options, and objective criteria—is also a source of negotiation power. If the other side is strong in one area, you can try to develop strength in another. To these five we would now add a sixth, the power of commitment, and seventh, the power of effective communication, including process management.

如何提升谈判能力？本书旨在解答这个问题。谈判能力的来源有很多。其中之一是拥有一个好的替代方案（BATNA）。只要对方相信你，告诉他们你有一个更好的选择就很有说服力。但本书第二部分概述的谈判方法中的四个要素——人（关系）、利益、选择和客观标准——也都是谈判能力的来源。如果对方在某个方面很强，你可以尝试在其他方面增强自己的优势。除了这五个要素之外，我们还要加上第六个要素：承诺的力量；以及第七个要素：有效沟通的力量，包括流程管理。

There is power in developing a good working relationship between the people negotiating. If you understand the other side and they understand you; if emotions are acknowledged and people are treated with respect even when they disagree; if there is clear, two-way communication with good listening; if there is mutual trust and confidence in one another’s reliability; and if people problems are dealt with directly on their merits, not by demanding or offering concessions on substance, negotiations are likely to be smoother and more successful for both parties. In this sense, negotiation power is not a zero-sum phenomenon. More negotiation power for the other side does not necessarily mean less for you. The better your working relationship, the better able each of you is to influence the other.

在谈判双方之间建立良好的工作关系至关重要。如果你理解对方，对方也理解你；如果双方的情绪得到认可，即使意见相左也能互相尊重；如果双方进行清晰的双向沟通，并认真倾听；如果双方彼此信任，对彼此的可靠性充满信心；如果能够根据问题的本质而非实质上的让步来直接处理人际关系问题，那么谈判就更有可能顺利进行，对双方都有利。从这个意义上讲，谈判的力量并非零和博弈。对方谈判能力的增强并不一定意味着你的谈判能力减弱。你们的工作关系越好，彼此就越能有效地影响对方。

Contrary to some conventional wisdom, you will often benefit from the other side’s increasing their ability to influence you. Two people with well-deserved reputations for being trustworthy are each better able to influence the other than are two people with reputations for dishonesty. That you can trust the other side increases their ability to influence you. But you also benefit. You can safely enter into agreements that will benefit both sides.

与一些传统观念相反，对方影响力的增强往往会让你受益。两个信誉卓著、值得信赖的人，比两个名声不佳、不诚实的人更能影响彼此。你对对方的信任会增强他们对你的影响。但你也会从中受益。你可以安心地达成对双方都有利的协议。

When the British ambassador to the United Nations, Lord Caradon, was seeking agreement on a Security Council resolution to set a framework for peace in the Middle East after the 1967 war, it appeared he had consensus except for the Soviet vote. The Soviet representative, Vasily Kuznetsov, approached Caradon to request a delay in the vote for two days. Caradon resisted, fearing that the Soviets would use the delay to win more votes for their alternative resolution. Kuznetsov persisted, “You may have misunderstood me. I am personally asking you for two days.” As soon as Caradon heard the word “personal,” he knew he had to grant Kuznetsov his wish. Why? “I knew Kuznetsov very well. I had worked with him on other difficult issues. I greatly respected him. I knew he could not work against me. . . . I knew I could trust him as he could trust me.” So Caradon went to the Security Council and requested a delay in the vote. Two days later the Security Council met to vote. “I raised my hand to vote,” recalled Caradon. “And then there was a cheer from the galleries. I looked to my right and saw Kuznetsov’s finger raised voting for our resolution and withdrawing his own, thus making the vote for the British Resolution 242 unanimous. He had made good use of the two days. He had come to the conclusion that a unanimous vote and full agreement were essential. He had gone back to his Government and, I have no doubt, to Arab Governments, too, and he had persuaded them.” [9] U.N. Resolution 242 remains central to Middle East peace negotiations to this day.

1967年战争后，英国驻联合国大使卡拉顿勋爵正努力就安理会一项旨在为中东和平建立框架的决议寻求各方共识。当时，除了苏联的投票外，似乎已经达成了一致。苏联代表瓦西里·库兹涅佐夫找到卡拉顿，请求将投票推迟两天。卡拉顿犹豫不决，担心苏联会利用这段时间争取更多票数支持他们的替代决议。库兹涅佐夫坚持说：“您可能误会我的意思了。我是在亲自请求您推迟两天。”卡拉顿一听到“亲自”二字，就知道自己必须满足库兹涅佐夫的请求。为什么呢？“我非常了解库兹涅佐夫。我曾与他合作处理过其他棘手的问题。我非常尊重他。我知道他不会与我作对……我知道我可以信任他，就像他信任我一样。”于是，卡拉顿前往安理会，请求推迟投票。两天后，安全理事会召开会议进行表决。“我举手投票，”卡拉顿回忆道，“这时旁听席上响起一片欢呼声。我向右望去，看到库兹涅佐夫举起手指，投了赞成票，并收回了他自己的赞成票，从而使英国提出的第242号决议获得一致通过。他充分利用了这两天时间。他得出结论，一致投票和全面协议至关重要。他回到英国政府，而且我毫不怀疑，他也与阿拉伯各国政府进行了沟通，并成功说服了他们。”[9] 联合国第242号决议至今仍是中东和平谈判的核心。

Kuznetsov’s example shows the power of a trustworthy reputation, even independent of the organization you may represent. Your reputation for honesty and fair-dealing may be your single most important asset as a negotiator.

库兹涅佐夫的例子表明，即使不考虑你所代表的组织，值得信赖的声誉也至关重要。作为一名谈判者，你诚实守信、公平交易的声誉或许是你最重要的资产。

There is power in effective communication. Good communication is an especially significant source of negotiating power. Crafting your message with punch, listening to the other side, and showing that you have heard can all increase your persuasiveness. Skillfully managing the negotiation process—making game-changing moves as needed—can dramatically affect the quality of the outcome you achieve.

有效沟通蕴含着强大的力量。良好的沟通尤其能增强谈判筹码。精心措辞、认真倾听对方意见并展现出你已理解对方意思，这些都能提升你的说服力。巧妙地掌控谈判进程——必要时采取关键性举措——能够显著影响最终结果的质量。

President John F. Kennedy was justly famous for his skill at the first of these, crafting a forceful message: “Let us never negotiate out of fear. But let us never fear to negotiate.” [10]

约翰·F·肯尼迪总统因其在第一点上的技巧而闻名，他精心炮制了一条强有力的信息：“我们绝不因恐惧而谈判。但我们也绝不害怕谈判。”[10]

A message does not have to be unequivocal to be clear and effective. In many cases, helping the other side understand your thinking—even when you are of two minds about something—can reduce their fears, clear up misperceptions, and promote joint problem-solving. Consider the supplier who makes what she thinks is a competitive bid for a business supply contract. The purchaser likes the bid and the bidder but is worried that the bidder’s firm, which is new to the market, may not be able to manage the volume needed to meet his peak requirements. If the purchaser says simply, “No, thank you” and then pays more to hire another firm, the bidder may assume that the purchaser disliked her bid. And the bidder would have no opportunity to persuade the purchaser that she could handle the needed volume. It would be better for both if, instead, the purchaser shared both his interest in the bid and his concerns.

信息不必非得一丝不苟才能清晰有效。很多时候，即使你对某件事犹豫不决，帮助对方理解你的想法也能减轻他们的顾虑，消除误解，并促进双方共同解决问题。例如，一位供应商自认为对一份商业供应合同的报价很有竞争力。采购方对这份报价和投标人都很满意，但担心这家新公司可能无法满足其高峰期的需求量。如果采购方只是简单地说“不，谢谢”，然后支付更高的价格聘请另一家公司，投标人可能会认为采购方不喜欢她的报价。这样一来，投标人就失去了说服采购方自己能够处理所需订单量的机会。如果采购方能够坦诚地表达自己对投标的兴趣和担忧，对双方都更有利。

Good listening can increase your negotiation power by increasing the information you have about the other side’s interests or about possible options. Once you understand the other side’s feelings and concerns, you can begin to address them, to explore areas of agreement and disagreement, and to develop useful ways to proceed in the future. Consider, for example, the elderly man whose doctors wanted to move him from his current hospital to one with specialized facilities. The doctors repeatedly explained how the specialized hospital would be better for him, but the man refused to budge. Knowing that the man was acting against his own best interests, the doctors dismissed his reasoning as irrational. One intern, however, took the man seriously and listened carefully to why he did not want to move. The patient told of how he had suffered repeated abandonments in his life and his fears that moving might result in another. The intern set about addressing this concern directly, and the man happily agreed to be moved.

良好的倾听能力可以增强你的谈判筹码，因为它能让你更了解对方的利益或可能的选择。一旦你理解了对方的感受和顾虑，你就可以着手解决这些问题，探索双方的共识和分歧，并制定未来可行的方案。例如，一位老人的医生想把他从目前的医院转到一家拥有专科设施的医院。医生们反复解释专科医院对他更有利，但老人拒绝让步。医生们知道老人的做法违背了自己的利益，便认为他的理由不合理。然而，一位实习医生却认真对待老人，仔细聆听他不愿转院的原因。老人讲述了他一生中多次被抛弃的经历，以及他害怕转院会让他再次遭受同样的痛苦。实习医生直接针对老人的顾虑展开讨论，老人最终欣然同意转院。

Showing that you have heard the other side also increases your ability to persuade them. When the other side feels heard by you, they are more apt to listen to you. It is comparatively easy to listen when the other side is saying something that you agree with. It is harder to listen to things with which you disagree, but that is the very time it is most effective. Listen before you launch into a rebuttal. Inquire. Make sure you understand their view, and make sure they know you understand. Once the other side knows that you understand what they have said, they cannot dismiss your disagreement as simple lack of understanding.

表明你认真倾听了对方的观点，也能增强你的说服力。当对方感到被你倾听时，他们更愿意听取你的意见。当对方的观点与你一致时，倾听相对容易。倾听与你相悖的观点则更难，但这恰恰是倾听最有效的时候。在反驳之前，先认真倾听。询问对方。确保你理解他们的观点，并让他们知道你理解了。一旦对方知道你理解了他们所说的话，他们就无法将你的异议简单地归咎于缺乏理解。

Your awareness of negotiation process and your ability to make game-changing moves increases your negotiation power because the process of the negotiation affects the kind of outcomes you can achieve. Positional bargaining frequently results in odd, arbitrary results that are difficult to explain to constituents and of little value as precedents in future negotiations. It also tends to bruise relationships.

你对谈判过程的了解以及你采取关键性策略的能力会增强你的谈判筹码，因为谈判过程会影响你最终能达成的结果。立场式谈判往往会导致一些奇怪且武断的结果，这些结果难以向利益相关者解释，也难以作为未来谈判的先例。此外，它还容易损害双方关系。

As discussed in Chapter 8, recognizing a tactic or move allows you to name it and begin an explicit negotiation over process. Another way to “change the game” is to change the frame. In other words, move the focus in the negotiation from positions to interests, options, or standards. If the other side says, for example, “$10,000 is the most we will pay,” when you think $50,000 would be fair, you could respond in several ways:

正如第八章所述，识别对方的策略或举动，就能指出其含义，并开始就谈判流程展开明确的谈判。另一种“改变游戏规则”的方法是改变谈判框架。换句话说，将谈判的重点从立场转移到利益、选择或标准上。例如，如果对方说“我们最多只能支付1万美元”，而你认为5万美元比较合理，你可以采取以下几种回应方式：

  • Reframe to interests: “I hear that is your position. Given how far that seems below the market price, help me understand your interests. Are you experiencing a serious cash flow crisis?”
    换个角度思考：“我听说这是您的投资方向。鉴于这个价格远低于市场价，请您帮我了解一下您的投资动机。您是否面临严重的现金流危机？”
  • Reframe to options: “$10,000 is one option, just as $100,000 or $200,000 would be attractive options from our point of view. I think we’ll get a lot further brainstorming options likely to be acceptable and attractive to both of us. What if we were to . . . ?”
    换个角度思考：“1万美元是一个选择，就像10万美元或20万美元在我们看来也是很有吸引力的选择一样。我认为，如果我们集思广益，想出更多双方都能接受且有吸引力的方案，会更有成效。如果我们……呢？”
  • Reframe to standards: “You must have good reasons for thinking $10,000 is a fair offer. How did you arrive at that number? Why that number, instead of, say, $0 or $100,000? My understanding is that the market price is $50,000. Why should we agree on less?”
    换个角度问：“你肯定有充分的理由认为1万美元是合理的报价。你是怎么得出这个数字的？为什么是1万美元，而不是0美元或者10万美元？据我了解，市场价是5万美元。我们为什么要接受更低的价格？”
  • Reframe to BATNA: “Of course, that’s your decision to make, and perhaps someone else will accept that. I think we need to think hard now about whether an agreement is possible here that would make sense for both of us.”
    重新表述为最佳替代方案：“当然，这是你的决定，也许其他人会接受。我认为我们现在需要认真考虑，是否有可能达成一项对我们双方都有利的协议。”

One of the greatest powers you have is to reframe, using statements and questions to change the focus of negotiation to interests, options, and standards—and thus to change the game from positional bargaining to principled negotiation. [11]

你拥有的最强大的力量之一就是重新构建，通过陈述和提问，将谈判的重点转移到利益、选择和标准上——从而将游戏从立场谈判转变为原则谈判。[11]

Let’s return to the neighbors from Chapter 3 who are concerned about an unwanted and unsafe construction site. Consider the difference between beginning their negotiation with the construction company by saying, “We demand that a fence be built around the site immediately!” or instead beginning, “I have a simple question for you: Does your company adhere to industry standards of safety?” That is certainly a question to which the company cannot afford to answer “no.” And once they say “yes,” the neighbors only need standards collected from competitor companies to make their point persuasively, and on the merits. “Well, Turner Construction said they would put a two-meter-high fence around anything bigger than a pothole, and always before beginning any construction activity.”

让我们回到第三章中提到的那几位邻居，他们担心一个不受欢迎且不安全的建筑工地。想想看，如果他们一开始就对建筑公司说：“我们要求立即在工地周围建起围栏！”，和他们先问：“我有个简单的问题：贵公司是否遵守行业安全标准？”，结果会有什么不同？对于这个问题，建筑公司绝对不能回答“不”。一旦他们回答“是”，邻居们只需要收集一些竞争对手的标准，就能更有说服力地证明自己的观点。“特纳建筑公司说，他们会在任何比坑洼大的地方周围建起两米高的围栏，而且总是在开始任何施工活动之前就建好。”

There is power in understanding interests. The more clearly you understand the other side’s concerns, the better able you will be to satisfy them at minimum cost to yourself. Look for intangible or hidden interests that may be important. With concrete interests like money, ask what lies behind them. (“For what will the money be used?”) Sometimes even the most firmly stated and unacceptable position reflects an underlying interest that is compatible with your own.

了解对方的利益至关重要。你越清楚对方的顾虑，就越能以最小的代价满足他们的需求。寻找那些可能很重要的无形或隐藏利益。对于金钱这类具体的利益，要追问其背后的原因（“这笔钱将用于什么用途？”）。有时，即使是最坚定、最令人无法接受的立场，也可能反映出与你自身利益相符的潜在利益。

Consider the businessman who was trying to buy a radio station. The majority owner was willing to sell his two-thirds of the station for a reasonable figure, but the one-third owner (and current manager of the station) was demanding what seemed an exorbitant price for her third. The businessman had raised his offer several times to no avail, and he was beginning to consider abandoning the deal. Finally, the businessman inquired more deeply into the second owner’s interests. He learned that the second owner had less interest in money than she did in continuing to manage a radio station of which she was a part owner. The businessman offered to buy only that portion of the owner’s share he needed for tax reasons and to keep her on as manager. The second owner accepted this offer at a price that saved the businessman almost a million dollars. Understanding the seller’s underlying interests had greatly enhanced the buyer’s negotiating power.

设想一下这位商人试图收购一家广播电台。大股东愿意以合理的价格出售他所持有的三分之二的股份，但持有三分之一股份的股东（同时也是电台的现任经理）却要价过高。这位商人多次提高报价，但都无济于事，他开始考虑放弃这笔交易。最终，这位商人深入调查了第二位股东的利益所在。他了解到，第二位股东对金钱的兴趣远不如继续经营她所拥有的电台来得重要。于是，这位商人提出只购买出于税务考虑所需的股份，并保留第二位股东的经理职位。第二位股东接受了这一提议，最终成交价为这位商人节省了近一百万美元。了解卖方的真正利益极大地提升了买方的谈判筹码。

There is power in inventing an elegant option. Successful brainstorming increases your ability to influence others. Once you understand the interests of each side, it is often possible—as in the radio-station example above—to invent a clever way of having those interests dovetail. Sometimes this can be done by devising an ingenious process option.

构思出一个巧妙的方案蕴含着强大的力量。成功的头脑风暴能够提升你影响他人的能力。一旦你了解了各方的利益所在，通常就能找到一种巧妙的方法——就像上面提到的电台案例一样——让这些利益完美契合。有时，这可以通过设计一个精妙的流程方案来实现。

Consider the sealed-bid stamp auction. The auctioneer would like bidders to offer the most they might conceivably be willing to pay for the stamps in question. Each potential buyer, however, does not want to pay more than necessary. In a regular sealed-bid auction each bidder tries to offer slightly more than their best guess of what others will bid, which is often less than the bidder would be willing to pay. But in a stamp auction the rules state that the highest bidder gets the stamps at the price of the second- highest bid. Buyers can safely bid exactly as much as they would be willing to pay to get the stamps, because the auctioneer guarantees that they will not have to pay it! No bidder is left wishing that he or she had bid more, and the high bidder is happy to pay less than was offered. The auctioneer is happy knowing that the difference between the highest and second-highest bids is usually smaller than the overall increase in the level of bids under this system versus a regular sealed-bid auction. [12]

以密封投标邮票拍卖为例。拍卖师希望竞标者出价达到他们愿意为目标邮票支付的最高价格。然而，每位潜在买家都不想支付超过实际所需价格的费用。在常规的密封投标拍卖中，每位竞标者都会尝试出价略高于他们对其他竞标者出价的最佳预估，而这个预估价格通常低于竞标者愿意支付的价格。但在邮票拍卖中，规则规定最高出价者只需支付第二高出价即可获得邮票。买家可以放心地出价达到他们愿意支付的最高价格，因为拍卖师保证他们不必支付这个价格！没有竞标者会后悔出价过高，而最高出价者也乐于支付低于其他竞标者出价的价格。拍卖师也乐于看到，最高出价和第二高出价之间的差价通常小于这种拍卖方式下整体出价水平相对于常规密封投标拍卖的增幅。[12]

There is power in using external standards of legitimacy. You can use standards of legitimacy both as a sword to persuade others, and as a shield to help you resist pressure to give in arbitrarily. (“I would like to give you a discount, but this price is firm. It is what General Motors paid for the same item last week; here is the bill of sale.”) Just as, by finding relevant precedent and principles a lawyer enhances his or her ability to persuade a judge, so a negotiator can enhance his or her negotiation power by finding precedents, principles, and other external criteria of fairness and by thinking of ways to present them forcefully and tellingly: “I am asking for no more and no less than you are paying others for comparable work.” “We will pay what the house is worth if we can afford it. We are offering what the similar house nearby sold for last month. Unless you can give us a good reason why your house is worth more, our offer remains firm and unchanged.” Convincing the other side that you are asking for no more than is fair is one of the most powerful arguments you can make.

运用外部合法性标准蕴含着力量。你可以将合法性标准作为说服他人的利剑，也可以作为抵御被迫无端让步的压力的盾牌。（“我很想给你打折，但这个价格是固定的。这是通用汽车上周购买同款产品的价格；这是销售单。”）正如律师通过寻找相关的先例和原则来增强其说服法官的能力一样，谈判者也可以通过寻找先例、原则和其他外部公平标准，并思考如何有力且清晰地呈现这些标准来增强其谈判优势：“我要求的价格不多不少，与你们为类似工作支付给其他人的价格相同。”“如果我们负担得起，我们会支付房子应有的价格。我们给出的价格是附近类似房屋上个月的售价。除非你能给我们一个合理的理由说明你的房子值更多，否则我们的报价不变。”让对方相信你所要求的只是合理的，这是你能提出的最有力的论点之一。

There is power in developing a good BATNA. As we argue in Chapter 6, a fundamental way to increase your negotiation power is by improving your walk-away alternative. An attractive BATNA is a strong argument with which to persuade the other side of the need to offer more. (“The firm across the street has offered me 20 percent above what I am now earning. I would rather stay here. But with the cost of living, unless I can get a good raise soon, I will have to consider moving on. What do you think might be possible?”)

制定一个好的替代方案（BATNA）至关重要。正如我们在第六章中论述的，提升谈判能力的一个根本途径是完善你的“退而求其次”的方案。一个有吸引力的BATNA能够有力地说服对方，让他们意识到需要提供更高的薪资。（“街对面的公司给我开出了比我现在高20%的薪水。我当然更愿意留在这里。但是考虑到生活成本，除非我能尽快获得大幅加薪，否则我不得不考虑跳槽。您觉得有什么办法吗？”）

In addition to improving your overall BATNA (what you will do if the negotiations fail to produce an agreement), you should also prepare your “micro-BATNA”—if no agreement is reached at this meeting, what is the best outcome? It helps to draft in advance a good exit line to use if a meeting is inconclusive. (“Thank you for sharing your views and for listening to mine. If I decide to go forward, I will get back to you, perhaps with a fresh proposal.”)

除了完善你的整体最佳替代方案（BATNA，即如果谈判未能达成协议，你将采取的行动）之外，你还应该准备你的“微观最佳替代方案”——如果本次会议未能达成协议，最佳结果是什么？事先拟定一个合适的结束语很有帮助，以便在会议没有结果时使用。（例如：“感谢您分享您的观点，也感谢您倾听我的意见。如果我决定继续推进，我会再联系您，或许会提出新的方案。”）

Sometimes it is possible, quite legitimately, to worsen the other side’s BATNA. For example, a father we know was trying to get his young son to mow the lawn. He offered a significant amount of money, but to no avail. Finally, the son inadvertently revealed his BATNA: “But Dad, I don’t need to mow the lawn to get money. You, uh, leave your wallet on the dresser every weekend. . . .” The father quickly changed his son’s BATNA by not leaving his wallet out and making clear that he disapproved of taking money without asking; the son started mowing the lawn. The tactic of worsening the other side’s BATNA can be used to coerce or exploit, but it can also help ensure a fair outcome. Efforts to improve one’s own alternatives and to lower the other side’s estimate of theirs are critical ways to enhance our negotiating power.

有时，我们完全可以合理地降低对方的最佳替代方案（BATNA）。例如，我们认识的一位父亲想让他的小儿子帮忙割草。他开出了相当可观的报酬，但儿子却不为所动。最后，儿子无意中透露了自己的BATNA：“可是爸爸，我不需要割草就能拿到钱。你，呃，每个周末都把钱包放在梳妆台上……”父亲迅速改变了儿子的BATNA，不再把钱包放在外面，并明确表示不赞成未经允许就拿钱；儿子这才开始割草。降低对方BATNA的策略既可以用来胁迫或剥削，也有助于确保公平的结果。努力改善自身的替代方案，并降低对方对其替代方案的评估，是增强谈判能力的关键途径。

There is power in making a carefully crafted commitment. One additional source of persuasive power deserves attention: the power of making commitments. You can use a commitment to enhance your negotiating power in three ways: You can commit to what you will do, for example, by making a firm offer. You can, with care, make a negative commitment as to what you will not do. And you can clarify precisely what commitments you would like the other side to make.

精心措辞的承诺蕴含着强大的力量。还有一种说服力值得关注：那就是做出承诺的力量。你可以通过三种方式利用承诺来增强你的谈判能力：首先，你可以明确承诺自己将要做的事情，例如，提出明确的报价；其次，你可以谨慎地做出否定性的承诺，表明自己不会做什么；最后，你可以清晰地阐明你希望对方做出哪些承诺。

Clarify what you will do. One way to enhance your negotiating power is to make a firm, well-timed offer. When you make a firm offer, you provide one option that you will accept, making it clear at the same time that you are not foreclosing discussion of other options. If you want to persuade someone to accept a job, don’t just talk about it; make an offer. By making an offer you give up your chance to haggle for better terms. But you gain by simplifying the other side’s choice and making it easier for them to commit. To reach agreement, all they have to say is “yes.”

明确你的计划。提升谈判能力的一个方法是提出一个坚定且时机恰当的报价。当你提出一个坚定的报价时，你便提供了一个你唯一接受的选择，同时也明确表示你并未排除讨论其他选项的可能性。如果你想说服某人接受一份工作，不要只是空谈，而是要提出报价。提出报价意味着你放弃了讨价还价的机会，但你却能简化对方的选择，让他们更容易做出承诺。为了达成协议，他们只需要说“是”即可。

Making an offer of what you will do if they agree to the terms you are proposing is one way to overcome any fear the other side may have of starting down a slippery slope. Without a clear offer, even a painful situation may seem preferable to accepting “a pig in a poke,” especially if the other side fears that a favorable indication will encourage you to ask for more. In 1990, the U.N. Security Council sought to influence Iraq to withdraw from its military occupation of Kuwait by imposing sanctions. The Council’s resolutions clearly stated that Iraq must withdraw, but did not state that upon withdrawal sanctions would end. If Iraqi President Saddam Hussein believed that sanctions would continue even after Iraq withdrew from Kuwait, then those sanctions, though unpleasant, provided no incentive for Iraq to leave.

向对方提出如果接受你提出的条件你将采取的行动，是消除对方对步入歧途的担忧的一种方法。如果没有明确的提议，即使是痛苦的局面也可能比接受“盲目接受”要好，尤其是在对方担心你表现出的积极态度会鼓励你提出更多要求的情况下。1990年，联合国安理会试图通过实施制裁来促使伊拉克从其对科威特的军事占领中撤军。安理会的决议明确指出伊拉克必须撤军，但并未说明撤军后制裁就会终止。如果伊拉克总统萨达姆·侯赛因认为即使伊拉克从科威特撤军后制裁仍将继续，那么这些制裁虽然令人不快，却无法促使伊拉克撤军。

The more concrete the offer, the more persuasive. Thus a written offer may be more credible than an oral one. (A real-estate agent we know likes to have a client make an offer by stacking bundles of hundred-dollar bills on the table.) You may also want to make your offer a “fading opportunity” by indicating when and how it will expire. For example, President Ronald Reagan’s inauguration in 1981 created a fading opportunity in the negotiations for the release of the American diplomatic hostages held in Iran. The Iranians did not want to have to start negotiating again with a new U.S. administration.

报价越具体，就越有说服力。因此，书面报价可能比口头报价更具可信度。（我们认识的一位房地产经纪人喜欢让客户把一捆捆百元大钞堆在桌子上，以此来提出报价。）你还可以通过说明报价的截止日期和方式，使你的报价成为一个“稍纵即逝的机会”。例如，1981年罗纳德·里根总统的就职，使得在伊朗释放美国外交人质的谈判中，机会稍稍溜走。伊朗方面不希望不得不与新一届美国政府重新开始谈判。

In some cases, you may also want to clarify what you will do if the other side does not accept your proposal. They may not realize the consequences of your BATNA for them. (“If we can’t get heat in our apartment this evening, I will have to call the health department’s emergency line. Are you aware that they charge landlords a $250 fine when they respond and find a violation of the statute?”)

在某些情况下，您可能还需要明确说明，如果对方不接受您的提议，您将采取什么措施。他们可能没有意识到您的最佳替代方案（BATNA）会给他们带来哪些后果。（“如果今晚我们公寓里没有暖气，我将不得不拨打卫生部门的紧急电话。您是否知道，如果卫生部门出警后发现房东违反了相关法规，将会对其处以 250 美元的罚款？”）

Consider committing to what you will not do. Sometimes you can persuade the other side to accept an offer better than their BATNA by convincing them that you cannot or will not offer more (“Take it or leave it”). You not only make an offer; you tie your hands against changing it. As discussed in Chapter 1, locking into a position has significant costs; locking in early limits communication and runs the risk of damaging the relationship by making the other side feel ignored or coerced. There is less risk in locking in after you have come to understand the other side’s interests and have explored options for joint gains, and it will do less damage to your relationship with the other side if there are credible reasons independent of your will to explain and justify your rigidity.

考虑一下你不会做什么。有时，你可以通过让对方相信你不能或不会提供更多（“要么接受，要么放弃”）来说服他们接受比他们的最佳替代方案（BATNA）更好的提议。你不仅提出了提议，而且还限制了自己更改提议的余地。正如第一章所述，锁定立场会带来巨大的代价；过早锁定立场会限制沟通，并有可能让对方感到被忽视或受到胁迫，从而损害彼此的关系。在你了解对方的利益并探索了共同获益的方案之后再锁定立场，风险会更小；而且，如果你有合理的理由（而非仅仅出于你的意愿来解释和证明你的立场坚定），那么对你们关系的损害也会更小。

At some point, it may be best to put a final offer on the table and mean it. Doing so tends to influence the other side by worsening their micro-BATNA. At this point if they say “no,” they no longer have open the possibility of reaching a better agreement with you.

在某些时候，最好提出最终报价并坚定不移。这样做往往会通过恶化对方的微劣替代方案（micro-BATNA）来影响他们。此时，如果他们拒绝，就意味着他们已经没有机会与你达成更好的协议。

Clarify what you want them to do. It pays to think through the precise terms of the commitment you want the other side to make. This ensures that your demand makes sense. “Susan, promise never to interrupt me again when I am on the telephone” could easily be disastrous if Susan took her promise literally in an emergency. You want to avoid a sloppy commitment that is overbroad, fails to bind the other side, leaves out crucial information, or is not operational.

明确你希望对方做什么。仔细思考你希望对方做出的承诺的具体条款至关重要。这能确保你的要求合情合理。“苏珊，答应我以后打电话时永远不要再打断我”这样的要求，如果苏珊在紧急情况下真的按照字面意思理解，后果可能不堪设想。你要避免做出含糊不清、范围过广、缺乏约束力、遗漏关键信息或根本无法执行的承诺。

Especially when you want the other side to do something, it makes sense to tell them exactly what it is you want them to do. Otherwise they may do nothing, not wanting to do more than they have to. In the fall of 1990, for example, the ability of the United States to influence Saddam Hussein was undercut by ambiguity about what would satisfy the United States. At different times, the withdrawal of Iraqi troops from Kuwait, the destruction of Iraqi nuclear facilities, the dismantling of Iraq’s military capability, and the overthrow of Saddam Hussein all seemed to be possible U.S. goals.

尤其当你希望对方采取某种行动时，明确告知对方你的具体要求至关重要。否则，他们可能什么都不做，因为他们不想做任何不必要的事情。例如，1990年秋季，由于美国对自身诉求的模糊不清，其对萨达姆·侯赛因的影响力受到了削弱。在不同的时期，伊拉克军队撤出科威特、摧毁伊拉克核设施、削弱伊拉克军事能力以及推翻萨达姆·侯赛因政权似乎都曾是美国可能的目标。

Make the most of your potential power

充分发挥你的潜在力量

To make the most of your potential negotiating power, you should use each source of power in harmony with other sources. Negotiators sometimes look for their strongest source of power and try to use it alone. For example, if a negotiator has a strong BATNA, he or she may confront the other side with it, threatening to walk away unless the last offer is accepted. This is likely to detract from the persuasive power of the negotiator’s arguments about why the offer is fair. If you are going to communicate your BATNA, it would be better to do so in ways that respect the relationship, leave open the possibility of two-way communication, underscore the legitimacy of your last offer, suggest how that offer meets the other side’s interests, and so forth. The total impact of such negotiation power as you have will be greater if each element is used in ways that reinforce the others.

为了最大限度地发挥你的潜在谈判优势，你应该协调运用每一种力量来源。谈判者有时会寻找自己最强大的力量来源，并试图单独使用它。例如，如果谈判者拥有强有力的最佳替代方案（BATNA），他/她可能会以此与对方对抗，威胁说如果对方不接受最后的报价，就放弃谈判。这很可能会削弱谈判者关于报价为何公平的论证的说服力。如果你要表达你的最佳替代方案，最好以尊重双方关系的方式进行，保持双向沟通的可能性，强调你最后报价的合理性，并说明该报价如何满足对方的利益等等。如果你的每一项力量都能相互加强，那么你所拥有的谈判优势的整体影响力将会更大。

You will also be more effective as a negotiator if you believe in what you are saying and doing. Whatever use you are able to make of the ideas in this book, don’t wear them as though you were wearing someone else’s clothes. Cut and fit what we say until you find an approach that both makes sense and is comfortable for you. This may require experimentation and a period of adjustment that is not so comfortable, but in the end, you are likely to maximize your negotiation power if you believe what you say and say what you believe.

如果你相信自己所说所做，你的谈判效率也会更高。无论你如何运用本书中的理念，都不要生搬硬套。要根据自身情况灵活调整，找到既合理又适合自己的方法。这可能需要一些尝试和一段不太舒适的适应期，但最终，如果你言行一致，你的谈判能力很可能会得到最大程度的发挥。

[ 4 ] We do think that, in addition to providing a good all-around method for getting what you want in a negotiation, principled negotiation can help make the world a better place. It promotes understanding among people, whether they be parent and child, worker and manager, or Arab and Israeli. Focusing on interests and creative options helps increase satisfaction and minimize waste. Relying on standards of fairness and seeking to meet the interests of both sides helps produce agreements that are durable, set good precedents, and build lasting relationships. The more a problem-solving approach to negotiation becomes the norm in dealing with differences among individuals and nations, the lower will be the costs of conflict. And beyond such social benefits, you may find that using this approach serves values of caring and justice in a way that is personally satisfying.

[4] 我们认为，除了提供一种在谈判中达成目标的有效方法外，遵循原则的谈判还能让世界变得更美好。它能促进人与人之间的相互理解，无论是父母与子女、员工与经理，还是阿拉伯人和以色列人。关注利益和创造性方案有助于提高满意度并最大限度地减少浪费。依靠公平标准并努力满足双方的利益，有助于达成持久的协议，树立良好的先例，并建立长久的关系。当以解决问题为导向的谈判方法成为处理个人和国家间分歧的常态时，冲突的代价就会越低。除了这些社会效益之外，您或许还会发现，运用这种方法践行关爱和公正的价值观，会给您带来个人满足感。

Introduction
